en: O Śrī, may this commentary on the *Tarkabhāṣā*, whose objective is unerring, be favorable to my intellect.
May she be the one who brings about correct understanding at every single sight. || 1 ||
Following the instruction of the authoritative and venerable masters,
I compose this commentary on the *Tarkabhāṣā*, which is neither too brief nor too extensive.

Commencing this treatise, which has the determination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as its primary subject, [the author] introduces the work by first showing the subject matter and purpose of the treatise he intends to undertake, with the passage beginning "Here...
and ending with "...the means of valid cognition must be determined.

It is understood that the direct purpose of this treatise is the determination of the means of valid cognition in terms of its essential nature (*svarūpa*), its definition (*lakṣaṇa*), and its result (*phala*).
Furthermore, it is established by implication that the subject matter of this treatise is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Although at the conclusion of the work the fourfold distinction between the views of the Vaibhāṣikas and others is indicated merely as a general direction,
nevertheless, valid cognition holds primacy.

The supreme purpose is the accomplishment of human goals for those who act after having determined the path of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the phrase "by those who follow valid cognition as the cause for the accomplishment of all human goals," it is not the case that all who strive in this way necessarily attain their goal; for indeed, the undertaking of the dull-witted is seen even in matters devoid of purpose.
Even among those who seek an object, not all follow a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Many commoners, like animals, are observed to act for the sake of an object even without having investigated the nature of valid cognition. Furthermore, even among those who act with foresight, those whose desires have been fulfilled—or those who are free from desire—have no need for valid cognition.
However, those who are intent on discernment and seekers of a goal would certainly follow the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of accomplishing that human aim (*puruṣārtha*).

Having this in mind, he says: "by those intent on discernment and seeking [the goal]. Thus, it is made clear that the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*) are the necessary factors for the engagement of discerning persons in a treatise.

Although those possessed of discernment must determine the nature of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) for the sake of accomplishing human goals, nevertheless, since the establishment of the objects of knowledge depends upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the nature of the means of valid cognition must be determined prior to the determination of the objects of knowledge;
it is with this intention that it is said: "at the beginning."

By this, the preeminence of this treatise—which is devoted to defining the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—is understood over that treatise which is devoted to defining the nature of the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*).
Now, he states the general definition of the means of valid cognition: "The means of valid cognition is correct knowledge whose object is not previously [known].
Here, "the means of valid cognition" is the indication of the definiendum (*lakṣya*).
"Right knowledge has as its object that which has not been previously apprehended"—this is the definition.
He explains the correctness (*samyaktva*) of knowledge by stating "non-contradictory.
Describing the purpose of the qualification "correctness," he says: "doubt... and so forth.

The point is this: although doubt and error may have as their object something not previously known, they nonetheless lack non-contradiction (*avisaṃvādakatva*); thus, there is no over-extension [of the definition].
Demonstrating that doubt and error lack non-contradiction, he explains what non-contradiction is: "But when the object—that is, the thing standing in its place, such as a jar—is present."

"Non-contradictory" (avisaṃvādaka) means that knowledge which, having indicated an object, causes one to attain it. By the inclusion of the two negative particles (nañ), errors such as the optical illusion of a moving tree are excluded.
For example, the direct perception of water causes a person to act toward water and thereby attains water.
The delusion of water in a mirage, however, causes a person to set out for water but does not actually result in the attainment of water.
Therefore, there is neither the fault of non-application (*aprasaṅga*) nor the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

By including "fitness" (*yogyatva*)—specifically, "fitness for attainment"—there is no room for the suspicion of under-extension (*avyāpti*); he explains this by way of resolving such doubts with the words beginning with "nanu."
Sometimes— that is, in the absence of desire and so forth—
it might cause one to reach [the goal], or produce [it], or cause one to reach it, or incite one to act.
Just as knowledge, by producing discernment, brings about [attainment], or as Devadatta, by engaging Yajñadatta in actions, brings him wealth; in that case,
there is no production of an existing thing by means of right knowledge.
Furthermore, not every cognition brings about the attainment of an object,

for we observe that even when an object has been ascertained, no activity may follow; thus, the sense is that non-contradiction, defined as the capacity to effect the attainment of an object, is under-extended (*avyāpta*).
He refutes [the objection] with the word "not" (na).
The meaning is this: non-contradictoriness does not consist in the actual attainment of the object, but rather in the mere capacity for attaining the object.
And that [capacity] is characterized by the power to induce activity,
and that [power] consists precisely in the establishment of a determination regarding the object;
for by means of such a determination, a person who has acted shall, provided there is no obstruction, certainly attain the object as it was presented.

And the teacher Dharmottara said: "The quality of being an instigator [of action] is nothing other than the capacity to indicate the object of activity; for consciousness cannot compel a person to act by force, as a human agent might.
(Nyāyabinduṭīkā, p. 3)

And Kamalaśīla says: "Non-contradiction (*avisamvāditva*) consists in the capacity to lead one to an object capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*), but it does not consist in the actual reaching of the object" (*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p.

312). While defining the specific determination of the object (*arthaparicchitti-viśeṣa*) as the function of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he establishes that the validity of a means of cognition is fulfilled merely by its producing that [determination], thereby making it fit for the attainment of an object capable of causal efficiency—beginning with the words "But when this is of such a nature," etc.
This means that the restriction must be understood as: "this clearly appearing form which is being manifested is [the object], and not another."
This very ascertainment is the function of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); such is the intention [of the author].

And Kamalaśīla says in the *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*: "Perception, although free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), arises as it delimits an object such as fire—which is excluded from things of its own class and of other classes—by virtue of the arising of a manifestation in its own form. And because it grasps an entity of a restricted nature and because it conforms to the form of an entity excluded from things of other classes, it brings about both affirmation and negation with respect to that very entity."
"This is fire, not that cluster of flowers and so forth" (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p.

390). And he says immediately following that very point: "For knowledge, arising in the form of the object, as if delimiting the object, becomes as if possessed of activity; this alone is the activity of knowledge consisting in the attainment of the object" (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 399).
And this is stated later on: "That which brings about the desired object for one seeking purposeful action (arthakriyā) is called a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
It does not become a 'bringer' (prāpaka) by moving the person to the location of the object, nor by bringing the object to the location of the person;
rather, it does so by impelling the person [toward the object]."
And it does not set that person in motion by seizing him with the hand; rather, what does it do?
It indicates the object of activity.
Such indication is nothing other than the determination of an object as it appears.
(Tattvapañcikā 783) By this much alone— that is, simply by the production of certainty—
the validity [of the cognition] is uncontradicted; that is to say, its validity remains intact because it possesses the capacity for attainment (*prāpaṇa*).

In some cases there is an absence of activity, and in other cases, even when activity occurs, there is no attainment of the object; this is caused by the absence of their respective causal complexes (*sāmagrī*). Thus, he demonstrates that the validity of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) remains entirely unimpaired: "But the person...
The fruit of the means of knowledge is the determination of the object;
once the object is determined, the cognition of its being a purpose (*prayojana*) is the cause for activity.

The point is that even if activity occurs, the non-attainment of the result is due to an obstruction; thus, because of the distinction between the cause and the effect, or because of non-activity resulting from non-attainment, the validity of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not obstructed.
Intending this very point, he says: "What does that have to do with the cognition? And Śāntarakṣita says:
"Furthermore, the apprehension of the object is here intended as the fruit of the means of valid cognition" (*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā* 398).
He raises this objection with "But is it not this...":

the underlying intention is that for one looking at something present before them, there immediately arises a perception that is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), devoid of the construction of names, universals, and so forth, and consisting of non-determination.
The cognition that takes the form "this is precisely this" is a determinate (savikalpaka) apprehension.

Since that [determinate cognition] arises immediately upon the perception [of the object], its validity—characterized by non-contradiction and the capacity to lead to the attainment of the object—is not known without the actual attainment of purposeful action (arthakriyā).
Therefore, how can it be called "correct knowledge"?
[The opponent argues: "For once rightness (*samyaktva*) is understood, activity would ensue.
[The author] refutes this, saying: "This is not a fault.
The underlying intention is as follows: this refers to the lack of understanding regarding the capacity to attain the object in the case of a perception that has just arisen.
This is not a fault,
for its innate capacity to bring about purposeful action does not depart by that much alone;
rather, activity indeed occurs through the possibility of attaining the object.
However, there is this distinction: a person of dull intellect, at the very moment water is perceived, is unable to ascertain its validity;

rather, observing from afar others performing actions such as bathing and drinking, he ascertains it as "water," and thus there arises the apprehension of its fitness for achieving the intended purpose.
One of sharp intellect, however, by virtue of the clarity of the manifestation, immediately ascertains "this is this very thing," and simultaneously ascertains its validity.
He raises an objection: "Now, even though...

The underlying intention is this: although visual perception, by bringing about the attainment of an object within its own range that is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), possesses non-contradiction characterized by the attainment of such causal efficiency; yet...
But in the case of direct perception, such as that of hearing, this is not possible;
for sound is manifested solely by the auditory organ.
When someone instructs another on something, at that time only those words are apprehended.
"Even when an object is illuminated by the eye, there is no stability whatsoever regarding its causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsthiti*). He refutes this, saying "no.
The intended meaning is this: the very determination of the intrinsic nature of an object is non-discrepancy (*avisaṃvāditva*), and that itself is, in some cases, the stability of causal efficiency.

For one who gazes upon the moon, the sun, clouds, paintings, and so forth, there arises the appearance of the moon and other such objects; yet, unlike the performance of functions such as bathing or drinking when water and the like are seen, no such functional efficacy (arthakriyā) exists therein.
Rather, it is the very knowledge of the true nature of the object of cognition that constitutes the intended function established in that case.

"In the same way, the ascertainment of the object to be manifested occurs merely by hearing the word; and thus, the validity characterized by the ascertainment of the object to be manifested is exactly the same for auditory cognition as it is for visual cognition.
Refuting the Mīmāṃsaka position that "the validity of cognitions is apprehended intrinsically," he says: "For this very reason..."

The meaning is: because for one of dull intellect, validity is determined only after the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) regarding an object whose specific features were not ascertained at the very moment the perception arose;
whereas for one of keen intellect, the apprehension of validity occurs from the very beginning regarding an object whose specific features were ascertained at the very moment the perception arose.
Therefore, [it is said] "for this very reason."
"Of perception" means "of someone," that is to say,
of one of dull intellect.
"From another source" means by means of a logical mark (liṅga), such as causal efficiency (arthakriyā) and so forth.
Regarding "the cognition of a yogin":
since the direct perception (pratyakṣa) arising from the power of yoga is indeed of a nature characterized by vivid manifestation, its validity is apprehended intrinsically (svataḥ).
And regarding "of self-cognizable knowledge":
this means, in effect, of the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of pleasure and so forth.
For when pleasure is being directly experienced, there can be no doubt concerning it.
"But because inference consists of certainty" means,
in other words, "because it possesses a determined particularity.
By this, it is stated that for us there is no such rule as that the validity of a cognition is apprehended only intrinsically (*svataḥ*).
And it was said by Śāntarakṣita:
"By some earlier [teachers], a restriction was stated that [validity] arises from itself alone;
by others, it was held that some [validity] arises from itself and some from another, while yet others maintained there is no such restriction."
And Kamalaśīla has explained: "By some— the Mīmāṃsakas— and by others— the Buddhists—

certain things are accepted as self-validating (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*), such as self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), the cognition of a yogin, the cognition of causal efficiency (*arthakriyājñāna*), inference, and perceptual experience resulting from repeated practice."
For that [cognition] is ascertained by itself alone,
because its causes of error have been discarded through the power of repeated practice.
Some [cognitions], however, are [ascertained] from another— namely, the cognition produced by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*), which is the subject of dispute.
"And perception [is that] which has not yet departed from the causes of error" (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā 775).

He states the purpose of including "having an object not previously apprehended" in the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with the words beginning "from the very first," and so forth.
The intention is this: for the purpose of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is to incite those who act with deliberation toward purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*).
And its capacity to incite arises from its quality of revealing an object;

and although this quality of revealing an object is no different in a continuous stream of cognition (*dhārāvāhin*)—such as a second or subsequent cognition—than it is in the first cognition that initially arose, [the first alone possesses the status of a *pramāṇa*].

Furthermore, since the object is already determined by the very first cognition that has arisen, a person acts based on that alone without depending on a second or subsequent cognition; thus, the second and subsequent cognitions are established otherwise (anyathāsiddha) and are not auxiliary factors for the activity. Consequently, they do not possess the status of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*). Therefore, to exclude them, the definition of valid knowledge includes the qualification "having an object not previously [cognized]" (*apūrvagocara*).

And it has been stated by the teacher Dharmottara: "For this very reason, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has as its object that which has not yet been apprehended; for by whichever cognition an object is first apprehended, by that very [cognition] is the person impelled to act and the object attained."
"In that very matter, what further purpose would be served by another cognition? (Nyāyabindu, p. 4).

This has been explained by us elsewhere: those who engage in purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*) do so for the sake of cognizing an object capable of that action, which manifests that object; they do not act because the object has already been apprehended.
For that [cognition] is of no benefit to them.

However, when it illuminates such an object and, by removing ignorance, benefits that person, then, with respect to that person, it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that object. But that which does not benefit anything at all does not attain the status of being a means of valid cognition, even though it illuminates the object.

However, it is precisely this—the removal of the non-apprehension of an object—that must be accomplished by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Prior to the ascertainment of an object through a valid cognition, there exists a non-apprehension of that object characterized by ignorance; this is indeed destroyed by the first valid cognition, which is characterized by the ascertainment of that object.
But that which manifests an already apprehended object is not brought about as its result.
Because ignorance itself is non-existent;
since it is incapable of producing any effect, it is called invalid.
But surely, direct realization is valid knowledge?

Anticipating the objection that "the sense organ, being the instrument of that [cognition], is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and therefore a definition of the means of valid cognition applicable to it must be stated," he says: "Valid cognition is the means of valid cognition" has been stated.
For an insentient sense organ, the status of being a means of valid cognition is simply untenable.
For this is the very nature of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa): that it is the delimitation of an object;
and the delimitation of an object is the very nature of cognition itself.
The eye merely comes into contact with the object, like light;
however, the determination of the object occurs through cognition alone.

Therefore, since it [the sense organ] is not included within the category of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the definition should not be formulated as something common to both. This is the intended meaning.

If this is so, it would follow that direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and if that were the case, the distinction between the result and the instrument—namely, that "this is the valid cognition" and "this is the instrument of valid cognition, which is called the *pramāṇa*"—would not be tenable. To this we shall reply immediately upon reaching the occasion for defining perception (*pratyakṣa*).
By this, the disagreement regarding the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been refuted.
Now, refuting the disagreement regarding its number, he says: "That is twofold.
He states the etymological derivation of the word *pratyakṣa*: "gone toward" (*pratigata*).
He explains the term "pratigatam" (gone toward) as "āśritam" (supported).
And being supported by the sense-faculties is simply being connected to the sense-faculties;
and this connection is its arising from them.
There is no other relation for a real entity (vastu) than identity (tādātmya) or causality (tadutpatti).
Having this in mind, it is said: "Therefore, the meaning is that perception is cognition produced [from that object].

Now, an objection is raised: since objects are also causes of the cognition of form and so forth, just as the sense organs (akṣa) are, why is there not the designation "pratyartham" (with respect to each object), intending to show its dependence on the object?
Not so;

for while the connection with the object is common to mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the connection with the sense organ (*akṣa*) is unique [to sensory perception]. Therefore, it is appropriate that it be designated by the very term "perception" (*pratyakṣa*).
And Dignāga said: "Because it has a unique cause, it is designated by means of the sense organs" (*Pramāṇasamuccaya*, verse 4).
And the commentary says: "Consciousness arises from the support of the object; why then is it said to have the sense-faculties as its support?
Why does it not have the object as its support?"
If this is argued, he says: "The uncommon," and so forth.
In that context, objects such as color-form (*rūpa*) are common to mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
yet, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is observed based on what is uncommon, as for example, the word "barley" (*yava*) is used for a barley sprout.
He raises an objection with "nanu" (but surely).
Regarding the phrase "in mental [perception] and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (ādi), self-awareness and the direct perception of yogis are included.
He refutes [the objection] with the words "To this it is said.

This is the point: dependence upon the sense organs (*akṣa*) is the etymological basis (*vyutpatti-nimitta*) for the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), but it is not its operational basis (*pravṛtti-nimitta*);
rather, the operational basis is the quality of directly manifesting an object (*arthasākṣātkāritva*).
By the expression "that which has gone toward the sense-organ" (*pratigatamakṣam*), the etymological derivation of the word *pratyakṣa* is merely demonstrated.

And by that etymological ground, its actual basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*)—namely, the quality of being a direct perception (*sākṣātkāritva*), which inheres in the same object as that ground—is indicated.

Just as, for example, by the etymological ground of the word *paṅkaja* (lotus), namely "the agent of arising from mud," there is indicated the property of being a lotus (*padmatva*), which inheres in the same object as that ground.

And it has been stated by the teacher Dharmottara: "The state of being dependent (*āśritatva*) is the etymological basis (*vyutpattinimitta*) of the word, but not its operational basis (*pravṛttinimitta*);

however, by this dependence upon the sense-faculties (*akṣāśritatva*), the quality of directly perceiving an object (*arthasākṣātkāritva*), which is inherent in the same substrate as that [dependence], is indicated."
That alone is the ground for the application of the term [perception].
Consequently, whatever direct cognition of an object there may be, that is called perception (*pratyakṣa*).

He states the etymological ground for the word "inference" (*anumāna*) with the passage beginning with "is measured" (*mīyate*) and ending with "inference is the means of measuring" (*mānamanumānam*).
Now, he states the ground for the application [of the term] with the passage beginning with "liṅga" and ending with "iti.
Regarding the phrase "by virtue of conventional usage" (rūḍhivaśāt):
this means that although this word is etymologically derived in a general sense, it conveys a specific meaning through conventional usage.
And it was stated by the teacher Diṅnāga: "Inference is the perception of an object through its mark" (*Nyāyapraveśa*, p. 7). [The opponent] is the Mīmāṃsaka Kumārila Bhaṭṭa.
A general term culminates in a specific one.
With the words "In that regard" (*tatra*) and so forth, he refutes the Cārvāka doctrine that maintains perception alone is the means of valid cognition.

The underlying intention is as follows: while formulating definitions of various things according to his own system in order to eliminate another's lack of comprehension or misconception, how does this author himself come to know that other person’s lack of comprehension or misconception?
Regarding the phrase "the activity of another's body and speech":
likewise, even by one who does not know [the specific intention], the inference of a cause from an effect is accepted.

Similarly, when a person employs a statement to communicate their own intention to another, even by one who does not know that the statement being employed serves as an inferential mark (*liṅga*) for the speaker's intention, this is nonetheless accepted.
And it was said by Śāntarakṣita:
"Some of evil view, even while expressing their intention through these words, declare that inference is not a means of valid cognition."
Thus [it is said]. (Tattvasaṃgraha 425) He refutes the authority of verbal testimony as accepted by the Sāṅkhya and others with the words "And verbal cognition," etc.
[The phrase] "must be accepted" [is used].
For one who asserts that verbal cognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), validity must be admitted on the basis of non-contradiction with external objects.
This non-contradiction consists in the capacity to bring about the attainment of that object, and that capacity consists in the determination of that object;
furthermore, the fact that a specific word serves as the cause for the determination of a specific object is not possible without a relationship between those two—the word and the object.
The capacity to delimit objects such as color-form (*rūpa*) is not inherent to the eye;

for if it were, then just as there is the cognition of blue and so forth as soon as the eye is opened, there would be a cognition of the object for everyone—including even those who have not mastered linguistic conventions—as soon as a particular word is heard.

Therefore, the relationship between word and meaning must be stated. Having raised the question of what that [relationship] might be, he refutes the various alternatives with the words beginning: "The relationship between word and meaning being... and so forth.
"Even though there is a difference in appearance":
because of the difference in location, the difference in time, and the difference in object, the appearance of these two is not one and the same;
the word is perceived by the ear and the object by the eye.
The sound is heard in one place, while the object is seen elsewhere; thus there is a difference in time as well.
Therefore, the point is that because they do not share the status of being the object of a single cognition, there is no identity between the word and its referent.
And Śāntarakṣita said:
"Because they are apprehended by different sense organs and so forth, there is neither identity nor origination [of the word] from that [referent]."
And because it is subject to deviation, it is not logical for anything else to possess non-deviation.
Thus, (Tattvasaṃgraha 440),

if the word were the cause with respect to the object, or the object were the cause with respect to the word, then a relationship consisting of the nature of cause and effect between the two would be possible.

He states that neither of these two exists by means of the passage beginning with "nor" (*nāpi*) and ending with "because it arises from the operation of the palate and so forth" (*tālvādivyāpārādeva tadutpatteḥ*).
Although no relation between two entities other than identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) is accepted,
he nevertheless refutes it by restating what is admitted by others, beginning with "now" (*atha*).

Since the relationship between the lamp and the jar as the illuminator and the illuminated is natural, just as the lamp illuminates an object by its mere existence, so too, if the relationship between word and meaning known as the signifier-signified (vācyavācaka) were natural, a word heard for the first time would convey its meaning without distinction even to one who does not know the convention. To this he says: "If that were so... [evam tarhi]. He states, "an unprecedented person" [abhinava], pointing to a specific individual, in response to the question: "What worldly person could there be who is ignorant of the convention between a specific word and a specific meaning?"
This means that [the person] has not come from that continent where the term "fire" is not even conventionally used.
Now, although there exists a natural relationship between a word and its meaning in the form of the signifier-signified relation (*vācyavācakabhāva*),
the capacity to convey the meaning nevertheless depends upon convention (*saṅketa*).
With the intention that there can be no cognition of an object without the apprehension of that [word], he raises an objection with the words "Now, however" (*atha*).
Regarding the phrase "only that which is capable":

the syntactical connection is to be understood by shifting the order of the words as follows: "Only that which is born as capable of conveying an object arises precisely in dependence upon convention."
"He rejects it, saying 'not that'"—for in this way its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) does not remain.
The meaning is: such being the case, its validity does not indeed persist.
Why? He says: "Because of convention alone.

And Kamalaśīla says: "For lamps and the like, which are by nature causes for the cognition of objects, do not depend upon convention; otherwise, it would be through the positive and negative concomitance of convention alone that there would be capacity for the cognition of objects, and not of an inherent relation" (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā 438). Therefore.
The meaning is that there is no relationship between word and object.
"It is not known" means,
in other words, that it cannot be ascertained.
The sense is that only when a relationship exists can there be a determination that "this very meaning is to be understood by this word.
Because of the absence of a relationship, due to the lack of distinction, there could never be a determination that "only the intended meaning is to be understood by this word.
He refutes [the opponent's position] even after accepting the relationship—on the principle of "let it be so for the sake of satisfaction"—despite its logical untenability, saying: "Or let it be."
"Exactly this"—meaning something other than identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*).
With the intention that there is no occasion for an implication regarding the restricted nature (*svabhāva*) of a thing, he raises an objection: "Now, it must be said.
He rejects it: "That is incorrect."

The meaning is that when the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no occasion for an objection; however, if it were merely being postulated (*kalpyamāna*), there would certainly be occasion for doubt.
For example:

With the intention that fire, when being produced, is produced as characterized by a burning power by its very nature, and likewise that a particular word is produced as characterized by a power to convey a particular meaning,
[the author] restates the objection raised by the opponent and refutes it with the words "And it should not be said thus," etc.,
[concluding with] "the non-deviation from a restricted object."
And it should not be stated in this way; such is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). He states the reason for that with the words beginning "for thus" (*tathāhi*).

Furthermore, he refutes the claim made by others—that a sentence uttered by a reliable person (*āpta*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—with the words "nor [is there validity] of words composed by a reliable person."

He refutes the position of the Mīmāṃsakas—who maintain that a sentence uttered by one who is not trustworthy is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and who describe the Veda as having intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) due to its being authorless—by means of the very critique of the [word’s] relationship [to its meaning].

Anticipating the objection that if the validity of words is thus rejected, it would entail the total destruction of worldly linguistic practice (*lokavyavahāra*), he provides a rebuttal starting with the words “How then...”:
“[It occurs] by the force of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣāvaśāt*).”
The meaning is that the speaker’s intention to convey a specific sense serves as an indicator (liṅga) for the words.
And Śāntarakṣita has said:
"This very intention to speak is inferred from all words whatsoever."
For that [causal relation] is indeed ascertained through perception and non-perception.
Thus [it is said] (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā 441): that intention (*vivakṣā*) is the cause of that; it is the cause of the speech being employed.
The meaning of that [statement] is that the causal relationship between those two is ascertained through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*).
Now, while refuting the validity of comparison (*upamāna*) as maintained by the Naiyāyikas, he restates their position with the words "of the Naiyāyika.
[He says] "the elaboration" (*prapañca*).
It is being examined;
this is the ellipsis.
[The phrase "assisted by the recollection of the meaning of the authoritative analogical statement" means: assisted by the recollection of the meaning of the authoritative statement of analogy.
The meaning is: that for which the recollection of the meaning of the extended statement (*atideśavākya*) serves as an auxiliary cause.
"Cognition of similarity" means, in other words, that which is produced by the words of a reliable authority (*āpta*).
"Being pervaded by having an object" means that a cognition becomes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by illuminating an object not previously known;
the sense is: in the absence of such an object, how could there be validity for the cognition?
He establishes the impossibility of an object [of perception] with the words "tathāhi" (for it is thus).
Regarding the phrase "the relationship of designation":
this is the underlying intention.

Having heard the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*), when one goes to the forest and perceives a particular object (*piṇḍaviśeṣa*), then there is for him merely the direct perception (*aparokṣa*) of that object. However, its similarity (*sārūpya*) is remembered alone.
But memory is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it apprehends what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitva*).
But surely, immediately after seeing the individual object, there occurs the apprehension of the relationship of the name, namely, "this is what is denoted by the word *gavaya*";

this very [apprehension] is called analogy (*upamā*), and it is said to be the fruit of the means of knowledge known as analogy; therefore, there exists an object, which is the relationship between the word and its referent, namely the name.
And he rejects it, saying that it does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality;
furthermore, this common assertion that "there is a relation" is mere words.

The point is that no entity distinct from the two related things is perceived which could be intended as the true nature of the relation (*sambandha*). He refutes the mere concept of a relation by means of the passage beginning with "if it were perceptible" (*dṛśyatve*), and so forth.
One who asserts that "these two are related" and "this is the relation between them" must state whether this relation is perceptible or imperceptible.
The existence of something imperceptible is not established; if it were perceptible, [it would be perceived].
The point is this: when a relation is perceived, that [related object] should also be perceived;
yet it is not perceived.

Therefore, the relation is not ultimate. Consequently, the claim that the relationship between word and meaning is one of designation (*samākhyā*) and that analogy (*upamā*) possesses validity as a means of knowledge because it reveals that [relation] is simply untenable.
Now, in a case where the very collection of conditions for perceiving the related term is itself the collection of conditions for perceiving the relation,
the relation would indeed be perceived at the very time the related term is seen. But where these collections are distinct, the relation would not be perceived at that same time.
Therefore, it is not the case that it is entirely invisible;
for this reason, he states another objection, beginning with "furthermore" (kiñcit).
Now, [the opponent might argue that] a relation is simply the production of a cognition of connection.
The intention is this: surely the relation is indeed distinct from the two related entities, for it is characterized by being the cause of the cognition that [the two] are related.
For the mere existence of a jar and a cloth is not the cause of the cognition that "the jar and the cloth are conjoined."
Because such a cognition would arise even in the state where they are separated,
one must therefore accept that conjunction (*saṃyoga*)— which is distinct from those two— is the regulator of the cognition of their specific relation (*vaiśiṣṭya*);
likewise, even though both the word "gavaya" and the particular individual exist, there is no apprehension of the designation [of the object as "gavaya"].

[The opponent claims: "One apprehends that relationship of denotation immediately after perceiving a specific individual object, even while possessing knowledge of the meaning of the authoritative extended statement (*atideśavākya*).
[The author] rejects this, stating: "That is not tenable;
for [the cognition arises] even from two related things."

The meaning is: "from the two things themselves, independently of any other entity called 'relation'. This is the intended sense: since all existing things are momentary, those two objects that are the focus of a cognition of conjunction are distinct from those that are the focus of a cognition of separation; and since it is precisely these two that serve as the cause of the cognition of being related, there is no need to postulate a related entity distinct from them. Therefore, a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*) is not capable of postulating a relation as something over and above [the two relata].
This is what must be understood here: the perception "that which is similar to a cow is a gavaya" is auditory perception (*śrautra-pratyakṣa*).
That [perception], by virtue of manifesting a specific word, is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the word alone;
however, the subsequent observation of a specific individual object, by virtue of manifesting that specific individual object, is a means of valid cognition with respect to that object alone.

The recollection of similarity previously understood through instruction that occurs upon seeing a particular individual object is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it apprehends what has already been apprehended in the form of memory.

Furthermore, the subsequent grasping of the relationship with the name once that particular object has been seen also does not go beyond memory, as it pertains only to the conceptual entity that is the universal "gavaya."
Moreover, there are other means for grasping the relationship of a name as well; for example, when asked, "What is a *pika*?", someone replies, "That which sings sweetly is a *pika*.
Following the hearing of the sweet song, the grasp of the name *pika* occurs within the conceptual form of the universal *pika*.
Otherwise, even [cognitions] such as these would result in having independent validity.
And it has been stated by Śāntarakṣita: "It is said that water and the like are not indistinguishable because of their momentariness."
Likewise: "It has been established that there is no relation existing apart from the related entities. (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā 220)
Long before, at that time, the sound was already grasped by the auditory consciousness.
This animal standing directly in front is seen by the eye;
however, this connection between two things perceived separately is not a valid means of knowledge.
Because it involves the apprehension and subsequent synthesis [of what was previously perceived], like the fragrance and sweetness [of a flower];
therefore, that cognition of yoga does not transcend the nature of memory.
Furthermore, cognitions resulting from the application of names and the conjunction [of words] produced by infinite means arise even in men,
dogs, and other beings, regardless of their similarity [to others].
The lord of men, whose feet are covered by the white parasol,
is said to be in their midst according to the specific instruction.

When that [object] is seen at a later time, the cognition that "this has that name" is a distinct means of valid knowledge (pramā) at that moment, because it does not depend upon similarity or other such factors.
Thus [it is said].
(Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā 454) Now, he refutes the Mīmāṃsakas' demonstration of the validity of analogy (*upamāna*) with the words beginning "in this way" (*evam*).
[The phrase] "even of that described by the Mīmāṃsakas" refers to this.
The word "of the standard of comparison" (*upamānasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

An individual (*piṇḍa*) qualified by similarity, or similarity qualified by an individual, is the object of the standard of comparison; it is by means of that [object] that [the subject] is described.
This is the underlying intention: having previously seen a cow in a village, one later goes to the forest and sees a *gavaya*.
Then, there immediately arises for him a cognition consisting of indeterminate perception (*ālocana*) regarding the specific object;
and from that follows the determinate (*savikalpaka*) ascertainment: "This animal is similar to a cow.
And this [determinate cognition], being produced by the sense organs, is indeed characterized as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
And from that arises the cognition: "The cow is similar to this animal.

This very cognition is called the means of valid knowledge known as comparison (*upamāna*), and its object is either the cow as qualified by similarity to the *gavaya*, or the similarity residing in the cow.
Now, surely similarity is apprehended through perception,
and the cow is the object of memory;
so what new thing is being asserted as the object of the means of knowledge called analogy?
True.
The object of analogy (upamāna) is that very reality characterized by similarity which has not yet been apprehended.
And so it was stated by Kumārila:
Therefore, that which is remembered, as qualified by similarity,
would be the object of knowledge (*prameya*) for analogy (*upamāna*), or else it is the similarity itself as qualified [by the remembered object].
When the similarity is apprehended through perception and the cow is remembered,
comparison (upamāna) possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge because the qualified [object] cannot be established by any other means.

Thus [it is said]. (Ślokavārttika, Pratyakṣa 444) He refutes similarity—which is claimed by others to be the object of the means of valid cognition known as comparison—by the words "And not," and so forth.
That pair, the cow and the gavaya, which are mutually similar, are established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
One has been seen previously and the other is now [seen];
what similarity, moreover, exists beyond these two that could be called the object of comparison?
As for the claim that there is further similarity of parts, that does not exceed what is already accounted for by the arrangement of those parts;
and that [arrangement] is indeed directly perceived.
The meaning is that this so-called "similarity," which is distinct from the two perceived individual objects, does not fall within the scope of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
He establishes its lack of proof by valid cognition with the words beginning "for instance" (*tathāhi*):
it is simply swallowed up by the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*).
For the non-perception of that which is capable of being perceived indeed leads to the understanding of the non-existence of the object.
As for the cognition of similarity—this is the underlying intention: surely, this very cognition, "This is similar to that," is itself the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for similarity.
If it is argued that [the universal] is established through an inference based on an effect— since cognition arises from an object— that is not so.
For consider the cow and the gavaya, which are perceived as being similar to one another.
Those two things, having arisen from their own respective causes, serve as the grounds for the cognition "these two are similar to each other";
thus, no entity called "similarity" is established as something distinct from them.

Furthermore, the resemblance of many parts is nothing other than a specific arrangement of those parts; therefore, its establishment does not result from an inference based on an effect as a logical mark (*kāryaliṅgaka-anumāna*).
"By that proponent" means by the Mīmāṃsaka.

Since he himself asserts that the object of the means of knowledge called comparison (*upamāna*) is merely the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) between two objects of similarity whose existence is already established by other means of knowledge, [the opponent asks: "By what means of knowledge is similarity itself established?"
The meaning is that one might ask how he could say, "It is established by this very means of knowledge, namely comparison," for such a statement would be contradictory.

This is what should be understood here: just as when a gavaya, which resembles a cow, is seen, there arises the cognition regarding a previously experienced cow, "A cow is similar to this [gavaya]," so too, regarding a previously experienced horse, there arises the cognition, "A horse is dissimilar to this [cow]."
Therefore, why should this cognition of dissimilarity (*vaisādṛśya*) not also be a distinct means of valid cognition?
Nor can it be subsumed under the means of valid cognition consisting of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*),
for this cognition is based on a positive entity (*bhāva*).

Thus, when a row of trees is being perceived, although the "firstness" (ādyatva) was not apprehended upon the sight of the first tree, that firstness is apprehended immediately after the sight of the second tree in the form, "That tree is the first. Consequently, this cognition too would result in being a distinct means of valid knowledge (pramāṇāntara), because its object is something previously unapprehended.
It has been stated by Śāntarakṣita: "But when a gavaya is perceived,
that cognition of its dissimilarity which arises with respect to a horse and so forth— is that not another means of valid cognition?"
If it is argued that [the cognition] is not included within non-existence, it is not so, because it relies upon existence;
and in the case of mutual non-existence, the same applies to cognitions of similarity.
When a row of trees or the like is perceived, from the sight of a single tree and the subsequent cognition of a second tree, there arises the certain conviction: "This is that very same one."
Another means of valid cognition is engaged [therein], because it is independent of similarity.
(Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā 450). "It would not be possible as something separate" means that it would not be possible as something distinct from inference.
Presumption (arthāpatti) does not possess validity at all;
if it were valid, it would simply be included within inference (anumāna). Demonstrating this very point, he says: "In this regard, the following is considered."

"That object which is seen through valid means of knowledge" refers to an object established by *pramāṇa*, such as the fatness of one who does not eat during the day, or the absence from home of one who is alive, and so forth. "The object being postulated" refers to [the inferred] eating at night, being outside, and so forth.

"There is a necessary connection (pratibandha). That which is the conceptualizer perceived through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and that which is the object to be conceptualized which is imperceptible— if there exists a necessary connection between these two, it is included within inference (anumāna).
And in the absence of that [cause] for that object, there is no validity at all.

For example, in the case of one who does not eat during the day, his corpulence and his eating at night stand in a relationship of cause and effect; since there is a necessary connection (*prabandha*), corpulence—the effect—can serve as the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for eating at night, which is the cause.
Therefore, in that instance, presumption (*arthāpatti*) has no separate validity apart from inference (*anumāna*).

As for what the Mīmāṃsaka says—that because one hears of a person's corpulence despite not eating during the day, the sentence "he eats at night" is inferred—this is untenable due to the lack of connection; thus, there is no proof whatsoever for that.
And it has been said by Śāntarakṣita:
"A person associated with eating at night is understood as the desired [subject],
by virtue of being fat despite the absence of eating during the day, just like anyone other than him."

Since corpulence is determined to follow from the presence of food through positive and negative concomitance, there is a cognition of the thing-in-itself from the thing itself by virtue of that relationship.
For how can a sentence, which is devoid of all connection, be understood?
Otherwise, everything would be understood from a single sentence.
(Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā 465).
Thus, he refutes the means of valid cognition called non-existence (*abhāva*) with the words beginning "of non-existence" (*abhāvasya*), stating:
"we do not perceive even its own nature."
The phrase "because of being non-existent" (avastutvāt) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Regarding the expression "of perception and so forth" (pratyakṣādīnām), by the word "and so forth" (ādi), inference, comparison, verbal testimony, and presumptive testimony are included.
"It is stated by the Mīmāṃsakas.
And Śabarasvāmin said: "Non-existence (abhāva) is also the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāva), regarding an object that does not exist and is not in contact [with the senses].
And Kumārila says:

"Where the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇapañcaka*) do not arise with respect to the nature of an object, there the status of non-existence as a means of valid cognition (*abhāvapramāṇatā*) exists for the sake of cognizing or not cognizing that object" (Ślokavārttika, Chapter 473).

He refutes the non-arising of the five means of valid cognition—which is intended to be the means of valid cognition known as non-existence—by means of the analysis beginning with "In that case, what is this... and so forth.
"Because it is devoid of all power.
The meaning is that since the mere negation of origination is of the nature of non-existence, it is not a real entity.
"For this very reason," [he says].
The meaning is: "precisely because it is not a real entity.
For non-existence is not the apprehension of anything;
that is to say, it is not the apprehension of any object whatsoever.
How, then, is that [non-existence] apprehended?
The meaning is: since non-existence is not a real entity (*avastu*), how could its apprehension possibly occur?
Now, one might argue that the non-arising of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇānutpatti*) is merely a particular state of the cognizer, the self (*ātman*).

Kumārila said: "The non-arising of perception and the other [means of knowledge] is intended as the absence of a means of valid cognition; that [absence] is either the non-modification of the self. (Ślokavārttika, Abhāvapariccheda, verse 475)
Thus, it is the non-arising of perception and the other means of knowledge;

its meaning is the non-modification of the self— that is, the state of not being modified into the form of cognition of objects such as jars which are intended to be negated— and the substance of the self in its state of equilibrium.
If it is argued that, in this way, it is not a non-entity,
what is the use of that [nature] which is common to the state of deep sleep?
Thus it has been said by Śāntarakṣita:
"Or, even if there were no transformation of this [consciousness], it would still be subject to deviation;
for even when that [transformation] exists during states such as sleep or fainting, the object does not exist."

(Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā 474). [Objection: But we speak of the non-arising of perception and the other means of knowledge by way of *paryudāsa* (relative negation); and that [non-arising] is the abiding in another cognition.

And it has been stated by Kumārila: "Or consciousness [arises] regarding another object. If this is raised, it is refuted by the phrase "nor even this," etc., through the refutation of the second alternative.

Regarding the statement "the non-occurrence of perception and so forth," with the intention of considering the alternative as to whether what is intended is cognition in general or a specific type of cognition, he refutes the position of cognition in general with the verse beginning "deśakāla... and so on.
Sumeru is remote in terms of space;
the Śaṅkha universal monarch is remote in terms of time;
and beings such as yakṣas are remote in terms of their intrinsic nature.
He refutes the position that [the cognition] is a particular kind of knowledge with the words: "Now, if it is connected with a single cognition.

This means: in a single cognition, such as a perception qualified by a jar, the ground—which is connected as its object—is perceived as mere ground; it is precisely the perception of that object that is expressed by the phrase "the non-arising of perception and so forth."

The expression "a single cognition" (*ekajñāna*) is stated with the intention that they have a single object (*ekaviṣayakatva*). The point is this: the perception of the bare ground (*bhūtalamātra*) has as its object the very same specific location that the qualified perception (*viśiṣṭapratyakṣa*) has; therefore, this perception is called the means of valid cognition consisting in non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*). To this, he says: "At that time... (*tadā*).
He defines direct perception (pratyakṣa) with the words "therein, direct perception.

"Therein" means between direct perception and inference. The syntactical connection is established by way of the relationship between the subject and the predicate: that which is free from conceptual construction (kalpanāpoḍha) and non-erroneous (abhrānta) is direct perception.
By the negation "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*), it is established by implication that [the object] is cognition (*jñāna*).
Now, one might object: "The nature of perception (*pratyakṣatva*) being enjoined must be stated as distinct from the form of the subject (*uddeśya*).
It is replied: That which consists in direct perceptual cognition (*sākṣātkārijñānatva*)—which is agreed upon by both disputants—is what is denoted by the word "perception."
He states that very conceptual construction (kalpanā), which is excluded from what is called perception, with the words beginning "prior and posterior," etc.
[The phrase] "the form associated with words" [is explained as follows].
And conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is to be understood as twofold according to name: namely, "Ḍittha" and "the staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*).
And it has been stated by Diṅnāga: "In the conjunction of name, genus, and so forth."
And this has been explained in the *Vṛtti*: "Now, what kind of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is it? He says: 'The association with name, genus, and so forth.

In the case of arbitrary words (*yadṛcchā-śabda*), there is the name such as 'Ḍittha'; in the case of genus-words, likewise 'cow', and so on" (Pramāṇavārttika 1.2). Since infants, the mute, and others lack a cognition capable of contact with words, he says: "having the form of internal speech."
He establishes the testimony of a reliable authority by stating, "And so it has been said. This means by Dharmakīrti.
That cognition in which there is an appearance capable of being associated with a verbal expression is "that which has an appearance capable of association with verbal expression."
By the inclusion of "fitness" (*yogyatva*), there is the inclusion of that conceptualization which takes the form of internal discourse (*antarjalpa*) in the case of infants, the mute, and others.
This has been explained by the master Dharmottara: "'It is expressed by this,' thus it is expression (*abhilāpa*); [it refers to] the expressive word (*vācaka-śabda*).

Connection with expression is the repeated association (*śīlana*) within a single cognition of the form of the signified (*abhidheya-ākāra*) together with the form of the signifier (*abhidhāna-ākāra*) as an objective aspect (*grāhya-ākāratayā*)."
Therefore, when the forms of the signifier (*abhidhā*) and the signified (*abhidheya*) are both present within a single cognition, then the signifier and the signified are conjoined.
That cognition in which there is an appearance of the signified that is capable of being associated with verbal expression is described as such [i.e., "conceptual"].
(Nyāyabinduṭīkā, p. 10)
He establishes that even infants, the mute, and others possess a cognition in the form of internal discourse (*antarjalpa*) with the words "the meaning of conceptual construction" and so forth.
And Śāntarakṣita said:
"In the form of 'tree' and so on, it is capable of connecting a word with its object..."
Or that which, even in the absence of the employment of speech, arises as if it were accompanied by verbal expression.
"Due to the continuity of the latencies from the cultivation of the names and objects of past existences,
even one just born becomes skilled in what is to be done through their connection."
(Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā 367).
Thus, it is determined that this conceptualization exists even in infants through specific activities such as smiling, crying, and suckling at the breast.
Now, one might ask: why is it that from a determinative conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), such as "this is indeed a cow," there arises the attainment of the object?

With the intention of questioning how it is determined that those two are not valid cognitions—since it is observed that even one who has acted upon the error of seeing a moving tree or seeing a yellow conch shell attains the object—the author raises the doubt with the words, "But what [is the case]?
[The answer is: "It is not a valid cognition."
The meaning is "not a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) in this context;
that is to say, what is the proof that it is not a means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?
It is agreed upon by everyone.
The intention is that while there is disagreement among disputants regarding the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*),
there is no disagreement concerning the essential nature of perception as consisting in the direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) of an object.
He states with the words "and not" (*na ca*) and so forth that this is not the case for conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*) or for error (*bhrama*).
It is logical that a cognition which is capable of directly realizing an object is "one that realizes that object";
however, how can that which is not so capable possess the nature of a cognition that realizes an object?
He states—“neither conceptual construction nor error [is such]”—because conceptual construction and error lack that capacity.
He establishes the lack of capacity with the words beginning "For instance" (*tathāhi*), etc.:
"They know [it] to be the state of being the object of apprehension;
it is precisely the state of being a cause."
The logical connection is that those who know reasoning understand that being a cause is precisely what constitutes the state of being an object of cognition (*grāhyatva*).
He establishes this causality by stating "capable of imparting its own form to the cognition.
The meaning is that because the object of cognition is capable of imparting its own form to the cognition.
Regarding the phrase "but conceptual cognition" (*kalpanājñānam tu*):

that cognition which is associated with the conceptualization of names, universals, and so forth, arises solely through mental impressions (*vāsanā*) even without an object such as the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of blue and the like; thus, it does not have an object as its cause.
Since it is not caused by an object, it does not apprehend an object; therefore, how could it possibly be a direct perception (*sākṣātkārin*) of that object? This is the intended meaning.
He points out the undesirable consequence if conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*) were produced by the object, with the words "And therefore" (*tataśca*).

The idea is this: since the perception of conceptualization—which expresses names, universals, and so forth—occurs even for a blind person who hears the word "blue," if one were to admit that conceptualization is also produced by the object, it would follow that such a person would possess visual perception of form;
for it has already been stated that there is no relation between the apprehended and the apprehender other than the relation of cause and effect.

Here, he provides authoritative corroboration: "Therefore it has been said," meaning that [the object] does not appear [as a distinct entity] in the same way as it does in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). He refutes the view of the Grammarians by restating it with the words beginning "by this" (*etena*).
"By this" means by the refutation that is about to be stated.

"To explain" (tathāhi): this is the underlying intention—let it be granted that for a person looking at something standing before them, there occurs a cognition permeated by a name, such as "this is a jar";
nevertheless, when the jar is thus perceived, the ground which serves as its locus is necessarily perceived as well, since it has come within the range of the eyes.
And yet that name is not uttered; thus it is untenable that every cognition whatsoever is permeated by a name. This objection has been stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position].
In reality, direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) is indeed devoid of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);
as soon as it is opened, the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) object standing before one is directly perceived,
while the appearance of conceptual construction occurs only immediately thereafter.
And that [error] occurs even for one who closes their eyes and reflects;
furthermore, there is no dependence on the sense-objects here.
He demonstrates the impossibility of error being perceptual with the words beginning "even though it is erroneous," and so forth.

The meaning is that those who know the nature of error declare that only that which arises with respect to an object capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*) in a distorted manner is called "erroneous.
The point is that a cognition whose appearance is distorted lacks the capacity to apprehend an object as it actually exists, and therefore it does not possess the status of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
It is for this very reason that the Teacher said [the following].
The master Dharmakīrti says— meaning, in the *Nyāyabindu*—
that the word "timira" (darkness/dimness) is an indicator for ocular defects.
By this—namely, by the fact that it is produced by the defect of *timira* (an optical disorder)—he raises an objection: "Now, if [it is argued]...
The underlying intention is as follows: if the perception of moving trees, a yellow conch-shell, and so forth, is erroneous, then it is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The definition of valid cognition as "non-erroneous knowledge" is untenable, because it leads to over-extension;
for that [knowledge] also brings about the attainment of an object that performs a causal function.

One who acts upon seeing a moving tree reaches that very tree or its location; likewise, one who acts upon the appearance of a yellow conch reaches the conch. Therefore, since it is governed by the definition of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), its inclusion within a specific category of valid cognition must necessarily be stated.
Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition other than perception and inference;
and since this [alleged] inference is not such, it must be admitted that its inclusion lies within perception itself.
Thus, the qualification "non-erroneous" need not be applied to the definition of perception.
He refutes this: there is no attainment of the object from that [cognition],
but rather from another cognition.
Therefore, there is no attainment of the object manifested by the perception of moving trees and so forth; rather, it is the attainment of something else entirely,
namely that which is manifested by another cognition.
Only that which is capable of causal efficiency (arthakriyāsamartha) is denotable by the word "real entity" (vastu).
A moving tree and the like are not capable of causal efficiency; rather, only a tree situated in a specific location is capable of causal efficiency.
The meaning is that it is illuminated by a subsequent cognition alone.
This is the intention: the perception of a moving tree is not non-contradictory, for no object is actually reached in accordance with how it appears.
A tree, appearing in another cognition, is apprehended as being in a fixed location,
and that location belongs to the stationary tree;
likewise, the appearance of a yellow conch is not non-contradictory.
Yellow is indeed seen,
yet white is obtained;
for white is certainly something other than yellow.
Therefore, it does not cause one to attain an object as it was manifested by itself;
rather, it is non-contradictory precisely because it causes one to attain the object exactly as it was manifested.
But is it not the case that the very same conch-shell is what is attained?
Is that which has entered the path of appearance as "yellow" [the conch]? No;
rather, the conch is not other than its form (rūpa), for there is no difference between the form and the possessor of form (rūpin).
And it has been said by Śāntarakṣita:
"A configuration does not arise as something distinct from color;
nor is correspondence admitted for the color that is actually appearing."
(Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā 395). By this, it should be understood that the argument establishing non-contradiction based on the unity of the continuum (*santāna*) is also refuted.
And Kamalaśīla said: "A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), in order to exist, must exist by way of two aspects."
Because there is non-contradiction either with respect to the appearance as it is or with respect to the conceptual determination;
however, in this case, there is no non-contradiction with respect to the appearance as it is.
Because there is the appearance of something yellow,
yet that thing as it truly is is not attained;
nor is there non-discrepancy according to the conceptual determination.

"Because there is a determination [of the object] precisely as yellow due to its performing a specific purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), yet there is no attainment of a purposeful action corresponding to that form," so it is said (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā 395).
And Ācārya Dharmottara says: "If it is a false cognition, how is it that from it one attains a tree?"
From that [cognition], the tree is not obtained;
for the tree, which moves through various locations, has been delimited by it,
and yet the tree is obtained as restricted to a single location.
"Therefore, the location where the moving tree was seen is not reached by the boat, and the location that is reached was not seen.
Thus, since the very definition of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is the capacity to lead one to the object as it appears, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

This is what is being stated: An object such as a moving tree, while being perceived, is indeed different from another cognition-perceived tree located in a fixed place that is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, because it lacks either the capacity to manifest an object capable of causal efficiency or the quality of being a cause for a corresponding determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*), the perception of a moving tree and so forth does not possess validity (*prāmāṇya*);
for validity consists precisely in non-contradiction (*avisamvādakatva*).
The term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) is used to exclude over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to inference (*anumāna*).
Since the object of inference is exclusively the universal (*sāmānya*), it is not free from conceptual construction.
Now, if perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed free from conceptual construction, how can it serve as a factor for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)?
For that which manifests what is inexpressible is not capable of leading to either engagement or withdrawal.
True;

even though it manifests what is inexpressible and devoid of conceptual construction, it becomes a constituent of worldly transaction by way of producing a determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) such as "this is a cow," which brings about engagement.
And Śāntarakṣita said:
"Even non-conceptual cognition possesses the power to produce conceptualization;
therefore, by means of that [power], it becomes a factor for all worldly transactions."
(Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā 390). Thus,
although the perceived object is one thing and conceptual construction is another,
for everything is indeed momentary.
The particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is the object of perception,

whereas conceptual construction (vikalpa) has a universal nature (sāmānyātman); nevertheless, activity occurs because of the determination (adhyavasāya) of the identity between the perceived and the conceptualized.

It is therefore appropriate that [conceptual cognition] is a factor in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) by virtue of possessing the capacity to produce a determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding an object manifested by itself.

Now, one might argue that conceptual cognition (*savikalpa*) should also be accepted as valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is a correct cognition (*samyak-jñāna*). This is not so; only a correct cognition whose object is something previously unknown (*apūrva-gocara*) is valid knowledge.

Furthermore, determinate cognition does not have an unprecedented object as its domain; for it grasps only what has already been grasped by perception, and it grasps it precisely as non-different [from that prior apprehension].

And Kamalaśīla has said: "Perception, although free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), arises by determining an object such as fire—which is excluded from both similar and dissimilar classes—through the production of an appearance in its own form.

And because it grasps an entity established in a specific form and conforms to the form of the entity as excluded from dissimilar things, it brings about affirmation and negation with respect to that very entity: 'This is fire, not that cluster of flowers.'"
"Furthermore, although the two types of conceptual cognition are non-deceptive because they are indirectly connected to the real object, they are not accepted as valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*).

This is because, through the determination of the identity between the perceived and the conceptualized, one acts [upon the object], yet there is no apprehension of the nature of the object that has not already been apprehended.
(Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā 390)

If it is objected: "But that which is obtained is indeed different from what was seen and determined; therefore, since perception does not cause one to obtain the object as it appeared to itself, how can it possess validity?
We say: no, for its validity is established through the identity of the continuum (*santāna*).
And it has been stated by Pārśvadeva: "The continuum (*santāna*) alone is what must be reached by perception" (*Nyāyapraveśavṛttipañcikā* 77).
He divides perception [as follows]: "That is fourfold," [meaning] "by means of the five sense-faculties, such as the eye."
And their status as the basis [of consciousness] is due to their being the uncommon cause.
Regarding the phrase "having form as its object": that which is transformed (*rūpyate*) is "form" (*rūpa*), which is merely the visible.

Anticipating the objection that since the sense organ is also a cause for the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of form and so forth, one could just as well say it is "based on the object" (*viṣayāśraya*), he says: "of the designation 'sensory direct perception' (*indriyapratyakṣa*). And it has been stated: "Because of its unique causality, it is designated by means of the sense organs (*akṣaiḥ*). Furthermore, this [perception], such as visual perception, which is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatā*) only by way of producing a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) regarding the object manifested by itself;
however, when the conceptual cognition has not yet arisen, it does not possess the status of a valid means of knowledge.
There is no harm in this, for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is defined as that which serves as a constituent factor of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

Even though indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) may occur for one whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been entirely removed, it is not considered a means of valid cognition with respect to that [person], because determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) does not arise for them.
With the intention that the doorkeeper is not established as something other than the door because the door does not arise [without him], he says "And this... and so forth.
Now, he defines mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) with the words "its own object" (*svaviṣaya*).
This definition was stated by Dharmakīrti in the *Nyāyabindu*.
He explains the defining statement with the words "by the word 'own' (*sva*)," and so forth.
For it is logical that the word "own" (*sva*), which constitutes a qualifier, refers to the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
[The phrase] "by the auxiliary" (*sahakāriṇā*) means:

And its "concomitance with the object" (sahāritva) is due to their performing a single function. That is to say, sensory cognition and the second moment of the object— such as a jar— which exists within the continuum of that object and arises immediately after it, both combine to produce mental perception.
Regarding the term "designated as the immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyayasaṃjñaka*):
*pratyaya* means cause (*kāraṇa*).
And it has been said: "Cause (*hetu*), condition (*pratyaya*), motive (*nimitta*), and instrument (*karaṇa*)—these are synonyms."
*Samantaraḥ*: By the prefix *sam*, equality (*samānatva*) is understood; and this equality is in terms of being knowledge (*jñānatvena*).
*Anantaraḥ* means "uninterrupted" (*avyavahita*), that is, having no interval immediately preceding it.

The designation *samanantarapratyaya* (immediately preceding condition) refers to that cognition existing within a single continuum which serves as the cause for a subsequent cognition. And it will be stated: "It is well-known by convention as the appropriation (*upādāna*) existing within one's own continuum.
When the activity of the eye has ceased, the cognition that arises moment by moment is produced by that visual cognition acting in conjunction with an object immediately following its own object.
Thus, it is concluded that this is mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*). Furthermore, regarding its non-utility in linguistic convention (*avyavahāritva*):
this defect—that mental perception, characterized by the aforementioned definition, does not fall within the scope of linguistic usage—does not apply here.
For there is neither over-extension nor non-extension of the definition: when the causal complex is present, it falls within the scope of conventional discourse;
and when it is absent, it does not.
The sense is: "What defect could there be for him on that account?

In response to the doubt—"Why is it accepted as being beyond the scope of empirical usage (*vyavahāra*), i.e., not a constituent part of empirical usage?"—he says: "It is well-known from scripture (*āgama*).
This means that scripture alone is the authority (*pramāṇa*) for its existence.
He shows the very scripture [that supports this] with the words "as it has been said.

Now, one might object with the intention that accepting this [principle], which is in no way useful for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) as found in scripture, is pointless; thus he raises the doubt with "nanu" (but surely).
He refutes this with "īdṛglakṣaṇa" (of such a characteristic).
This is the intended meaning: for a thing cannot be denied merely because it is of no use in worldly transactions;
this [object] is indeed perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣa), though its true nature must be discerned by means of a definition (lakṣaṇa).
And by means of the definition already stated, that perception is distinguished. By this distinction, even the suspicion held by others regarding the impurity of the scripture is refuted.
And the teacher Dharmottara has said: "And this mental perception is established by our own tenets (*siddhānta*)."
"And there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes this;
[the definition was stated] so that one might say, 'If such a thing existed, there would be no fault whatsoever. (Nyāyabinduṭīkā 14)
Now, he defines self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedanapratyakṣa*) with the words beginning "of all minds and mental factors" (*sarvacittacaittānām*).
The meaning is that whatever constitutes the self-cognition of minds and mental factors, that alone is called self-cognition.
He explains this very point with the words beginning "mind" (*cittam*).

"Grasping the mere object" means perception that grasps only the external object, such as blue and so forth. "Mental factors" (caitta) are those which exist in the mind; these are not external, but rather internal sensations and so forth, which are entirely distinct from external objects like blue and the rest.
