The specific distinctions of cognition that grasp the particular states of an object being perceived, such as blue and so forth—characterized by pleasure, pain, or indifference—arise when objects like blue are being directly experienced.
That form in which these [states] are cognized is called self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*).
For this too is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*).
This is what is being stated: at the time of the direct perception of external objects such as blue and so forth, that perception does not remain unmanifested, just like the blue object itself;
likewise, pleasure and so forth are also [not unmanifested].
Therefore, because their manifestation arises by its own very nature, it is called self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) as a form of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

And the teacher Diṅnāga said: "The mind, too—such as [the cognition of] objects, passion, and so forth—is non-conceptual with respect to self-awareness. And the commentary states: "The mind, having perceived forms and so forth, exists in the form of the experience [of them]."
That [cognition] is indeed non-conceptual.
For desire, anger, delusion, pleasure, pain, and so forth, arise without depending on the sense faculties; thus, they are self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*).
(Pramāṇasamuccaya 17)

Now, one might object: by the term *svasaṃvedana*, it is implied that "it is perceived by itself through itself"; yet, within a single action, it is not logically possible for one and the same entity to possess both the status of agent (*kartṛ*) and the status of object (*karman*). With this intention, he raises an objection: "In this regard, some say... [and so on].
This word does not function here by virtue of its etymological derivation from its constituent parts (*avayavārtha*).

However, with the intention that [consciousness] is called "self-aware" (svasaṃvedana) by referring to its nature as a light that does not depend on another light, he provides the resolution beginning with "To this it is said," etc. Regarding the phrase "by way of the relationship between the established and the establisher":
every object, arising through the power of causes, arises with distinct and specific natures; thus, it is precisely the respective cause that establishes the particular nature of each object.
Therefore, the meaning is that there is a specific reason which establishes the intrinsic nature of a thing, and there is a specific intrinsic nature of a thing which is established by that [reason].
He demonstrates the state of having an intrinsic nature of manifestation that is independent of any other illuminator with the words beginning "just as" (*yathā*).
He refutes the Naiyāyika-accepted insentience (*jaḍarūpatā*) of cognition with the words beginning "nor" (*na ca*).

Having raised the dilemma as to whether a cognition is manifested by another cognition existing at the same time or by one existing at a different time, he refutes each in turn, beginning with "not first" (*na tāvat*).
For the relationship between the manifested and the manifester is characterized by the relationship between the beneficiary and the benefactor.
And that [causality] is not possible for two things that exist simultaneously;
for there is no relationship of mutual benefit between the left and right horns of an ox—this is the sense. Nor indeed... [the rest of the sentence].
It is not tenable that cognition is manifested by another cognition arising immediately after it, in the form of a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) such as "I know this.
Since every entity is momentary, that [first] cognition perishes in the second moment; what opportunity, then, is there for its manifestation?
Consequently, cognition alone would be non-luminous in nature.
For the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas), who accept that cognition persists for two moments, establish its status as an object of reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*).

There is no room for their doctrine [of momentariness] here, because we have already established the momentary destruction of all things. This is so provided that cognition is indeed imperceptible (*parokṣa*).

Since this momentary cognition cannot be known by another cognition, and since its self-cognizability is not admitted, it would be imperceptible like a jar or other objects; thus, being of the same nature as external objects such as jars, what is the meaning of this designation "cognition," which is supposedly distinct from objects? The point is that since nothing can manifest this imperceptible thing, by what means could its own nature be characterized?

He brings forward an undesirable consequence (aniṣṭa-prasañjana) by means of the words "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth, [arguing] that if the self-cognizability (*svasaṃvedyatva*) of cognition is not admitted.
The phrase "not unapprehended" (*nāgṛhīta*) means that in a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) is the cause.
Now, there indeed arises the cognition "this is a visible form," and yet the eye is not itself perceived;
nevertheless, even though unperceived, that eye is cognized as a qualifier of the form.
Therefore, the rule that "a cognition of a qualified object does not occur when its qualifier has not been apprehended" is not absolute;

thus, with the intention that it is logical for even unperceived cognition to appear as a qualifier of the object—such that one can say "the object is known"—he raises an objection with the words, "As for what was said...
In the cognition "this is a visual color," the eye does not appear as a qualifier.

Furthermore, visual consciousness—and this would not be possible without the self-cognizability (*svasaṃvedyatva*) of consciousness—is established; thus, with the intention that our own position alone is proven, he replies: "That is incorrect.
The self-cognizability of knowledge does not exist by way of the relationship between object and agent.
However, he concludes this by means of the relationship between the established and the establisher with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
He corroborates his own stated point with the words of an authoritative person (*āpta*) using the phrase "as it has been said.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*), being distinct from—i.e., different in nature from—objects such as blue which are insentient by nature, arises from its own cause as something whose very essence is light. It is indeed of a non-material form.
That which is this non-inert nature of this cognition is precisely the self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvitti*) of this cognition; the meaning is that it is self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*).
And this verse [is] by Śāntarakṣita (*Tattvasaṃgraha* 559), and was commented upon by Kamalaśīla: "For self-awareness is not intended here in the sense of being a subject (*grāhaka*)."
What then?
[It is] "by itself—by its very nature as luminosity, like the light in the expanse of the sky.

But surely, just as a lamp that illuminates other things possesses the nature of self-illumination, so too should cognition, which illuminates external objects such as blue and so forth, possess self-luminosity.
How could that [pleasure] belong to a pleasure that does not manifest an object?
Furthermore, pleasure and the like are distinct from cognition and are manifested by a cognition residing in their own substratum.
To this it is replied: the experience of pleasure occurs at the very same time as the experience of form and other objects.
This being the case, it must be stated by what pleasure is manifested.
One cannot say, "By this very manifestation of form," for how could the manifestation of internal pleasure be possible through this external object of perception?
If it is argued that [the pleasure] is known by another mental cognition (*mānasa-jñāna*), then the established rule that cognitions occur in a temporal succession would be violated.
[Objection: Is it not the case that immediately after the cognition of a blue object, a mental cognition arises by which pleasure is manifested?
However, while there is indeed a fixed order regarding the arising of cognitions, their simultaneous existence is not precluded;
for it is not contradicted by the fact that the experience of pleasure occurs at the very same time as the perception of an external form. No.
Because it is impossible [for pleasure] to exist in that way since all things whatsoever are momentary.
Furthermore, if pleasure were manifested by another cognition—just as blue and other objects are—it would follow that it is perceived as something distinct, like blue and the like.
And this has been explained at length by Śāntarakṣita:
"How indeed can they [the external objects] be partakers of self-cognition if they are non-experiencers of another?
If it is argued that these [objects] become cognizable by a consciousness residing in the same substrate [as the cognition],
then, since the perception of external things proceeds in uninterrupted succession,"
"Why is pleasure and so forth experienced continuously at that time? (Tattvasaṃgraha 396), and so on.
He defines the knowledge of the yogi [with the words] "the real object," etc.
The meaning is that the knowledge produced at the ultimate limit of the intensification of the cultivation of the true object is "yogic knowledge.
He explains the definition-statement beginning with the words "Yoga is... and so forth.
[He comments on] "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder), etc.
Through one-pointedness of mind, wisdom that discerns all principles without exception is accomplished;
that very [wisdom] is expressed by the word "yoga," because the means is metaphorically applied to the end— this is the intended meaning.
"That perception" means the perception arising for that yogin.
He explains the defining statement beginning with "an object as it has been" (bhūtārtha).
Dispelling the misconception that the word *bhūta* refers to a specific time, he explains it as "an object established by valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇopapannārtha*).
What is its cultivation (*bhāvanā*)? What constitutes cultivation?
He said: "It is the repeated mental superimposition.
Its excellence is the stage at which the clarity of the object being cultivated begins;
its culmination is that state which has not yet abandoned its prior condition but is oriented toward clarity.

The teacher Dharmottara illustrates that state by means of an analogy: "When one perceives the object being meditated upon as if it were veiled by mica, that is the state produced at the ultimate limit of excellence" (*Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā* 15).

Therefore, the knowledge born from that ultimate limit of excellence—which consists of a vivid manifestation of the real object like the perception of an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of the hand—that is what is meant by "yogic direct perception."
And since this [perception] is indeed non-conceptual, the definition of perception as "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) is established.
With this in mind, he says: "free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous.
And it was stated by the teacher Diṅnāga: "For yogins, there is the vision of the mere object unmixed [with other factors], due to the instruction of the Guru."
(Pramāṇasamuccaya 17) "Just as the mind is non-conceptual, so too is the knowledge of yogins.
Yoga is meditative concentration (*samādhi*); one who possesses that is a yogin."
In this context, the object is used to indicate the subject.
The word "nirdeśa" (indication) expresses the conceptual nature (*savikalpatva*) of the scripture; thus, the meaning is that it is "unmixed," that is, free from that [conceptuality].
By this, its quality of appearing with vivid clarity (*sphuṭābhatva*) is also understood.

The word *mātra* has the sense of excluding what is superimposed (*āropita-vyavaccheda*); this is explained in the *Ṭīkā*. In this context, he defines the "real object" (*bhūtārtha*) with the words beginning "the real object," etc.
What are the real objects?
And how are they to be cultivated?

That yogic cognition which arises from the ultimate limit of the intensification of such cultivation is what is expressed here by the passage beginning with "the real objects are the four noble truths" and ending with "is to be realized."
The four noble truths are suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Among these, suffering consists of these four great elements, these objects such as form and so forth,
and these sense faculties such as the eye and so forth.
All this is called suffering because it consists of a single mass characterized by the transformation into suffering.
That cause by which its origination occurs is called the origin.
That which is the cessation of this suffering, characterized by the state of nirvāṇa, is called "cessation.
That which is the gateway to cessation, such as right knowledge and so forth, is called the "path.
[The phrase] "having the five aggregates as its intrinsic nature" [is used].
The five aggregates are the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
Because suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are each included within one or another of these, they are said to have the nature of the five aggregates.
However, the distinction between the aggregate of form and the others should be understood from other sources.

To the question, "How can there be a contemplation of the momentariness of everything that is recognized as being 'this very same thing'?", he says: "By the inference that 'whatever exists is momentary'.

This recognition—just like the recognition [of a flame] as "this is that same lamp-flame"—is of the nature of an error because it is sublated by the means of valid cognition known as inference; such is the meaning.
The investigation of this inference should be understood from other sources.

Dispelling misconceptions regarding the subject matter, he says: "Of that," and so forth. He explains that very same statement of his own: "'Of that fourfold [pramāṇa]'—the *lakṣaṇa* (definition) is that by which a thing is characterized; it is the form (*rūpa*) of the object."
That which is the unique form is called "its own" (sva);
it is stated that the unique reality of a thing is its *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic).
He says this very thing: "The *svalakṣaṇa* is the unique nature of the object, determined by place, time, and form."
That universal which is asserted by others to be the object of perception is one whose place, time, and form are not fixed;
the meaning is that such a thing is not the object of perception.
He clarifies this very point with the words "the jar, etc. and so forth.
For the object-domain of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is twofold: the apprehended (grāhya) and the attainable (prāpaṇīya).
That which is the form according to which a cognition arises is the apprehended.

That form by which one determines [an object] is what is to be attained; in that regard, perception arises precisely with the form of the unique particular (svalakṣaṇa), such as a jar, restricted by place, time, and aspect—thus the object of perception is called the unique particular.
Another moment of the jar existing within that continuum is determined by the conceptual determination (adhyavasāya) arising immediately after the perception.
"Indifferent to manifold properties such as impermanence" means that it is not qualified by such properties as impermanence.
"By this" means by the demonstration that only the particular (svalakṣaṇa) is the object of perception.

Among the six categories beginning with substance (*dravya*), he states— thereby clarifying the position held by others that the triad of substance, quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*) constitute a single group through their connection with the universal (*jāti*) "existence" (*sattā*)— that just as a composite substance, a quality, and an action [are related to universals],
the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) is exclusively the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) of the universal and the particular, and not their sub-stratum-ness (*anuyogitā*).
Thus, there is a single category for those two;
however, in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), neither of those two exists, which is its distinction from them. [The phrase] "as intended by others" refers to this.

"By others"—meaning by the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas) and those of Akṣapāda (the Naiyāyikas). Others maintain that [reality] is twofold, divided into the categories of eternal and non-eternal.
In that regard, since eternal substances are refuted precisely by establishing the momentariness of all things, their status as objects of perception is thereby refuted.
Now, he refutes the status of the composite substance (*avayavidravya*) as an object of perception by means of the passage beginning with "tathā hi ghaṭādau" and so forth.

This is the underlying intention: although a gross object such as a jar is indeed perceived, it does not follow that, merely because it is gross, it is a distinct entity consisting of parts (*avayavin*).
Those very atoms, when aggregated, appear as gross objects;
it is not that atoms are by nature invisible.
Furthermore, the claim that atoms are eternal and invisible—based on the principle that "whatever exists is momentary"—is thereby refuted.
That which is perceived as "gross" consists only of parts and only of portions; indeed, no whole (*avayavin*) exists apart from its parts.
When a preceding portion is seen among the divisions such as front and back, the subsequent portion is not seen;
and when the subsequent portion is beyond the range of the eye, there is no determination of blue or other colors at all.

What other distinction could there be [between blue and white] than the doubt itself as to whether it is blue or white? If a composite whole were perceived, the systematic arrangement of parts— both determined and undetermined— would not be possible.
Therefore, a single hair is not perceived; that very same hair is perceived when aggregated.
In this way, these atomic parts are perceived when they are aggregated.
There might be some whole (avayavin) as a part-possessor distinct from its parts.
If this whole were concealed even in part by flies and the like, it would be entirely concealed and thus could not be perceived at all.
Therefore, it is logical that only the parts appear.
Here, he shows the agreement with authoritative tradition, stating: "As the Supreme Lord of Nyāya has said."
In such and such a manner they are situated— that is, they are situated as prior and posterior parts (or situated as the neck and the shell);

apart from these constituent parts, no other possessor of those parts— namely, a "portion-possessor" (*bhāgavān*) or a "division-possessor" (*vibhāga*), which is to say a whole (*avayavin*)— is ever perceived.
For no composite whole called "cloth" is perceived as something distinct from the threads; rather, it is simply the threads themselves that are perceived arranged in such a manner.
The same logic should be applied to the threads as well.
And the refutation of qualities, actions, and so forth should be understood as follows:

this method of refutation is that when a large object such as a jar situated inside a house is being perceived by light passing through a small aperture like a keyhole, blue color is observed in part;
yet for those who maintain that a single whole (avayavin) is partless and inherent in its parts, the perception of even a single part would be impossible.
It would be perceived everywhere.
Likewise, when a mango fruit is being tasted, the sweet flavor perceived in the portion being tasted would be perceived in every part;
yet it is not so.
Therefore, there is no distinction between the quality and the possessor of the quality;
rather, it is firmly established that only parts are perceived. In this same manner, the refutation of other qualities should be understood by following the same logic.
Since all entities perish in a single moment, what possibility is there for action?

The refutation of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth should also be understood from other sources. Now, he begins by dispelling misconceptions regarding the result (*phala*) of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), starting with the words: "But [the result] consisting of the cognized object," and so on.
According to the etymological derivation of the term *pramāṇa* as "that by which something is correctly cognized" (*pramīyate 'nena*),
it is established that a *pramāṇa* is that which serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the act of valid cognition (*pramiti*). Furthermore, it is accepted that this *pramāṇa* is knowledge (*jñāna*).
What is this valid cognition (pramiti), and what is its instrument? Furthermore, what is that distinct knowledge which constitutes the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)?
For the relationship between cause and effect must be established through their distinction.

The intention of the objector is that, since [cognition] is accepted as being a direct means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*), the distinction between the means of valid cognition and its result (*pramāṇa-tatphala*) is difficult to establish. He dispels this doubt with the words beginning "It is said" (*ucyate*).
[He explains: "From the object such as blue, etc. (*nīlāderarthāt*).
The meaning is that the cognition which arises apprehending external objects such as blue arises with two forms.
He states these two forms: "having the form of blue and the nature of the awareness of blue."

Thus, when a single perception possesses a twofold nature, that which is the "blueness" of the cognition— characterized by the exclusion of non-blue forms— is its very validity (*prāmāṇya*); and that which is the "nature of the cognition of blue"— characterized by the exclusion of the cognition of non-blue— is its very form as a result (*phala*).
With the intention of explaining the distinction between the fruit and its result (*phala-phalibheda*), he says "therein" (*tatra*) and so forth.
He states the distilled meaning (*nirgalitārtha*) with the words "the aforementioned object" (*yathoktamartha*) and so forth.

Of this—namely, of the perception (*pratyakṣa*) which has external objects such as blue as its objective support—the aforementioned conformity to the object (*arthasārūpya*) consists in the conformity to blue and so forth, characterized by the exclusion of non-blue forms.
The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is stated [as follows].
As has been said—the comprehension of the object "blue," characterized by the exclusion of what is not blue, is called the result (*phala*). This is the meaning.
Now, one might ask: how can there be a distinction between the result and the means within a single act of perception?
Anticipating the doubt that "this [relationship] is indeed based on the relation between the means and the goal," he says "and this" (*etacca*).
The intention is as follows: the relationship between the fruit and the fruition is not restricted solely to the relation between the means and the goal;
for even in the case of a single entity, that relationship is possible through a difference in its aspects (*ākāra*), even though in reality there is no ontological difference in the thing itself.
Perception, however, is in reality only one.
Nevertheless, it is established as distinct through the differentiation of its aspects, such that "this is the means of valid cognition" and "this is the fruit of the means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, this establishment of the relationship between the fruit and the means of attainment is determined by the conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) arising immediately after the perception.

And the teacher Dharmottara said: "Therefore, by the exclusion of dissimilarity (*asārūpya*), similarity (*sārūpya*) is the cause for establishing the cognition; and by the exclusion of the cognition of non-blue, the nature of being a cognition of blue is to be established.
Furthermore, the conceptualizing consciousness (*vikalpapratyaya*) arising through the force of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) should be understood as the establisher.
(Nyāyabinduṭīkā 19)
Regarding this, Śāntarakṣita says:
"In this context, either the cognition of the object is intended as the fruit of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
or self-awareness is the means of valid cognition, while similarity [to the object] and capacity [are its characteristics]."

Thus it has been explained by Kamalaśīla: "When an external object is the object of cognition (*prameya*), the apprehension of that object is the fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇaphala*), while similarity [to that object] is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
but when cognition itself is the object of cognition, self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is the fruit."

"Yogyatā (capacity) is the means of valid cognition. And in the commentary on the immediately preceding verse: "The cognition having blue as its locus is not [the cognition] of yellow; thus, for the determination of the apprehension of an object, conformity with the object (*arthasārūpya*) alone is the basis, and nothing else. By way of the relationship between that which is determined and that which determines, it is established that "therefore, cognition is indeed endowed with form (*sākāra*); it is not formless (*nirākāra*). And this determination is to be understood through the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) obtained subsequent to that [direct perception]."

This is what must be understood here: the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the conformity (*sārūpya*) with an external object such as blue is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while the comprehension of the object such as blue is the result (*phala*).

The Sautrāntikas maintain that the form deposited in cognition by an external object such as blue is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is the result (*phala*); it is not the appearance of the object itself.
For, according to them, the external object is imperceptible.
For these [cognitions] are proponents of the object as inferable;
rather, that very form of cognition— which, though produced by beginningless latent impressions (*anādivāsanā*), appears as if external—
is itself the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

The Yogācāras maintain that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a cognition is its own form (*svākāra*), which is also called its "subjective capacity" (*grāhakatā-yogyatā*); and self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is the result (*phala*).

These are the proponents of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only). Keeping this difference of opinion in mind, the Master Diṅnāga said: "Because it is perceived as possessing an operation, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed that very result (*phala*)."
The metaphorical designation of "valid cognition" (pramāṇa) does not apply to that which is devoid of activity;
rather, its very objective form is the means of cognition (pramāṇa), because by means of it the object is measured.
Alternatively, self-awareness (svasaṃvitti) is the fruit here, since the determination of the object arises from the [cognition's] possessing that [objective] form.

"That which appears is the object of cognition; that [cognition] is the means of knowledge, and then its fruit is the awareness of the form of the apprehender. Therefore, these three are not made separate."
[This refers to] Pramāṇasamuccaya, verses 9–11.

He cites the words of Dharmakīrti as authority for the point that there is no ontological difference between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), stating: "As it has been said.
Now, one might ask: what is this "conformity" (*sārūpya*) of cognition with the object?
Warding off the doubt that cognition is indeed formless (*nirākāra*), he says: "If, however...
Thus ends the section on perception (*pratyakṣapariccheda*). 61.
The section on inference (*anumānapariccheda*).
Now he analyzes inference: "Inference is of two kinds. [Objection:
But surely, it is improper to divide inference before its general definition has been determined; for it is precisely upon the definition that the desire to know first arises.
True.
When a common characteristic exists, that alone must first be defined; but when it does not exist, only the two specific characteristics need to be defined.

The [inference] for one's own sake consists of cognition, whereas that for the sake of others consists of speech; therefore, since these two are of different natures, a single definition is not applicable to both.
Thus, it is logical to provide a division, stating their definitions only after first distinguishing them.
He explains the term *svārtha* (for one's own sake) as follows: that which is for oneself (*svasmai*) is *svārtha*.
He states the distinction from inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) by saying "consisting of cognition" (*jñānātmaka*).
He establishes its nature as being for one's own sake with the words beginning "on a mountain, etc. (*parvatādau*).
He explains this [term] "for the sake of another" (*parārtha*) as follows: "That which is for the sake of another is inference for the sake of another" (*parārthānumāna*).
He establishes its status as being for the sake of another with the words beginning "having the three characteristics" (*trirūpa*).
To the question, "How can the word *anumāna*, which denotes a specific kind of cognition, be applied to a verbal expression? he replies: "By way of metaphor" (*upacārāt*).

Now, an objection: in one case it is perception that makes known the three-featured logical mark (*liṅga*), while in another it is verbal testimony; how, then, on that basis alone, can there be a twofold division of inference?
If this were so, it would follow that even the visual organ (*cakṣus*) would be an inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
Not so;
a word indicates a logical mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics,
for a word indeed becomes an indicator of an object by means of the speaker's intention (vivakṣā).
The eye, however, directly causes the cognition of the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*);
it is merely indicative, whereas for us, *parārthānumāna* (inference for others) is defined as such.
Thus it has been stated by Śāntarakṣita:
Because it indicates the existence [of the object] through a statement of the three-featured logical mark (liṅga),
that which is called "inference for others" (parārthānumāna) is so designated from the perspective of the listener.
Thus, the status of being an inference is accepted here in a secondary and conventional sense;
because it indicates what is connected [to the object], no over-extension [of the definition] occurs.
(Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā 431). And Kamalaśīla has explained it thus: "That which was stated regarding speech being inference for the sake of others, that is from the perspective of the listener."
Therefore, the fault of not depending on a speaker does not arise.

Furthermore, with respect to the listener, it is called "inference" either figuratively—because it indicates a three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) and is thus a cause of inference—or by convention (*samaya*).

Since the designation "inference" is applied only to that which indicates what is connected [to the probandum], there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), such as the undesirable consequence that the sense organ or the knowledge of the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva-sambandha*) would also be considered inference for others (*parārthānumāna*).
"Because those two lack the capacity to indicate what is connected [to the probandum].
He defines inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) with the words: "Among these, that which is for oneself.
That is to say, inference for oneself is the cognition of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) produced by a mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa*).
What is that cognition of the inferable object which arises from the cognition of the three-featured mark? To this he says: "And that," and "the particularity of the locus" (dharmiviśeṣa).
The specific property of the subject— namely, the thesis— is the ascertainment of the mark's inseparable connection with the probandum; "in the mark" is the ellipsis to be supplied.

The meaning is that for one who perceives a logical mark (*liṅga*) as being connected with similar instances (*sapakṣa*), excluded from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), and connected with the subject (*pakṣa*), there arises a certainty regarding the mark’s inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*) with the property to be proven through a portion of the subject.
Others say this refers to the determination of fire;
that is to say, the certainty that "this is fire" or "this possesses fire."
It has already been stated previously that its object is the universal (*sāmānya*).
In the definition of inference, the three-fold characteristic (*trirūpa*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*) was introduced;
he now defines that introduced three-fold nature with the words beginning "saṃprati" and so forth.
Therein, he states the first characteristic, known as "presence in the subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*): "ascertained existence in the object of inference (*anumeya*) alone.
What is this "object of inference"?
He says: "in a locus (*dharmin*) such as a mountain."
Although the mountain is indeed apprehended through direct perception,
it is nevertheless not a property of fire;
therefore, "this mountain possesses fire" is what is to be inferred by way of its being qualified by fire.
In order to make this known, it was stated that "the mountain is the locus (*dharmin*).

Anticipating the point that even when the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) are present, inference does not arise if they are not ascertained, he says: "ascertained. Regarding the phrase "by the inclusion of the term 'existence' (*sattva*)": [it means] by the mention of *sattva*.
The mark (liṅga) possesses three forms or constituent members for the cognition of the object to be inferred (anumeya): existence in the similar instance (sapakṣa) and so forth.
If it were deficient in even one of these, it would be a fallacious mark (liṅgābhāsa).

In that regard, if the form of "existence in the subject" (pakṣasattva) were not required, there would be the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of [calling] unestablished (asiddha) marks as valid marks; therefore, the sense is that this form is included in order to exclude such cases.
He states the purpose of the particle *eva*— which serves to exclude non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*)— with the words "by the particle *eva*" and so forth.
He provides an example of that which is unestablished with respect to a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*), namely, "as in the Digambara's syllogism," [stating] "not in all trees."
This sleep, characterized by the closing of leaves, which has been pointed out as the reason,
does not exist in all trees;
for some indeed have their leaves uncontracted day and night.
By this [reason], the consciousness intended to be established in all trees would not be proven;

therefore, it would be unestablished with respect to a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*). If the particle *eva* were not used, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since sleep—the state intended [as the reason]—exists in some tree.
The point is that by means of the particle *eva*, the non-existence [of the reason] in the subject is excluded, and thus there is no over-extension.
He states the purpose of the term "ascertained" (*niścita*) with the words: "by the inclusion of the word 'ascertained'.
This is the underlying intention: suppose there is smoke on a mountain, and as one observes it, a doubt arises as to whether it is smoke or vapor.

In that case, this aggregate of elements, being suspected of being smoke and so forth, would be a "doubtful-unestablished" (sandigdhāsiddha) reason; or rather, it would be the vapor itself that is suspected of being such.
The point is that since the presence [of the reason] in the subject (pakṣasattva) would be known only through doubt, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
This is what must be understood here: a logical mark (liṅga) must possess three characteristics; if even one characteristic is lacking, it is indeed a non-existent mark.
If there is error regarding the aspect of the threefold nature, the cognition produced by that is not inference, but merely an error.
If there were no doubt regarding the three aspects [of the reason], inference would not occur at all;
for a logical mark (*liṅga*) is not capable of producing cognition by its mere existence, as is the case with the sense organs.
This being so, what is the point of investigating the definition of the logical mark or investigating the inclusion of the term "certainty" (*niścaya*)?
"Only after the word 'sattva' [is used] is the particle 'eva' [employed].

This is the intended meaning: if the nature of the logical mark (*liṅga*) were stated as "existence only in that which is to be inferred," it would be excluded from anything other than the subject (*pakṣa*).
If that were the case, the other characteristic—presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*)—would be contradicted;

and if that were so, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of [the definition] to the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason, which is excluded from both similar and dissimilar instances and resides only in the subject (*pakṣa*).
Now, he defines the second characteristic with the words beginning "only in the similar instances" (*sapakṣa eva*).
"It continues" means "and it continues in this way"— the sense is that this second form of the indicative (liṅga) also exists. In that context,
[the phrase] "by the mention of existence" [is used].
If the second form [of the reason] were not apprehended, then that very form would be abandoned;

such being the case, there would be the over-extension [of the definition] to the contradictory [reason], namely: "Sound is eternal because it is produced," for the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) indeed exists in the subject, sound.

Although the third characteristic—namely, its non-existence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)—is not contradictory and thus offers no occasion for over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), this purpose was stated with the intention that this particular form has not yet been explicitly mentioned. However, that [non-existence in the dissimilar instance] is actually understood through the second characteristic: "existence only in the similar instance" (*sapakṣa*).

When the absence [of the reason] in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) has already been established, the purpose of stating its presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) is to exclude it from what is not common (*asādhāraṇa*).

In the case of "Sound is eternal because it is audible," the property of audibility—which resides only in the subject (*pakṣa*)—is excluded from the similar instances just as it is from the dissimilar instances. By the word "only" (*eva*) placed before "presence" (*sattva*), the meaning is that one does not say "presence only in the similar instances," but rather says "presence only in the similar instances" (*sapakṣa eva sattvam*). Thus, it excludes the possibility of its being present elsewhere.
If it were stated that "it exists only [in the subject]," then by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), existence in all similar instances (*sapakṣa*) would be intended;
and this being the case, the proof of impermanence in sound by means of the mark (*liṅga*) of being produced immediately after an effort would be contradicted.
For whatever is produced immediately after an effort is observed to be impermanent, such as a jar and so forth.

For even if lightning and the like are ascertained to be impermanent, its status as a prover of impermanence is not lost merely because it lacks "being produced immediately after an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*).

However, if the particle *eva* is understood in the sense of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*)—meaning "existence only in similar instances" (*sapakṣeṣu sattvam eva*)—then its status as a logical reason (*hetutva*) is lost due to the absence of "being produced immediately after an effort" in lightning and the like. This is the intended meaning.
[The phrase] "not like lightning" (*na vidyudvat*) [expresses this].
The meaning is that jars and the like are to be understood as the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) in which this mark exists, whereas lightning and the like are not.
Now he states the third characteristic: "and in the dissimilar instance" (*asapakṣe ca*).
Regarding the phrase "by the inclusion of non-existence":
this is the intended meaning— since non-existence in the counter-example (vipakṣa) is already ascertained, if "non-existence" were not explicitly mentioned in this third characteristic,
it would mean "ascertained in the dissimilar instance" (asapakṣa).
That being the case, since this is the nature of the contradictory, how could it possibly be the nature of a logical mark (*liṅga*)?
By this [it is shown that]— how could there be the application of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the definition of a logical mark to that which is contradictory?
The doubt that the second form [of the reason], namely its existence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), is absent, is thereby refuted.
By the word "only" (*eva*), the term "of the common [reason]" (*sādhāraṇasya*) is implied;

the remainder is "of that which exists in a portion of the dissimilar class" (*vipakṣaikadeśavṛtteḥ*). When smoke is the probandum (*sādhya*) and fire is the reason (*hetu*), in the case of a common reason, there is existence in the subject (*pakṣa*) and existence in the similar class, such as a kitchen (*mahānasa*).
Furthermore, since all three characteristics would exist even if [the reason] were absent in some lake—which serves as a dissimilar instance (vipakṣa)—there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

However, by including the particle "eva" (only), one obtains the exclusion of non-connection (ayogavyavaccheda); thus, because one obtains the exclusion from *all* dissimilar instances, there is no over-extension, since fire does exist in a red-hot iron ball, which is a dissimilar instance.
[Objection: But was it not stated that the second characteristic consists of the inclusion of the restriction "existence only in the similar instance" (sapakṣa eva sattvam)?
And that [reason] would not exist in a common locus;
how, then, could there be occasion for an over-extension? No;
rather, the third characteristic has as its very purpose the restriction (avadhāraṇa) included within the second characteristic.
That very [definition] is now being examined; however, it should be understood that the second form consists precisely of the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (*niścita*).
He states the purpose of including the term "ascertained": "by the inclusion of the term 'ascertained'... and so forth.

Someone refutes by means of a formal argument (prayoga) a proponent who says, "Even one who is free from passion speaks this for the sake of the world's welfare," as follows: "This person is not free from passion, because he is a speaker, like a man on the street.
And this reason (hetu) is inconclusive due to doubt (sandigdhānaikāntika), for there remains the doubt: "Why might even one free from passion not speak?"

When the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is being established by means of the example of a stone fragment— that "whoever is not free from passion is not a speaker"— a doubt arises as to whether the speakerlessness of the stone fragment is caused by its being free from passion or is due to its own nature.
Therefore, since its absence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is not certain, this reason is inconclusive due to doubt (*sandigdhānaikāntika*).
The intention is that the word "ascertained" (*niścita*) is used to exclude this [fallacy].
By means of the particle "only" (*eva*), [the text] excludes those [reasons] that reside in only a portion of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), and so forth.

Furthermore, this sentence ought to have been placed precisely at the point "by the particle 'only,' [it excludes] the common (*sādhāraṇa*"), prior to the phrase "by the inclusion of the term 'ascertained'."

But here—the purpose of the particle *eva* must be stated, [namely] why it was not adopted [in the definition] as "non-existence only in the non-concordant instances (*asapakṣa eva asattvam*") prior to the mention of "non-existence" (*asattva*).

And this has been illustrated by the teacher Dharmottara: "If the restriction were placed before the word 'non-existence,' the meaning would be this: 'That which does not exist only in the discordant instances (*vipakṣa*) is the logical reason (*hetu*').
And in that case, the property of 'being immediately subsequent to effort' (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) would not exist even in all concordant instances (*sapakṣa*)."
Consequently, it would not be a cause;
therefore, it could not have been produced previously.
(Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā 23)
He raises an objection with "But surely" (*nanu*).
He refutes it with "No," beginning with "the ancient masters of old" (*pūrvavṛddhāḥ*), and so forth.

This is the underlying intention: opponents (*vipakṣa*) are of three kinds—those that possess the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavat*), those other than the locus of the probandum (*sādhyavadanya*), and those that are contradictory to the probandum (*sādhyaviruddha*).
In accordance with that, the determination of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) also occurs in three ways:
"where there is no fire, there is no smoke"; "whatever is without fire is without smoke"; and "where there is water, which is the opposite of fire."

"There is no smoke there. The intention is that [the word "only"] is used again to indicate the restriction to one of these three types. Alternatively, the restriction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the reason (*hetu*) exists only between those things that are related.
And the relationship is either identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from that (*tadutpatti*).
Where there is origination from that— as in the case of smoke [originating] from fire—
the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) arises through non-existence, such that where there is no fire, there is no smoke.
But where there is identity—as in the case of the *śiṃśapā* tree having identity with "tree"—there, by way of distinction, that which is not a tree is not a *śiṃśapā*.
In the statement "this place is hot because of fire," the opposite side (*vipakṣa*) is the cold place, which is contrary to heat;
whereas that which is hot possesses fire.
However, that which is cold does not possess that [fire], as it is characterized by coldness, which is its opposite.

The intention is that the third type is mentioned separately to clarify the distinction that, among these various counter-examples (vipakṣa), the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is to be understood according to what is appropriate.

"Some say it is for the purpose of restricting the formal application" means that in the formal application (*prayoga*) of an inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), it is for the sake of a restriction;

the intention is to make known that, just like the form of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the form of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) must also be employed: "Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire; whatever is without fire is without smoke."

Alternatively, the intention is that when a formal argument (*prayoga*) is to be made, it is for the purpose of making known the necessary rule (*niyama*): namely, that in a formal argument, only a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that possesses such a rule should be employed, not one devoid of it.
Otherwise, even the following argument would be valid: "This [person] is dark-complexioned because he is his son;
for whoever is his son is dark-complexioned, like another son."
For it is possible to employ positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) in the form: "He who is not dark-skinned is not his son.

However, there is no necessary connection whatsoever between being dark-skinned and being his son, such that there could be either a relationship of the produced and the producer (prayojya-prayojaka-bhāva) or identity (tādātmya) between the two.
The meaning is that positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) must be employed only when there is a necessary restriction;
however, once such a restriction exists, the employment of either one of the two is sufficient,
and it is stated separately to indicate that both are not required.
The teacher Dharmottara says this, beginning with "That is stated," and so forth (*Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā* 24).
He analyzes the logical mark (*liṅga*) by stating, "And those which possess the three characteristics."
The meaning is that the logical marks (*liṅga*), characterized by the definition of the three forms (*trairūpya*), are of three kinds.
He explains the term "possessing the three forms" (*trirūpāṇi*) as: "those which have three forms.
He states the distinction between the types [of these marks] with the words beginning "non-perception" (*anupalabdhi*).
He states synonymous terms for "marks" (liṅga) with the words beginning "the means" (sādhana).

For the sake of easy comprehension and because they are well-known, he defines those three by way of their application, following a sequence that deviates from the order of classification—beginning with "therein, the effect" (kārya).
He demonstrates the mark as an effect with the statement: "where there is smoke, there is fire."
For smoke is the effect of fire; therefore, this is called a "reason based on an effect" (kāryaliṅga), since an effect serves as the indicator of its cause.

Regarding inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), he states here, by way of a relevant digression (*prasaṅga*), the determination of the division of the members of the syllogism (*nyāyāvayava*): "There are only two, known as pervasion (*vyāpti*) and property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
Here, while refuting the position of others, he restates it with the words "But others... and so forth.
He refutes it with the words "And this is incorrect... and so forth.
This is the intention: this proposition (*pratijñā*) is useless, for the proposition is not a constituent part of the proof (*sādhana*).
If it is argued that it is required for the sake of making known the probandum (*sādhya*) which one intends to prove, [we reply: no.
How could a word express that which is unrelated?
For there is no relationship between a word and its object;
the absence of such a relationship was established previously during the refutation of verbal testimony (*śabdapramāṇa*).
But surely, the word conveys the speaker's intention;
therefore, because it is indirectly a cause for the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*), the proposition (*pratijñā*) is a constituent part of the proof (*sādhana*).
Or else, even so, it is not a constituent part at all.
For it does not indicate that [the probandum] is unattached;
nor is the initial awakening of the desire to prove it necessarily required.
Therefore, because it indicates what is unattached, the thesis (*pratijñā*) is not a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the inference.

Because inference is established by the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) alone. If it is argued that, just as the phrase "in the kitchen" is employed as an example even though it is not a formal member [of the syllogism], so too the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) should be employed at the outset of the formulation in order to make known what is intended to be proven—[we reply: if this were the case, one would be urging either the proponent (*vādin*) or the opponent (*prativādin*) toward the mere description of the formal formulation.
The speech of the instigator, such as "Prove the impermanence of sound" or "I shall prove its permanence," would likewise be [invalid].
Regarding this, Śāntarakṣita said:
"It is described by others that the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth constitutes inference for the sake of another (*parārtha*);
however, because it does not constitute a member of the proof (*sādhana*), the proposition is useless."
For that [cognition] is not directly capable of establishing the object when it is unconnected;
nor is it appropriate [to do so] indirectly, because it does not indicate what is unrelated.

If this [statement] is accepted as a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) because it possesses the status of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) by way of demonstrating the subject (*viṣaya*) characterized by the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*).
"But surely, there is a deviation here due to statements such as 'permission';
and in that case, the presentation of the subject matter would be fruitless."

(Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā - 418). Having established that the members [of a syllogism] are not auxiliary parts of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and thus useless, he asks: "What is the use of employing a reason ending in the fifth case? and answers: "Without the proposition," etc. He states that the conclusion (*nigamana*) is also not an auxiliary part of the members by saying: "Where the proposition itself does not exist," and so forth.

In this regard, the following should be understood: no additional meaning is established by the conclusion (*nigamana*) beyond what is already established by the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*).
Therefore, for those who accept that the conclusion is merely a restatement of the proposition, it results in the fault of redundancy (*punarukta*).
Thus, the Master Diṅnāga stated: "The conclusion is not a means of proof precisely because it is redundant."
Now, is it not the case that the conclusion (*nigamana*) has a specific purpose?
For the proposition (*pratijñā*) is merely the statement of what is to be proven;

by means of this [conclusion], those meanings expressed through the proposition, the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), and the application (*upanaya*) are brought together as a single coherent statement.
If it is argued that for this very reason the conclusion (*nigamana*) is stated, and by means of it the suspicion of sublation (*abādhitatva*) is dispelled—

this is not so. For there is no room for such a suspicion at all, since the probandum (*sādhya*) is ascertained in the subject (*pakṣa*) by the two statements of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and presence-in-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) alone.
For even by those two [means], a doubt that is not being excluded would not be warded off by this [third one].
Thus, this speculative construction is fitting only within one's own circle.
And it has been said by Śāntarakṣita:

"Since the proof is established by the very power of the statement of the three-featured reason, there is no possibility of doubt regarding its opposite; therefore, the statement of the conclusion is useless. (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, verse 421)
"Fire and so forth being the probandum" means that when fire and so forth are the probandum, smoke and so forth must be perceptible; that is to say,
smoke is perceived only when fire exists.
If it were not seen when [the cause] is absent—
namely, if smoke were not the effect of fire—
it would be perceived even in the absence of fire.
It is not perceived; therefore, the meaning is that it is determined through perception and non-perception that smoke is the effect of fire.
[The phrase] "in the case of the eye and so forth" refers to the probandum (*sādhya*).

The point is that because the eye and other [senses] are imperceptible, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*anupalambha*) are impossible; therefore, the fact that the cognition of color and so forth is an effect of the eye and other [senses] is determined by its occasional nature (*kādācitkatva*).
Now, one might object: "A necessary rule (*niyama*) applies only to things that are related, not to things that are unrelated."
Furthermore, there is no relation other than identity (*tādātmya*) and origination (*tadutpatti*);
therefore, a cause would be inferred through its effect,
or the essence of that [cause] would be inferred through its own nature characterized by identity.
Now, as to how the inference of form (rūpa) occurs from taste (rasa)—
for there is no causal relationship between the two,

nor is taste identical to form— this objection raised by others is answered as follows: the inference of form through taste occurs because both are dependent upon the same causal complex (ekasāmagryadhīnatvena).
He illustrates this with the words "form and so forth," etc.
He establishes the dependence upon a single causal complex with the words "here," etc.
Regarding the term "preceding":
The meaning is "immediately preceded.
That is to say, the production of each subsequent form from each preceding form;
that is, the production of a subsequent aggregate from a preceding aggregate.

This is the intended meaning: the relationship of part and whole (avayavāvayibhāva) as accepted by the followers of Kaṇāda and others is not approved by the Buddhists; nor is it the case that the form of the parts is the cause of the form of the whole, or the taste of the parts is the cause of the taste of the whole.
Nor, again, is there a distinction between the quality (rūpa) and the possessor of the quality (rūpin).
However—the production of a subsequent aggregate characterized by form and so forth from a preceding aggregate characterized by form and so forth;
in that case, the status of being "preceding" relative to the subsequent form is equally applicable to taste as well.
Nevertheless, the subsequent forms constitute precisely a continuum (*saṃtāna*) of the preceding forms.
Likewise, tastes possess an infinite continuity of taste;
and thus, with respect to its own continuum, the subsequent [moment] is itself the material cause (*upādāna*).
In that aggregate characterized by the continuum of form, the preceding taste is held to be the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*), because of the experience of taste in the subsequent aggregate.
Thus, in the continuum of taste, the preceding form is the auxiliary cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*).

This being so, the causal complex of form is constituted by taste, and the causal complex of taste is constituted by form; however, in terms of their status as material cause (*upādāna*) and efficient cause (*nimitta*), there is a reversal.
When that taste is perceived, its form—which is to be established by that same causal complex—would necessarily be inferred.
Now, he defines the essential nature (*svabhāva*) as a logical mark (*liṅga*) with the words beginning "essential nature" (*svabhāva*).
In the phrase "occurring merely through its own existence," "its own" (*sva*) refers to the reason (*hetu*).
That which has the nature of existing by virtue of the very existence of its cause is "that which exists merely through its own existence" (*svasattāmātrabhāvī*);
when that is the probandum (*sādhya*), the reason (*hetu*) is called its "essential nature" (*svabhāva*).
For example, the existence of a tree depends precisely upon the existence of a *śiṃśapā* tree.

The tree does not depend on anything other than that for its existence in its own abode; it exists by virtue of its own mere presence. The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: when that [existence] is to be proven, its own nature (svabhāva) is called the reason (hetu).
He provides an illustration with the words "for example" (*yathā*) and so forth.
He raises an objection with "but surely" (*nanu*).
"In unity" (*ekatve*) means "in non-difference" (*abheda*).

"Because it is a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*)": that is, because the object intended as the subject of the proposition— the tree— is [the locus] of the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
"Because it is a part of that"—the meaning is "because it is one of those [trees].

This is the intended sense: for the means of proof (*sādhana*) must indeed be cognized; and if the *śiṃśupā* tree, which is intended as the means of proof, is cognized as characterized by its specific configuration of leaves, branches, and so forth, [then the object is established].
[Objection: "Since that tree is already understood as established, how can it be something to be proven? [Response: He refutes this, saying "no.
This means that the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is employed for the sake of one who is deluded.

And the teacher Dharmottara says: "In a region abounding in *śiṃśapā* trees, a dull-witted person who is unacquainted with the linguistic usage of the term 'śiṃśapā' is shown a tall *śiṃśapā* by someone and told, 'This is a tree.
Then, due to his dullness, he determines that even the height of the *śiṃśapā* is the basis for the linguistic application of the term 'tree.
Consequently, whenever he sees a *śiṃśapā* that is not tall, he determines that very tree to be a non-tree."
"Then that deluded person is led to apply the conventional designation 'tree' solely on the basis of the specific characteristic of being a *śiṃśupā* tree.
(Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā 28).
He defines non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) as a logical mark (*liṅga*), stating: "Non-apprehension is, for example..."
"Of that which has reached the conditions for perception":
perception is cognition;
its "condition" (lakṣaṇa) is the causal complex (sāmagrī).
In that context, "attained" means having entered into the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) by way of being a producer;
that is to say, it is "perceptible."
The object, too, is included within the causal complex (sāmagrī) of cognition.
He raises an objection with "But surely" (nanu).
"Dṛśyatā" means the state of being within the range of the act of seeing (dṛśi-gocaratā).
What is intended here is not the actual state of being within the range of vision,
but rather the very fact of being capable of being conceived as being within the range of vision.

With the intention that this alone is what is called "having reached the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), he provides the resolution with the words beginning "by a single sense-organ," and so forth.
The jar and its locus, the spot of ground, are both perceivable by a single sense organ;
therefore, when the jar is present, that spot should also be perceived along with its locus.
If it is not perceived, then even though it is capable of being seen, it does not come within the range of vision; this very non-perception is called "non-apprehension" (anupalabdhi).
The meaning is that this very non-perception serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*) for the absence of a jar.
Regarding the phrase "by other conditions for perception" (*upalambha-pratyayāntara*):
*pratyaya* means cause.
Regarding the other conditions for apprehension—namely, the causes such as the sense faculties and so forth, which are distinct from the objective support—it is due to their completeness.
He states the intended meaning by the term "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) with the words beginning with "and that" (*sa ca*), etc.
And that—namely, the cause denoted by the term "non-apprehension."
Regarding the phrase "in the sense of being cast":

"associated with a single cognition" means that the two things— the locus and the object residing therein— which are capable of being directed toward by the sense organ, are called "associated with a single cognition" when they are mutually dependent.
The meaning is that among those two, whichever one is the single object— a particular location— is perceived alone; that is, [the cognition arises] from the perception of that [location].
Regarding the phrase "by way of the relationship between action and agent": the secluded place, serving as the objective support (*ālambana*), is called the "action" (*karman*);
the perception (*upalambha*) is called the "agent" (*kartṛ*) because it illuminates that [place].

The point is that both of these are intended here by the term "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*). He states its lack of probative force if it were intended merely as the cessation of apprehension with the words beginning with "but not... (*na tu*);
for that [cessation] is itself... [as follows].
The meaning is that the mere absence of knowledge certainly exists when the causal complex for knowledge is absent.
"Nothing" means "incapable of producing any effect."

He states that by resorting to the function of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the cognition of any other thing whatsoever should not be accepted as the meaning of the word "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*), saying: "Nor... (*nāpi*).
He concludes the meaning of the word "non-apprehension" with: "Therefore... (*tasmāt*).
[The phrase] "only the qualified" (*viśiṣṭameva*)...
The meaning is "excluded from others"— that is, a specific, distinct location and the specific cognition thereof; the sense is not that it refers to just any location or any random cognition.

And it has been stated by the teacher Dharmottara: "Therefore, that very spot devoid of the jar, as well as the cognition having that as its object, is called 'non-apprehension of the perceptible,' because it is the cause for the ascertainment of the non-apprehension of the perceptible" (Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā 26).

This non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the absence itself, but rather for the linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) regarding absence; thus he says, "For this very reason," and so forth.

When absence is cognized through perception, the corresponding linguistic convention would also arise from that very same [perception]; so why would there be any need for a further means of proof (*sādhana*) for it?
Regarding this, he says: "In response to the fool," and so forth.

He establishes the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*), which is non-apprehension, and the probandum (*sādhya*), which is the fitness for the conventional usage of non-existence, by means of the passage beginning with "of non-perception" (*anupalambhasya*).
The phrase "the position that [non-apprehension] is a property of the object" (*karmadharmapakṣa*) refers to this.

In the context of analyzing the meaning of the term "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), it was stated that the specific empty place is the object of apprehension, while the cognition of it—which illuminates it—is the agent; thus, both constitute the referent of the word "non-apprehension.

With this distinction in mind, he establishes the relationship of identity (*svabhāva*) when non-apprehension is treated as a property of the object, and the relationship of being an effect (*kāryatva*) when it is treated as a property of the agent—beginning with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*).
He states: "But the cognition is the effect of the place."
Because the object of cognition is the cause of knowledge.
[The opponent] raises a doubt: "But surely... [The author] refutes it: "There is a distinction because of the means of proof for the negation."
Here he provides corroboration from an authoritative source, stating "as it has been said.
This refers to the Master Dharmakīrti.
He states the purpose of the phrase "of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility" as follows: "perceptibility," etc.

The meaning is this: whatever is remote in terms of space, time, or intrinsic nature is indeed not "attained by the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*); therefore, there can be no apprehension of its absence, because the aforementioned non-perception is lacking.
And this non-perception is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) not only in the present time, but also at times in the past.

He states that in the future time, however, this is certainly not a means of valid cognition, using the words beginning with "And this... and so forth. As for what he says—"the proponent of logic"—this statement, from "of one whose memory-impressions are unconfused" up to "establishing," was spoken by the teacher Dharmakīrti in the *Nyāyabindu*.

(Nyāya-vārttika 1.1.4, p. 105) This is its meaning: that object, such as a jar, in which there exists an unimpaired—that is, unfallen—latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that generates memory is "one in which the latent impression for memory is unimpaired.
Of such a past [object], and likewise of a present one, which is perceptible to the cognizer—the object, such as a jar, that is directly perceived by the cognizer.
"The cessation of that [perception] is non-apprehension, which establishes the conventional usage of non-existence.
This statement is explained in detail in the *Nyāyabinduṭīkā* (Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā, p. 33).
He defines the different types of non-apprehension with the words beginning "In that regard," and so forth.
In this context, "here" is the indication of the locus (*dharmin*).

"There is no smoke" is the indication of the probandum (*sādhya*). Since non-apprehension of intrinsic nature consists in the apprehension of a distinct location and the apprehension of that [absence], the absence itself is apprehended precisely through the apprehension of the location; thus, there is no lack of provability regarding the absence.
Rather, it is precisely the state of being fit for the conventional usage of "non-existence" [that is established].
And this has been stated previously:
in other cases, such as the non-perception of an effect and so forth, it is non-existence and its conventional usage that are the objects to be proven. 1.
"Non-perception of the effect is as follows": the meaning is that it is the non-perception of that which is the effect of the object to be negated.
"Due to the absence of smoke," and so forth.

Even though non-existence is a logical mark (*liṅga*), nevertheless, that absence of an effect is accessible through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*); thus it has been analyzed among the specific types of non-apprehension.
All these [reasons], beginning with the non-apprehension of the effect, are capable of being subsumed under the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) alone.
Nevertheless, this elaboration arises from the variety of applications;
and he himself will state this with the words "these," and so forth.
It is simply that there is a distinction based on the difference in the manner of application.
Wherever there is an impossibility of perceiving the perceptible, it is precisely there that the non-perception of the effect must be relied upon as a reason;
otherwise, the [effect] would be established from that very [perceptible object] itself.
And in this case, because the cause of the smoke is obstructed and thus imperceptible, the non-perception of the effect serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*).
Even when a cause exists, the non-perception of its effect may occur due to the force of a continuous series;
therefore, it was stated that [the causes] possess unimpeded capacity (apratibaddhasāmarthya). 2.
As for the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*), it is as follows:

The non-perception of fire, which is the cause of the smoke to be negated, establishes this: "There is no smoke here because of the absence of fire. Now, one might object: if fire were visible, the smoke produced by it would certainly be visible as well; therefore, if that [fire] is not perceived, the other [smoke] is not either. Since the absence of smoke can be ascertained through the very non-perception of what is perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*), why is there the necessity of establishing it [through the non-perception of the cause]?

It is said: at the time of dawn when the darkness is very thin, a person who is in doubt as to whether it is smoke—having observed vapor spreading all around the cold water in a lake during the winter season—and not seeing a fire, determines it by means of inference due to the non-perception of its cause;
for fire, being of the nature of combustion, would certainly be perceived if it were present.

The absence [of the object] due to non-perception is understood through direct perception (pratyakṣa). (3) He provides an illustration of the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi): "The non-perception of the pervader is as follows.
This means the non-perception of that which is the pervader of the object to be negated.

And this non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*) for establishing the absence of a *śiṃśapā* tree for one who has cognized the universal of "tree" but has not cognized the particularity of the *śiṃśapā*.
However, for one who has cognized the particularity of the *śiṃśapā*, its absence is established by the very non-apprehension of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*). 4.
As for the apprehension of what is incompatible with the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*), it is as follows:
The meaning is: the perception of that which is contradictory to the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the object to be negated.
Now, one might ask: how can perception be a specific variety of non-perception?
It is said:
it is not the perception of just anything, but rather the perception of that which possesses a nature contrary to the nature of the object to be negated.
Through the negative particle (*nañ*), just as non-existence is understood, so too is contradiction (*virodha*).
And the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*) is established when there is the perception of a location devoid [of the object], by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa-vṛtti*);
the same applies to the perception of a contradictory nature.
And this is a perception of the contradictory [to cold] when the cold is not in contact [with the senses];
however, when it is in contact, it is simply the non-perception of the perceptible.
Fire, even from a distance, becomes perceptible due to the manifestation of its specific color.
But touch, due to its being obstructed, is not suitable for visual perception.
(5) "The perception of what is incompatible with the effect" means: the perception of that which is incompatible with the effect of the thing to be negated.
It is precisely that which has reached its final stage.
Since all things are momentary, not everything within the causal series of preceding moments possesses the capacity to produce the effect;

for if that were the case, it would follow that the effect would be produced at every preceding moment. Therefore, within the causal series consisting of preceding moments, that which consists of the final moment—namely, the moment immediately preceding the effect—is [the one capable of producing it].
The intention is that this very [cause] possesses unobstructed capacity. (6) Regarding "the perception of what is incompatible with the cause":
the meaning is the perception of that which is incompatible with the cause of the object to be negated.
By the words "not his," etc.:
"his" refers to a particular person as the subject (*dharmin*).
The absence of specific qualities such as horripilation and so forth is the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
The term "and so forth" (ādi) should be understood to include Dantavīṇa and others;
the reason (*hetu*) is "because of being a particular fire in close proximity. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has a particular fire in close proximity."
The word "viśeṣa" (specific) refers to what is abundant; by its inclusion, there is the exclusion of very small things such as lamps and the like, which do not oppose cold.
This application occurs when a person sees both a man and a fire from a distance.
For at that time, neither the bristling of the hair and so forth nor the cold is perceptible;
rather, the absence of the effect is inferred solely from the perception of something contrary to its cause.

However, when a person is present, since specific effects such as horripilation—which are capable of being perceived—are not perceived, their absence would be established by the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) alone.
Likewise, since cold, which is capable of being perceived, is not perceived, its [the fire's] establishment would occur through the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) alone.
(7) As for "the perception of that which is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*): this refers to that which is the pervader of the object to be negated.
The meaning is: "the perception of that which is incompatible with it.
He provides an example: "There is no sensation of frost here, because of fire.
When the sensation of frost is neither perceptible nor cold, this becomes a valid reason (hetu) due to the perception of fire alone.
Otherwise, however, there would be either the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) or the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

As for "the perception of the effect of that which is contradictory to the essential nature" (*svabhāvaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*): the meaning is the perception of the effect of that which is contradictory to the essential nature of the object to be negated.
He provides an example: "There is no sensation of frost here because of smoke.

For one who perceives merely smoke from a distance on the locus (*dharmin*), this serves as the reason for the cognition of the absence of the sensation of frost. However, when a thing's own nature (*svabhāva*) is capable of being perceived but is not perceived, its negation is established by the non-perception of its own nature alone; and when something contradictory to it is perceived, the negation is established precisely through the perception of that which is contradictory (*viruddhopalambha*).

It would be established. 9. Regarding "the perception of what is incompatible with the effect": the meaning is the perception of that which is the effect of something incompatible with the effect of the object to be negated.
He provides an example: "not here. This is the reason when neither the causes of cold, nor its effect—coldness—nor that which is opposed to it—fire—is capable of being perceived.

Otherwise, however, if the essential nature were capable of perception yet remained unperceived, the negation would be established by the non-perception of the essential nature itself (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
When an effect is capable of being perceived but is not perceived, its negation is established precisely through the non-perception of that effect.
However, when something contrary to the effect is perceived, its negation is established precisely through the perception of what is contrary to the effect.
(10) An example of the perception of an effect contrary to the cause is as follows.
The meaning is: from the perception of that which is the effect of what is contradictory to the cause of that which is to be negated. He provides an example: "not [due to] horripilation and so forth.
This reason functions when the thing to be negated—such as horripilation and so forth—and its cause, or something contradictory to that cause, are incapable of being perceived.
