Otherwise, however—when the essential nature (*svabhāva*) or the cause (*kāraṇa*), which are capable of being perceived, are not perceived, then negation would be established either by the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) or by the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*); or, when something contrary to the cause is perceived, negation would be established by the perception of what is contrary to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalambha*). || 11 ||

"Perception of the effect of that which is contradictory to the pervader" (vyāpakaviruddhakāryopalabdhi) means: the perception of that which is the effect of something contradictory to that which is the pervader of the object to be negated.
He provides an example: "Not here... [and so forth].

For one who perceives only smoke from afar, the inference that serves to negate it—namely, "there is no touch of frost here"—would be either a non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), or a perception of what is contradictory to the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). This is because the touch of frost, as well as its pervader, cold, would be unperceivable if they were present and perceptible, whereas fire, which is contradictory to them, is actually being perceived. 12.
"Perception of what is pervaded by that which is contradictory to the intrinsic nature [of the object to be negated]" means:
the perception of that which is pervaded by whatever is contradictory to the intrinsic nature of that which is to be negated.
He provides an example: "Not here," etc.
The mere experience of the touch of frost is the mark (liṅga) for the negation of fire.
Otherwise, if the nature [of the object] were capable of being perceived but was not perceived, it would be a non-perception of the nature (svabhāvānupalabdhi).
However, when coldness is being perceived, it would be the perception of something incompatible with the nature (svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi). 13.
"Perception of that which is pervaded by what is incompatible with the effect [of the negandum]" means:
the perception of that which is pervaded by something that is incompatible with the effect of that which is to be negated.
He provides an example: "Not here," etc.
When the cause of fire is capable of being perceived but is not perceived, there would be non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

When the effect, fire, is capable of being perceived but is not perceived, there would be non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*). However, when its opposite, cold, is actually perceived, the perception of what is incompatible with the effect (*kāryaviruddhopalabdhi*) alone would be the logical mark (*liṅga*).

Since only frost, which is pervaded by cold, is experienced, this is the logical mark consisting in the perception of what is pervaded by that which is incompatible with the effect (*kāryaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). 14.
"Perception of that which is pervaded by what is contradictory to the cause" means:
the perception of that which is pervaded by what is contradictory to the cause of that which is to be negated.
He provides an example: "There is no smoke here."
When the perception of the nature of smoke is not apprehended, there is the non-apprehension of its own nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*);
when a capable cause is not apprehended, there would be the non-apprehension of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*);
and when that which is contradictory to the cause is apprehended, there would be the apprehension of what is contradictory to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*).

In this case, however, only frost—which is pervaded by that which is contradictory to the cause—is perceived. Because smoke is negated by that [frost], there occurs a negation of the effect through the perception of that which is pervaded by what is contradictory to the cause (kāraṇaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi).

Regarding "the perception of that which is pervaded by what is contradictory to the pervader" (vyāpakaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi): the meaning is the perception of that which is not pervaded by that which is contradictory to whatever is the pervader of the object to be negated.
He provides an example: "This is not eternal.
If that which is contradictory to the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddha*) were perceived, the negation would be established simply through the perception of what is contradictory to the pervader.
However, in this case, the distinction is that the negation of the pervader occurs because of the perception of that which is pervaded by its opposite (*tad-viruddha-vyāpta*). 16.
The phrase "and so forth" has already been largely explained.
He states the distinction of others from the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) with the words beginning "here," etc.;
this too has already been largely explained.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Investigation of Inference for Others (parārthānumāna).
He defines inference for others with the words: "that which possesses the three characteristics" (trirūpa).
He explains the phrase "the statement of the three-featured logical mark" (*trirūpaliṅgākhyāna*) with the words "concomitance" (*anvaya*), etc.
Concomitance is presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*);
negative concomitance is absence from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

Intending the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) as "that by which something is explained is an explanation" (*ākhyāyate 'nena iti ākhyānam*), he explains [the term] with the words "by which statement.
Regarding the phrase "metaphorically" (*upacārāt*), the meaning is: "because of the metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of the effect to the cause."
From the word arises the comprehension of the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*); and from that, inference (*anumāna*) arises.
Therefore, by way of this succession, the sentence is the cause for inference.
Now, one might object: "Let there be some other form of inference for others (parārthānumāna) besides the figurative one;
let that too be examined.
Do not say so.
In inference, that which serves as the cause must be examined; and that is the three-featured logical mark (*liṅga*).
Its essential nature has been investigated in the section on inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
But here, that sentence which reveals it is being investigated;
therefore, there is no occasion for the investigation of just anything whatsoever.
He states its twofold nature with the words "That is of two kinds," and so forth.
The subject possessing the property to be proven is the *pakṣa*;
the subject of the example is the kitchen;
the similarity between these two consists in their both possessing the reason (*hetu*).
"Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, as in the case of a kitchen;
and this [subject] possesses smoke"—it is by means of this syllogistic statement (*sādhanavākya*) that [the conclusion] is understood;
this, then, is the syllogistic statement characterized by similarity (*sādharmyavat*).
The dissimilarity (vaidharmya) produced by the absence of the reason is as follows: "Whatever is without fire is without smoke;
and this [subject] possesses smoke"—this is understood through such a statement, which is a proof-statement possessing dissimilarity (vaidharmyavat).

Therein, he provides an example of an application possessing similarity (*sādharmyavat*) with the words "therein" and so forth. It appears that the phrase "in order to demonstrate the application possessing similarity" is a stylistic manner of expression resulting from negligence.
For the Blessed One did not set out to define the distinctions between formal applications (prayoga), but rather to establish the momentariness of all things;
and this [statement] ought to serve as an example of a formal application of a probans based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu) possessing positive concomitance (sādharmyavat).
Nor was this spoken by the Blessed One by relying upon the Sautrāntika view;
for the Sautrāntika school emerged only at a time immediately following the Blessed One.
By the phrase "relying upon the Sautrāntika view," it should be understood that [the teaching] was given by relying on the doctrine of the existence of all things (sarvāstitva-vāda).
However, if existence were merely that of consciousness (*jñāna*), the designation "all" would not be particularly natural.
Alternatively, the connection is as follows: [this] is being explained by relying on the Sautrāntika view in order to demonstrate an argument based on similarity (*sādharmya*).
What is being explained?
Regarding this, he says: "As for what was stated by the Blessed One," and so forth.
Your intended meaning is that whatever is conditioned is momentary, and all of this [world] is conditioned.
He begins to explain this statement of the Blessed One with the words, "That is being expounded.
By means of the prefix *sam*, he states the intended meaning: "having come together through causes.
As long as the causes do not assemble...
Until those [causes] are combined, there is no accomplishment of the effect; however, when they are combined, that effect is accomplished.
Intending to state that these combined causes are called "conditions" (pratyaya), he says: "by conditions."
They proceed toward each cause as further causes; that state of these things proceeding in this manner is called a "condition" (*pratyaya*).
This means that the causes are conjoined.
This momentariness is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the conditioned.
Just as the nature of a *śiṃśapā* tree is its being a tree,
this is therefore a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
The similarity of this essential nature reason to a flash of lightning should be understood.
Even in that regard, the opponents' claim that momentariness does not apply is contradicted by direct perception.
Furthermore, those who consider themselves Buddhists—the Vātsīputrīyas—accept that cognition, sound, and so forth are momentary, while jars and the like are non-momentary.
Against them, this formal argument is directed: "Everything is indeed momentary, because it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), just like cognition, sound, and so forth."

He explains this term "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) as follows: "in the very moment of its arising" means that its duration is limited to the mere moment of its production; this is what is meant by "momentariness. Now, one might raise the objection: "How can jars and other such things be momentary? For once they have arisen, they certainly persist even after their production. Dispelling this doubt, he says: "All things, indeed," and so forth. The underlying intention is this: when this jar or whatever else is produced by its own causes, is it produced with a perishable nature or an imperishable nature? [It is produced with a perishable nature.]
If its nature were indestructible, then its destruction would not occur even when struck by a mallet or similar instrument.
On the other hand, if it is produced with a destructible nature, then immediately after its production, it must necessarily perish.

Now, having raised the objection that things do not arise with either a non-perishable nature or a perishable nature, but rather arise with a nature of stability for a certain duration of time, [the author] refutes it by stating:
"But such indeed is its nature," meaning that even at the time of the proximity of a mallet or other such causes, this very same nature persists.

The intention is as follows: whatever limit is established by saying "having remained for a certain time," that very limit is itself indefinite; therefore, why should this [entity] not remain again for that same duration? Since there is no restriction on its inherent nature (*svabhāva*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

With the intent that this same infinite regress applies even to the proponent of a two-moment duration, he says: "Therefore... [The productive causal complex (*utpādakasāmagrī*) produces only that which has a stable nature.]

He raises an objection with the words "This might be so," etc., on the grounds that the causal complex for destruction (*nāśakasāmagrī*) is even more powerful than that [the cause of persistence] and thus brings about destruction; he then refutes it with the words "That is incorrect," etc.
The intention is as follows: it is logically untenable that a thing which is stable by nature should perish.
For a thing of a single nature cannot acquire a nature that is contradictory to itself.
Therefore, this conceptualization—that the power of the destroyer is superior to that of the producer—would not be tenable.
Now, one might ask: what is this dilemma?
Is it that something of a stable nature arises, or rather something of an unstable nature?
An effect is dependent upon a cause;
just as an effect such as a jar is dependent upon a cause for its own production, so too is the effect called destruction dependent upon a cause for its own production.
If it is asked: "Therefore, since destruction occurs when there is the presence of a destroyer, and does not otherwise, how can the proof of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅga) be established?
It is replied: True, an effect is dependent upon its cause.
The relationship of cause and effect exists only between two positive entities,
and destruction is not some kind of real thing. What need for a cause could there possibly be for a non-entity, which is a mere absence?
The arising of an entity occurs from its cause of production, and once arisen, it ceases of its own accord immediately.
And it has been stated by Śāntarakṣita:
“In that regard, whatever entities are produced, they are all subject to momentary destruction,
because they exist independently with respect to their own disintegration.”
Whatever does not depend upon any other cause for the production of a certain state should be known as restricted to that state, because it arises from its own causes in such a manner.
"Just as a causal complex is independent in producing its own effect,
so too all things that are born are independent with respect to their destruction.
(Tattvasaṃgraha 132)

And Kamalaśīla said: "For there is the production of an existent entity, not of a non-existent one; because it is characterized by the absence of all intrinsic natures that could be made into a causal basis, there is no form whatsoever that can be produced."

Therefore, that which consists of both existence and non-existence— that is, destruction consisting of the negation of existence— is not produced by anything, because it is a non-entity (*avastu*), like the horn of a donkey (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā 136).
However, upon the proximity of a mallet or similar instrument, there is the commencement of a subsequent series (*santāna*) consisting of potsherds and the like.
And for this reason, cessation is called "gross.

Demonstrating through formal reasoning (*prayoga*) that even that which has a perishable nature possesses momentariness, he says: "The formal reasoning (*prayoga*), moreover, is to be formulated as follows:
'Just like that which exists in its final moment.'"
The moment of proximity to a hammer or similar instrument, which produces a continuum of a different genus from the potsherd and so forth, is called the "final moment.
Anticipating the objection that if things are momentary, this contradicts recognition (*pratyabhijñā*),
he responds with the words "without interruption and similar," and so on.
"Uninterrupted" (*nirantara*) is a qualification of "arising.
Furthermore, "similarity" is in relation to each preceding moment.

Clarifying both the uninterruptedness in arising and the similarity of the subsequent to the preceding, he says: "At the very time of the destruction of the preceding moment, another moment similar to it arises."
The meaning is that at the very moment of the destruction of the preceding moment consisting of a jar, another subsequent moment consisting of a jar similar to it arises.
By the restriction "at the very moment of destruction," the absence of any interval between the preceding and succeeding moments is understood;
this is because there is no separation by means of non-existence (abhāva).
The meaning is that there is no specific moment devoid of the jar-occasion between the destruction of the preceding jar-moment and the subsequent jar-moment.
If such a moment existed, then the distinction between the former and the latter might at some point be perceived;
however, due to the absence of any interval, there is an opportunity for the delusion of non-difference.

The point is that similarity and contiguity are the causes for the determination of non-difference. He explains this as follows: "Because there is an absence of difference in form, and because there is no separation by non-existence"—the meaning being that there is an absence of separation caused by non-existence.
[This refers to] the cognition.
The meaning is that it is a cognition consisting of error.
He provides an illustration regarding the error of non-difference with the words "even in the case of things that are absolutely distinct";
that is to say, even in the case of things whose differences are manifest.
"Even here" means:
whereas in the case of the distinction of the unmanifest (*avyakta*) there is a delusion of non-distinction established by logic, what need is there to mention it here?
The intention is that this is an application of a "reason based on essential nature" (*svabhāvahetu*) without any qualifying attributes (*nirviśeṣaṇa*).
For the state of being conditioned (*saṃskṛtatva*) is indeed the very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities;
and its quality of being without qualification will become clear on the occasion of analyzing the reason (*hetu*) as an intrinsic nature that possesses qualifications.
To facilitate a clear understanding, he demonstrates another formal argument (*prayoga*), stating: "likewise, there is another [argument] as well."
Regarding the phrase "that which exists": for existence (*sattā*) is indeed the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of all things.
Now, one might object: "The pervasion (*vyāpti*) that 'whatever exists is momentary' is not established."

Dispelling the doubt rooted in the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the opposing school—which holds that entities such as the self (*ātman*) and space (*ākāśa*) are eternal—he clarifies what is encompassed by the word "all": "entities cognized through valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇapratītāḥ padārthāḥ*).
The sense is this: since there is no valid means of knowledge regarding the self and so forth, they are like the horns of a hare.
The use of the qualifying phrase is as follows: [he provides an example].
The meaning is that this is the formulation of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) together with its qualification.
He establishes the presence of this qualification by means of the passage beginning with "from those not yet arisen" (*anutpannebhyaḥ*).
The underlying intention is as follows: just as a cow is said to be "excluded from what is not a cow" (*agovyāvṛtta*), so too...
Just as that which is excluded from the non-blue is called "blue," so too, that which is merely excluded from the unarisen is called "arisen.
This arising and this possessor of arising do not constitute a distinction between property and property-possessor (*dharma-dharmin*).
Furthermore, exclusion is simply the very nature (*svabhāva*) of that which is excluded.
It does not exceed the exclusion itself.

That very exclusion, by relying on an imagined differentiation of properties (*dharmabheda*), is spoken of as if it were distinct through the delimitation of the nature of the exclusion of the non-blue, [and thus] as "the arising of blue.
Likewise here, [it is spoken of] as "the arising of the word."

Relying upon this imagined distinction between the qualified and the qualifier, this reason—"because of having an origin"—is employed; thus, this is a reason whose nature is qualified (*saviśeṣaṇasvabhāvahetu*). He raises an objection with "But surely" (*nanu*):
all words indeed function solely by way of exclusion (*apoha*).

The meaning is this: even the word "existent" (sat) functions by excluding the non-existent (asat) with respect to that which is excluded from the non-existent; therefore, the essential reason (svabhāvahetu) previously demonstrated—that "it is existent because it possesses existence"—should likewise be considered a reason with a qualification (saviśeṣaṇahetu), just like "possessing origination.
He refutes this, saying: "This is not so."
Regarding the phrase "of that which exists" (*sata eva*):
in the previous formulation, "Whatever exists is impermanent, and these entities exist," it is "existence" (*sat*) alone that is indicated as the subject (*dharmin*),
and existence is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
In this case, nothing is qualified by a conceptual distinction between existence and non-existence in the form of an exclusion (vyāvṛtti),
which would entail the consequence of having a qualifier.
Here, however, that which possesses origination is impermanent.

Regarding the statement "sound possesses origination," the subject (*dharmin*) is indicated specifically by its origination through the phrase "that which possesses origination. Thus, by means of an origination characterized as the exclusion of non-origination, the subject is indicated as if distinct from that [property].

Furthermore, in the expression "sound possesses origination," origination is presented as if it were a property (*dharma*) of the subject sound, though its distinction [from the subject] is merely superimposed.
Therefore, this formal argument ought to be based on a reason characterized by a qualification (*saviśeṣaṇasvabhāvahetuka*);
for the argument would be: "Whatever is produced is impermanent, and these entities are produced."
"In that case, there would be no inequality.
He states another method regarding the employment of a reason with a qualification: "of one whose qualification is distinct.
And "distinctness" means not being included within the essential nature [of the subject].

Not understanding the meaning of the word "produced" (*kṛtaka*), he raises an objection: "But [in the case of] 'the brindled cow' (*citraguḥ*)," and so forth. The sense is this: in the case of "the brindled cow," since the brindled cows—which are external to the subject (*dharmin*, Devadatta)—are intended as qualifiers, a distinct qualification is clearly perceived there.

However, the designation "produced" is no different from the designation "effect" (*kārya*); it conveys only the nature of being an effect, namely "product-ness" (*kāryatā*). Therefore, how can there be a distinct qualification? This is the point.
He refutes this with the words beginning "dependent" (*apekṣita*).
The word "produced" (*kṛtaka*) is not a synonym for the word "effect" (*kārya*);
rather, it indicates a specific nature characterized by having its own production dependent upon the operation of another.

And thus, just as in the case of the word *citragu* ("possessor of brindled cows"), because this qualifier conveys dependence upon an external operation that is not included within the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the subject (*dharmin*), the intention is that this formulation can be a syllogism based on a reason whose nature is a distinct qualifier (*bhinnaviśeṣaṇasvabhāvahetu*).
And Dharmakīrti said in the *Nyāyabindu*: "That which is produced is impermanent"—this is [stated] by way of a distinction in qualifiers (*upādhibheda*).
"For a thing (*bhāva*) is 'produced' (*kṛtaka*) when its own activity depends upon another" (Nyāyabindu, p. 109).

This has been explained by the teacher Dharmottara: "The connection is that there is an application of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) through a distinction of conditions (*upādhi*). An 'condition' (*upādhi*) is a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*);
the meaning is that the essential nature as a logical reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is applied as qualified by a distinction—that is, by a distinct condition."
In this context, sometimes the mere object is expressed;
sometimes it is qualified by an inseparable qualifier; and sometimes by a separable one.
"Devadatta" is [the name of] a pure [individual];
"long-eared" is [an individual] characterized by two unseparated ears;
"possessor of brindled cows" is [an individual] characterized by brindled cows that are distinct [from himself].

In the same way, "existence" (*sattva*) is a pure [essential property], while "having an origin" (*utpattimattva*) is an inseparable qualifier (*avyatirikta-viśeṣaṇa*), and "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is a separable qualifier (*vyatirikta-viśeṣaṇa*). ... Because that which depends on the operation of another is called "produced," therefore its nature (*svabhāva*) is said to be qualified by a separable qualifier.
Although a separate qualifying term has not been employed, nevertheless, a distinct qualification is already included within the word "produced" (kṛtaka) itself.
For this very reason, this word "produced" functions as a technical designation (saṃjñā).
Because this suffix *kan* is prescribed [after a word] in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*)—so it is said in the *Nyāyabinduṭīkā* (p.
30)—he now states another method regarding the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), namely: "of that which has an applied qualification."
That is to say, it refers to a qualifier that is conveyed by a distinct word.
In other cases, the qualifier is presented by the very same word "produced" (*kṛtaka*) which presents the qualificand;
here, however, it is presented by another word, namely *pratyayabheda*.
This establishes the nature of the applied qualification—by means of the passage beginning with "of the term 'difference of cognition'";
and it is also the demonstration of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*).
The meaning is that it is a demonstration of the three types of qualified essential reasons.

Or, the meaning is that it is a demonstration of the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding the essential nature as a logical reason (*svabhāvahetu*). Regarding the phrase "for the sake of removing delusion":
there might be a delusion on the part of an unintelligent person that this is not the essential nature.
The meaning is: "for the sake of its cessation.

Stating the cause of the delusion, he describes the method for its cessation: "Even by means of the conceptualization of a distinction between properties (*dharma*), it results in nothing other than the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*).
And the teacher Dharmottara said: "Thus, the threefold application of the essential reason has been demonstrated."
"It is [of two kinds]: pure (*śuddha*) and that which has a distinct qualifier (*vyatirikta-viśeṣaṇa*).
This was stated for this purpose:
so that there may be no confusion regarding even a *svabhāva-hetu* when it is employed, due to a difference in its verbal expression" (Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā 31).

Now, he provides an example of an application of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) that possesses negative concomitance (*vaidharmya*), beginning with the words "of the essential reason" and so forth:
"Whatever is not non-momentary does not have a perishable nature;
whatever has a perishable nature is non-momentary."

Just as "the pot existing at its final moment" is a formulation based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) that possesses similarity (*sādharmya*), this following formulation is one that possesses dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*): "Whatever does not remain non-transitory in the interval—
for example, space."

And this illustration is to be understood as follows: by those partial Buddhists who maintain the existence of all things (*sarvāstitvavādins*), the Noble Truths are subsumed under two categories—the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Within the category of the unconditioned, space (*ākāśa*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are counted as three; thus [space] is established.
However, in the position that does not accept space, it should be understood as being equivalent to examples such as the horns of a hare.
"In the formulation of negative concomitance" (vyatirekaprayoge) means:
in the formulation of negative pervasion (vyatirekavyāpti). "The absence of the probandum" (sādhyābhāvaḥ)—that is, the probandum which is intended to be established by positive concomitance (anvaya).

Its non-existence [is established] by the absence of the probans— that is, by the absence of that probans which one intends to prove through positive concomitance (anvaya)— because it is pervaded by it, meaning it is characterized by that pervasion.
In the positive concomitance (anvaya), the probans is pervaded by the probandum; in the negative concomitance (vyatireka), the absence of the probandum is pervaded by the absence of the probans.
Because it is so, that absence of the probandum is necessarily restricted to the absence of the probans, and does not occur elsewhere than where there is an absence of the probans.

Just as when it is stated that something is restricted to its own action (*svakarma*), it is understood that there is no connection with anything other than its own action, so too, by that [reason], the pervasion of the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) by the absence of the probans (*sādhana*) is obtained.
And thus, it should be understood that through the cessation of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), the cessation of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is established.

Since the nature of being imperishable (*avināśisvarūpatva*) is the pervader of the absence of non-momentariness (*anantarānavasthāyitvābhāva*), that [imperishability], while receding from color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest, causes the absence of non-momentariness to recede from them as well, thereby establishing their momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).
He establishes this: that which has been demonstrated as having a perishable nature, such as form and so forth, exists at the time of its arising;
thus, "wherein momentariness does not exist" is this application of dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*) when momentariness is to be proven by means of existence (*sattva*).
And this is the formulation of the negative concomitance (*vaidharmya-prayoga*) for a pure essential reason (*svabhāva-hetu*).

It demonstrates the formulation of the negative concomitance when impermanence is to be proven by means of having an origin: "Wherever impermanence is absent, there too having an origin is absent. This is to be connected with the word "absent" (*nivṛttam*).

This is the formulation of the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmyaprayoga*) for an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) whose qualification is non-distinct. He demonstrates the formulation of the dissimilar instance when proving impermanence by means of being produced: "Wherever impermanence is absent, there being produced is also [absent]. The word "is not" is to be connected with what precedes.
This is the formulation of the negative concomitance (*vaidharmya-prayoga*) for a *svabhāva-hetu* whose qualifier is distinct [from the subject].

It demonstrates the negative concomitance of a *svabhāva-hetu* whose distinct qualifier is presented by another word: "Where there is no 'being produced' (*kṛtakatva*), there is also no 'variation according to the variation of conditions' (*pratyayabhedabheditva*). The word "is not" (*nāsti*) is to be connected with the preceding statement.
Now, he demonstrates the formulations based on similarity and dissimilarity for the reason of effect (*kāryahetu*) by means of the words beginning with "yathā" (for example).
The phrase "by perception and non-perception" (*pratyakṣānupalambhābhyām*) means by means of both perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*anupalambha*).
The necessary perception of smoke when fire is perceived is called *pratyakṣa* (perception).
The non-perception of smoke when fire is not perceived is called *anupalambha* (non-perception).
Through perception, the concomitance (*anvaya*) between cause and effect is ascertained.
"When there is fire, smoke exists.
By the non-perception of smoke when fire is not perceived, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*) between the two is ascertained.
Thus, when the positive and negative concomitances of two things are determined through perception and non-perception, their relationship as cause and effect is understood.

The meaning is that if the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) were not established, one would be unable to ward off the opponent’s objection regarding the lack of logical necessity (*aprayojaka*). Therefore, by one who employs an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), the causal relationship must first be ascertained through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*).
This is as [stated] in the refutation of the composite whole (*avayavinirākaraṇa*).
The word "is applied" (*prayujyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
This reason of non-perception (*anupalabdhihetu*) is employed to refute one who asserts that there exists some whole (*avayavin*) distinct from its parts which inheres (*samaveta*) in those parts.
This is the application of that [reason] possessing similarity (*sādharmyavat*), beginning with "if in this... and so forth.
The probandum (*sādhya*) is the fitness for the conventional usage of non-existence; the logical reason (*hetu*) is non-perception while meeting the conditions for perceptibility.
In this regard, whatever is not perceived there, despite meeting the conditions for perceptibility, is fit for the conventional usage of non-existence in that place, just like a horn on a human head.

Thus is the statement establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*). "And here, in the potsherds, no whole (*avayavin*) postulated by the opponent—which meets the conditions for perception—is perceived"; this is the statement establishing the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
Now, one might object: "But a cloth is indeed perceived."
True.
In whatever manner a whole (avayavin) is conceived by others, it is not perceived in that way;

for a whole is not perceived as something distinct from its parts and serving as their substratum, like a jar on the ground, nor is it perceived as something distinct from its parts while serving as their substratum within those very parts.
However, it is only the threads themselves that are perceived when they have attained a particular state of conjunction;
the difference in designation as "cloth" is merely nominal.

When the probandum is the fitness for the conventional usage of "non-existent"—on the grounds of not being perceived despite having reached the conditions for perceptibility—then [the cloth is non-existent].

"That which is unfit for the conventional usage of 'non-existent' is not devoid of the absence of non-perception qualified by having reached the conditions for perceptibility"— this is the negative pervasion (*vyatireka-vyāpti*). In this case, since the locus possesses the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the absence of the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) consists in the absence of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇābhāva*).

However, [the author] intends that an absence qualified by a specific attribute existing in a locus possessing that attribute consists in the absence of the qualified object; and specifically, an absence of the aforementioned qualification—existing in a locus possessing the attribute of "being available for perception" (upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva), which is fit for the linguistic usage of "existent"—consists precisely in the absence of non-perception.
With this in mind, he demonstrates the negative concomitance (vyatirekavyāpti): "Whatever is existent and meets the conditions for perceptibility is necessarily perceived.
Conversely, whatever is existent yet not perceived is not fit for perception; thus, one should understand that in the absence of the qualification, there is an absence of the qualified.
"And it is not so here.
Here— meaning in a part, such as a potsherd, or in a specific location, such as the ground and so forth.
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "of a jar that has reached the conditions for perception, there is no such perception here.

Thus, by the cessation of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), the pervaded (*vyāpya*) must also cease to exist; therefore, the sense is that the very fitness for the conventional usage of non-existence (*asad-vyavahāra-yogyatā*) is established for the whole (*avayavin*) with respect to its parts.
And it is the statement of the necessity of the probans with respect to the probandum;
that is to say, the statement of the pervasion of the probans by the probandum. And it is the statement of the necessity of the absence of the probandum with respect to the absence of the probans.
This means stating that the absence of the probandum is pervaded by the absence of the probans.
The meaning of the word *niyata* has been explained.

In order to ward off the opponents' suspicion that the aforementioned formal arguments (*prayoga*) are non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*), he says: "Therefore, when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."

This is the intended meaning: for us, who accept that pervasion (vyāpti) is rooted in the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) of direct perception (pratyakṣa), there is no room for the "lack of probative force" (aprayojaka) objection raised by opponents.
We establish what we intend to prove either through the relation of cause and effect (kāryakāraṇabhāva) or through essential identity (svabhāva);
both of these are likewise rooted in direct perception.
For the relationship of cause and effect is established through the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) as perceived by direct perception;
and the essential nature (svabhāva) of the probandum and the probans is likewise accessible to direct perception.
Furthermore, both apprehension and non-apprehension ultimately resolve into the very nature of that which is being apprehended and that which is not being apprehended.
In this way, existence and non-existence are established.
The existence of a horn elsewhere and its non-existence in a rabbit are simply specific natures (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) of the rabbit and the horn respectively;
this is indeed accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
In the context of this incidental discussion, he raises the objection of others—that [the reason] is not a valid probans—by saying "where," and so forth.
"Of them" refers to the Naiyāyikas.
[The point is: "Let there be another omniscient being here, or let there not be one."

The Mīmāṃsakas, who do not accept an omniscient, eternal, and singular Lord capable of perceiving supersensuous objects, strive only to refute the existence of an omniscient being, due to their obsession with negating the omniscience asserted by the Buddhists and others. We, however, say: whether there be an omniscient being other than the Lord in this world or not, we have no obsession regarding either its establishment or its refutation.
However, the Blessed One is again the Lord, the omniscient one who is the creator of this world;
and it can be established that he exists.
He restates their method of proving the existence of God with the words "For instance" (*tathāhi*), and so forth.

At the outset, while demonstrating the division of the subject (*pakṣa*), the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) regarding the formal argument (*prayoga*) that will be set forth to prove God, he begins: "Indeed, there are three...
When "having an agent" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), things such as pots, whose agents are certain, constitute the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Those things such as space (*vyoman*) and so forth, which are certain to lack a creator, are the counter-examples (*vipakṣa*).
Furthermore, those others such as trees (*vanaspati*) and so forth, as well as the earth (*mahī*) and mountains (*mahīdhara*) and so forth, are those whose creators are doubtful.
[The reason] "possessing magnitude" (*mahattva*) and "possessing parts" (*sāvayavatva*), and so forth, brings about the presence of having a creator.
The non-perception of an agent establishes its absence,
or else doubt arises from conflicting views;
therefore, all these things— the earth, mountains, and so forth— are included within the scope of the subject (*pakṣa*).

And other states of existence are included within the category of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the category of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*); there is no fourth possibility among these states. Therefore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: whatever is an effect has an agent.
For example, a pot and the like. Furthermore, the earth and so forth are effects;
and whatever is not an effect is not possessed of an agent, such as space and the like.

And this effect, namely the earth and so forth, has an intelligent agent as its maker. By including "intelligent" within the body of the probandum (*sādhya*), the rule is understood that the agent must be one who possesses knowledge of the material cause, the instruments, and so on.
Therefore, there is no occasion for [the fallacies of] *arthāntara* (irrelevance) and so forth.

Anticipating the doubt that the reason (*hetu*) of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*), which was adduced as the proof for having an agent (*sakartṛkatva*), might be fallacious (*ābhāsa*), he says: "This is not... and so on.
The fallaciousness of a reason consists in its deficiency of constituent factors (*aṅgavaikalya*).
The members of the reason are threefold: presence in the subject (pakṣa), presence in the similar class (sapakṣa), and absence in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa).
By the establishment of these three, any suspicion of fallaciousness is refuted.
Therefore, he establishes them in due order:
"of all"— that is, of the earth, mountains, and so forth—
within the homologous class, such as a jar and the like.

"And it is not inconclusive": this doubt regarding inconclusiveness is rooted in the suspicion that the probans is irrelevant—that is, that the property of being an effect might exist while the property of having an intelligent agent as its cause does not; that suspicion is now refuted.
In the case of trees, the earth, mountains, and so forth, which are accepted as the subject (*pakṣa*),
there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the opposite of the probandum— that is, against the opposite of being produced by an intelligent agent;
because the opposite is undermined by such a subverting proof, there is no risk of the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).
What is that subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*)?
He states it with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*), etc.
First, as for the effect (*kārya*).
The meaning is: "first, effects such as a jar.
Regarding the phrase "by means of mental perception," the qualification "mental" here is merely a slip of the pen.

The mind arises only with respect to one's own pleasure and so forth, not directly toward external objects; merely because the mind is the instrumental cause [of their perception], it is not easy to claim that the direct perception of external objects is mental (mānasa).
Therefore, this [text] cannot in any way be interpreted as referring to something non-empirical (*alaukika*).

Since it has been observed many times that effects such as jars have potters and the like as their agents, the intention [of the author] is that the fact of every effect having an agent has been perceived through empirical perception (*pratyakṣa*)— specifically, through a non-empirical perception (*alaukika-pratyakṣa*) arising via the universal-characterized proximity (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā-pratyāsatti*) of "being an effect," which, aided by those repeated observations, apprehends that all effects whatsoever possess an agent.
The intention is that this very perception serves as the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the opposite of the probandum.

Thus, the root text beginning with "tathāhi" (for instance) must be explained by supplementing the ellipsis as follows: first, an effect such as a jar is seen to arise from a potter and so forth; therefore, by means of perception aided by repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*), it is apprehended that "an effect has an agent."
"Therefore, this is not [the case].

Since it is understood through perception that the state of having an agent is inherent to an effect, therefore this should not be doubted—that an effect might exist while being independent of an agent; such is the meaning.
"By a universal inclusion" means by an inclusion of all individual instances (*vyakti*).
For it is not possible for there to be a pervasion (*vyāpti*) between two universals merely through the observation of mutual concomitance among a few individual instances.
The point is that the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) between the universals of "jar" and "cloth" does not arise merely from observing the coexistence of a few individual jars and cloths.
He refutes [the opponent's position] by analyzing the state of having an intelligent agent (*buddhimatkartṛkatva*), beginning with the words "In that case, if... and so forth.
The underlying intention is as follows: for every specific effect, there is its own respective, determinate causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
For the causal complex that produces a jar is not the same as that which produces a cloth,
nor is that which produces a cloth the same as that which produces a jar.
However, it is observed that in the case of effects dependent upon the operations of the body, senses, and mind, there is an intelligent agent.
Just as some effects are observed to depend upon bodily activity,
so too are countless others observed to be independent of it,
such as grasses, trees, creepers, shrubs, and the like.
Therefore, the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is indeed deviant with respect to having an intelligent agent who possesses a visible body;
furthermore, those things which are observed to have an intelligent agent are exclusively those whose intelligent agents possess visible bodies.
To argue that there is no suspicion of deviation because even grass and the like are included within the subject (*pakṣa*) is not tenable.
For it is not appropriate to make the subject of a deviation (vyabhicāra) the locus of inference (pakṣa) in order to exclude that very deviation.

[This is because] "the statement of the reason (hetu) applies to what is doubtful. This is the intended meaning: once the positive concomitance (anvaya) of the probandum is ascertained, the employment of a reason is useless.
When the absence [of the probans] is certain, it is improper to rely on a reason, as this would result in the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*).
However, reliance on a reason is appropriate when there is doubt.
But in this case, since the absence of an agent with a visible body has been ascertained in the case of grass and such things, it is untenable to rely on a reason to prove its existence therein.
He raises an objection with "Now [if it be argued]... (atha). He refutes it with "That is not so" (tan na).
On a mountain difficult to ascend, the absence of fire is hard to ascertain.
Furthermore, in other cases, fire is observed to be invariably concomitant with smoke;
therefore, it is logical to establish the existence of fire on a mountain despite the presence of doubt.
In this case, however, the absence of the probandum is ascertained through the non-perception of a perceptible object; such is the sense in which there is a great disparity between the two.

He refutes another alternative by restating it: "Now, [if it is argued] 'by the invisible'. The meaning is that the pervasion is understood either by an intelligent agent possessing an invisible body, or by an agent who is merely intelligent.

If "having an invisible body" were included within the definition of the property to be proved (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*), there would be the suspicion of an inconclusive fallacy (*anaikāntya*) in the case of jars and the like, which are well-known to have visible agents such as potters; therefore, he resorts to another alternative, stating "or merely possessing intelligence.
The intention here is this: what is actually to be proved is simply "having an intelligent agent."
And that agent must either have a visible body or an invisible body;
let him exist where a visible one is possible, but not where it is not.
"In that case, it ought to be invisible.
[This means: "Because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established by the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*).
That is to say, the meaning is that the negative concomitance is not established through the non-perception of what is perceptible.
The point is this: non-existence (abhāva) is indeed cognized through the non-perception of the perceptible.
And that non-perception depends upon the perceptibility of the counter-positive (pratiyogin);
for the non-existence of an imperceptible thing, such as a ghost, cannot be apprehended by the eye in the form "there is no ghost here."

Likewise, since some counter-correlatives (*pratiyogin*) possess an invisible nature, the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*) is not possible regarding the absence of their general property (*sāmānyābhāva*).

Thus, if you were to admit that even among agents there exists an agent who is invisible, then the absence of the general property of agency—characterized by such an agent—could not be ascertained due to the absence of the non-perception of the perceptible.
In reality, even in the case of jars and the like, the intelligent agent admitted by you as the creator is some eternal self (*ātman*).
Since that [creator] would likewise be invisible, the absence of an intelligent agent could not be ascertained due to the impossibility of non-perception of a fit object (*yogyānupalambha*).

Thus, because there is doubt regarding the exclusion of an intelligent agent, and because there is consequently doubt regarding the exclusion of "being an effect" from that [agent], it follows that even in the case of grass and such things, there would be doubt precisely about that [exclusion]; therefore, there would necessarily be doubt concerning the dependence of an effect upon an agent, which constitutes the state of having a doubtful exclusion from the counter-example (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatva*).

"The reason would indeed be faulty"—this is what is being stated: when "having an intelligent agent" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is that which lacks an intelligent agent.
It is difficult to establish the definitive determination that "this has an intelligent agent" and "this does not."
Because non-perception of a perceptible object is impossible when the object is invisible;

and thus, due to doubt, its absence in grass and the like remains merely doubtful. Therefore, the "doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instance" (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatva*) results in the fallacy of "doubtful inconclusiveness" (*sandigdhānaikāntikatva*), which is indeed a defect of the logical reason (*hetu*). By demonstrating that "doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instance" constitutes a defect of the reason, the Master Dharmakīrti illustrated this: "Even when there is doubt regarding this very form [of the reason], it is simply inconclusive."

"Just as when a certain intended person is non-omniscient and possesses passion and so forth, the property such as 'being a speaker' is one whose exclusion from the heterologue (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful; for nowhere—in its entirety or in part—is an omniscient speaker perceived. This is because a non-perception of this kind, having as its object an invisible nature, is a cause of doubt. (Nyāyabindu 3.112). Now, [it may be argued that] grass and the like have been made the subject (*pakṣa*).
A jar and the like are the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), while space and the like, which are indeed eternal, are the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

As for the illustration—"that which is without an agent does not possess origination, just as space and the like"—it is indeed observed; to this he replies: "of that which is necessitated by the absence of the probandum" (*sādhyābhāvaprayuktasya*).
The intention is as follows: what is the point of this mere illustration?

For, regarding space (*vyoman*) and other things accepted as eternal, there is no determining factor to ascertain whether the absence of being an effect (*kāryatvābhāva*) is caused by the absence of an agent, or rather caused by the absence of other causes independent of an agent; thus, because there is no such determination, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished.
He provides authoritative corroboration regarding the aforementioned fault, stating "tathā ca" (and likewise).
Regarding the phrase "of being an effect":
this is for the purpose of eliminating its occurrence in the dissimilar instance—that is to say, to avoid the contingency of the reason being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
If an agent beyond the senses is postulated— then indeed, an intelligent agent must be characterized by a body, sense organs, and a mind;
for we observe that intelligence is dependent upon the body and so forth,
and because it is seen only in embodied beings.
Furthermore, no embodied agent is observed in the case of grass and such things.
The underlying sense is: if it is argued that an intelligent agent with a supersensible body is postulated as the creator of effects such as grass;
[we reply: how can a pervasion (vyāpti) be established when it is devoid of the proof of negative concomitance (vyatireka)?
In that case, since a perceptible non-apprehension is impossible regarding that supersensible [subject], its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) cannot be established.

Now, if—on the grounds of establishing negative concomitance—a creator who is perceptible is assumed even in the case of grass and the like, then because such a creator is not perceived there either, the reason (*hetu*) remains inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); this is the intended sense.
[Objection: But surely there exists an innate connection (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) between being produced by a creator and having an origin.
Likewise, the absence of having an agent is obtained through the absence of having an origin, by way of illustration:
"Whatever has an origin has an agent, such as a jar and so forth;
whatever lacks an agent does not have an origin, such as space and so forth. Thus, it is obtained from this example.
There is also a natural relationship between smoke and fire,
and that is ascertained through repeated observation;
however, it is not the case that there is no relationship other than identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) between the probans and the probandum.

And thus, since the absence of the probans is necessitated by the absence of the probandum, what is the use of investigating the relationship between the necessitated and the necessitator? Dispelling this doubt, he refutes the theory of an inherent connection (*svābhāvikatva*) between the reason and the probandum, which is favored by others, with the words beginning "As for that which [was said] by Trilocana.
The phrase "of that upādhi" means "of that upādhi of the connection."

The meaning is that, just as there is the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of contact with wet fuel in the relation of fire to smoke, there is no such limiting condition in the relation of smoke to fire.

And it has been stated by Vācaspatimiśra in the *Nyāyavārtikatātparyaṭīkā*: "For instance, the relation of smoke and the like to fire and the like is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), but not the relation of fire and the like to smoke and the like."
For these [entities] are indeed perceived even without smoke and the like;
however, when they experience a connection with wet fuel and so forth, they then become connected with smoke and the like.
Therefore, the connection of fire and the rest with wet fuel and other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is not intrinsic (*svābhāvika*).
Therefore, it is not contingent;
rather, the relationship between smoke and the like with fire and the like is inherent,
because no limiting condition (upādhi) is perceived.
Because deviation is not observed in some cases, and because it is illogical to postulate [a relation] even for that which is not perceived;
therefore, a necessary connection is a constituent factor of inference. (Nyāyavārttika-ṭīkā 165)
He rejects [the opponent's view], saying "that is not tenable.
Among the two ways of establishing an intrinsic relation (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) that have been described, he first refutes the former with the words beginning "since" (*yataḥ*).
The meaning is as follows: when there is a relation between one thing and another, whatever else is required by those two related entities is designated by the term "limiting condition" (*upādhi*).
"How can it be said that [the relation] does not exist at all merely because it is not observed?"—
the meaning is that it is said that the *upādhi* (limiting condition) does not exist at all.
The point is that, since the suspicion of an *upādhi* cannot be ruled out, the determination of an essential (*svābhāvika*) connection would not be possible.
He refutes the second reason with the words, "As for what was also said... [The phrase] "due to the deficiency of other conditions" means "due to the deficiency of other causes."
"And it is not thus.

The sense is that if this were the case, the worldly course of affairs as conducted by authoritative persons through inference would not be possible, because of the consequence that one would have to postulate a limiting condition (upādhi) in every instance.

"Because doubt is prescribed when there is an absence of both probative and subversive evidence. This objection was raised and refuted by Vācaspatimiśra: "It is not correct to say that an unperceived adjunct (upādhi), which is doubted due to the absence of probative and subversive evidence because it is unfit for perception, obstructs [the inference of] intrinsic nature."

"Since there is no restrictive factor, doubt must necessarily arise"—thus given its opportunity, this demoness of doubt, having transgressed the boundaries of worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), gains such a hold that it would not fail to exist anywhere; consequently, "this [person] would not act anywhere," as in the case where there is no difference in otherness (*anyatva*). (Nyāyavārttika-ṭīkā 165).
Just as [in the case] of "even though there is no difference in otherness."

When it must be stated that preceding moments are the causes of succeeding moments, an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) arises because "precedence" and "succession" are common to all preceding and succeeding [moments] among the innumerable ones. For those Buddhists who assert that everything—be it similarity by way of place, time, genus, and so forth—is distinct from one another due to being unique particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*), such a relation is impossible; for even though there is no difference in their distinctness, [the cause-effect relation] would apply to only a certain moment in relation to only a certain [other moment].

The intention [of the opponent] is this: "Just as the status of being a cause at a specific moment is accepted by you, so too is it my own view that for some [thing], there is an intrinsic (svābhāvika) relation with some [other thing].
To this, [the author replies]: "That is not tenable.

For us, who state that the relation between fire and smoke is precisely their causal relationship (*hetumadbhāva*) as established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is unreasonable for you to postulate an intrinsic relation between them that is devoid of any basis in valid cognition.
The sense is that there is indeed a great disparity [between the two cases].
Having analyzed the meaning of the term "intrinsic" (*svābhāvika*), he refutes it by asking: "What is the meaning of 'an intrinsic relation'?

With the intention that it is not logical for mere repeated observation alone to provide certainty regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*), he says: "Since there is merely an example, whether by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), there is no establishment of pervasion either."

"Even in the case of two things met by chance" means that even for a specific camel and a specific donkey who have met by chance, there would follow the erroneous determination of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) between them merely by observing them in many instances.
[Objection: If that is so, then what is the use of employing an illustrative example (*nidarśana*) in the context of a formal logical argument (*nyāyaprayoga*)?

To this, he says: "Therefore, [it is] the illustration. [This occurs] by means of the recollection of the means of valid cognition that grasped the invariable concomitance (pratibandha), which had been previously grasped but was subsequently forgotten. "Previously grasped" means...

Alternatively, the meaning is: "by means of the recollection of that means of valid cognition which apprehended the connection between fire and smoke—characterized as the relation of cause and effect—which was forgotten";
or rather, it means "by means of the recollection of that means of valid cognition which apprehended the connection, whether it had been grasped or forgotten."
"Not by mere proximity"—the meaning is: not by the mere presence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as an illustration.

For the intended sense here is that it is not [established] merely by observing the coexistence of the absence of having an agent and the absence of being produced in the case of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "For instance" (*tathā hi*).

Regarding the phrase "just as in the case of space": this is the intended meaning— by you, who seek to prove that whatever possesses origination must have an intelligent creator by demonstrating space and so forth as negative examples (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*), it is not tenable [for you] that space and such lack origination.

In that case, the absence of a cause other than that [intelligent being] exists for an insentient cause just as it does for an intelligent one. Thus, for those who maintain that grass and the like arise from their respective causes such as seeds even when presided over by an intelligent agent, why should the very absence of such a cause—which they themselves accept—be the reason for the non-arising of space and so forth? Why would that alone not be the determining factor for the non-origination of space and the like?

Therefore, since the absence of being produced by an intelligent agent is unestablished in relation to the absence of having an origin, the fact of having an origin cannot be established as being pervaded by being produced by an intelligent agent.

Nor is it appropriate to say that because the presence of an effect is observed in a jar to be concomitant with an intelligent agent, the absence of an intelligent agent in space must therefore entail the absence of agency;

for while the observation of the concomitance of the state of being an effect with an intelligent agent in a jar might mean that its production does not occur without such an agent, [it does not prove the necessary pervasion].
If space is unproduced, how can it be the causal factor [for its own production]?
The point is this: merely because a cause observed in one instance is not seen elsewhere does not mean that the non-production of the latter depends upon the former.
One might object: "Just as when fire and so forth are to be proven by means of smoke, the absence of smoke in the counter-example (vipakṣa) is understood to be caused by the absence of fire."

Anticipating the objection—"In that case, why could the absence of origination, which is observed in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) such as space, not be caused by the absence of an intelligent agent?"—he says: "Furthermore, merely by non-perception...

If the negative concomitance (vyatireka) of the reason were established merely by its non-perception in the dissimilar instance, then it might indeed be possible for the absence of the probandum to be caused by the absence of the probans.
The point is that the non-existence of a reason is not established merely by the non-perception of that reason. He demonstrates this as follows: "For instance...
Furthermore, the mere cessation of perception cannot serve as the determining factor for the absence of perception.
The cessation of apprehension is due to the absence of the causal complex for apprehending;
the cessation of the object of apprehension, however, is due solely to the absence of its own causal complex.
Furthermore, apprehension is not included within the causal complex that produces the object of apprehension.
However, the object of apprehension is included within the causal complex of apprehension,
because, like the eye and other sense organs, the object is also a cause for apprehension. Therefore, the absence of apprehension is caused by the absence of the object of apprehension.
However, the absence of the object to be perceived is not necessarily caused by the absence of perception;
for indeed, that which is situated inside a well or a hole is not perceived by anyone.

Therefore, only when there is a necessary connection between the probandum and the probans—either as a causal relation (hetu-hetumadbhāva) or as identity (tādātmya)—can the absence of the probans be necessitated by the absence of the probandum.
The point is that, in other cases, if the exclusion of the reason from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful, the defect is indeed unavoidable. As for what Vācaspati said:

this statement of the venerable Vācaspatimiśra means, "Therefore, by one who maintains the course of worldly conduct according to authoritative tradition, doubt must be entertained in accordance with what is observed."
Nor [can it arise] even with respect to something never seen before;
for doubt, which depends upon the recollection of specific features, does not occur regarding what is not recollected,
and recollection cannot pertain to that which has never been experienced.
"Therefore, by diligently searching for a limiting condition (*upādhi*) and failing to perceive one, we understand that it does not exist and conclude that the relationship is intrinsic.
(Nyāyavārttika-ṭīkā 165). This very point is restated in substance by the words "only depending on the recollection of the specific [condition]," and so forth.

The underlying intention is as follows: Surely, there must be a relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) either through identity (*tādātmya*) or through origination from that (*tadutpatti*).

If it were otherwise, the intended object of proof might not exist even if the means of proof were present; thus, because of the doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), a suspicion that the reason is non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*) would arise. To this we say: no. When the concomitance between fire and smoke has been repeatedly observed in many locations, and the connection of smoke with fire is established while no limiting condition (*upādhi*) is perceived, then for one who sees smoke on a mountain, there is no [such doubt].
There would be doubt regarding fire;
for doubt occurs only when there is a recollection of a distinguishing feature.
That is to say, it would arise only upon the recollection of some previously experienced location that possesses smoke but is devoid of fire.

Just as, despite observing the coexistence of smoke and fire hundreds of times, doubt regarding smoke might indeed arise when fire is seen on a mountain and so forth, due to the recollection of a previously experienced iron ball (*ayogolaka*) which possesses fire but lacks smoke; likewise, despite observing the coexistence of earthiness and being scratchable by iron hundreds of times, doubt regarding earthiness might indeed arise even when [something] is observed, due to the recollection of the diamond-gem (*vajramaṇi*), which is earthen but lacks the property of being scratchable by iron.
In some cases, there is doubt regarding the state of being inscribable by iron;
therefore, one should entertain suspicion only according to what is actually observed.
[This is stated] "by abandoning the relations of identity and causality."
"It is to be suspected" connects with what follows.
In that regard, it is precisely the observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) concerning "knowability" (*prameyatva*).

This is the intended meaning: even when "knowability"—which is common to both the seen and the unseen—is observed in a knowable object, despite its having been repeatedly seen to coexist with fire in certain knowable objects, it remains [uncertain] regarding fire, just as in the case of smoke.

Likewise, there would be doubt regarding smoke even when some instances of smoke have been observed to coexist with fire; for since the property of being smoke is common to both those where coexistence has been observed and those where it has not, if one does not accept a specific continuity [of the cause], then doubt regarding fire would certainly arise even upon seeing smoke. Similarly, since the property of being an effect is common to both those effects observed to require an agent and those not so observed, doubt would certainly arise regarding an observed effect such as a sprout.
When there is an expectation for an agent, doubt arises; thus, the occasion for doubt occurs exactly as it is observed.
The phrase "characterized by the censure of one who is not to be censured" implies "by means of a point of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*).

The meaning is this: when we have pointed out a valid refutation of the reason stated by the opponent—namely, that its exclusion from the contrary (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful—the opponent, speaking to us and claiming that this is the "point of defeat" called "the pointing out of a non-existent fault," becomes caught by his own words in the very point of defeat characterized as "questioning one who should not be questioned," even though no such point of defeat actually exists. And the definition of "questioning one who should not be questioned" is: "The charging of a point of defeat against one who has not been defeated is questioning one who should not be questioned" (Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.23).
He refutes the inference for God (īśvarānumāna) stated by others in another manner—beginning with "Furthermore" (kiñca).
Regarding the term "proving what is already established" (siddhasādhana):

this means that even if [the world] were created by a single non-omniscient intelligent being, or by many such beings acting together, it would still result in a "different matter" (arthāntara), because the intended object of proof has already been accomplished.
"By means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*).

This means that since it is well-established that objects such as pots have non-omniscient agents like potters as their makers, the property of having a single, eternal, and omniscient creator is not accessible through valid cognition; thus, because the example lacks the probandum (*sādhyavikalatva*), there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*).
Alternatively, [the opponent might argue] that they are taking the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in a general sense.
The pervasion of "being an effect" (kāryatva) by the mere fact of having an intelligent agent (buddhimatkartṛkatva), unqualified by attributes such as omniscience, is established in a general sense;

however, the specific quality of having an omniscient and single agent is proven through the force of the property of being a predicate of the subject (pakṣadharmatā), namely that "being an effect" resides in things such as grass, creepers, trees, mountains, and the earth. How so? [It is so] by the force of the property of being a predicate of the subject.
The sense is that their status as effects is not possible without being produced by a single omniscient creator.
He refutes this with the words "In that case, it is logical.

With the intention of asking how a specific quality can be established through the force of the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) when the property of being an effect is indeed possible even without the creator possessing specific qualities such as omniscience, he says "By which," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "even if [the agent] were not omniscient":
the point is that if even a creator of something as simple as grass is established by virtue of being an agent, then what is this restrictive rule that he must necessarily be omniscient?
Regarding the phrase "for if there were establishment of oneness":
if the creator of all things—such as grass, trees, creepers, the earth, mountains, and so forth—were indeed one, then he would necessarily have to be omniscient;
however, this is not an invariable rule.
The sense is that it could indeed be argued that "all this was created by those various [beings] acting together, who were each proficient in their respective materials and so forth.
He provides an illustration of an effect produced by multiple agents: "just as by hundreds of various ants," and so on.
This is intended to establish an intelligent cause that is eternal, unitary, and omniscient.
The meaning is: when the probandum (*sādhya*) is "having a single, eternal, omniscient creator.
Here, "eternality" (*nityatā*) is characterized by the absence of birth and death.
He demonstrates the contradiction as follows: because the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is pervaded (*vyāpta*) by an intelligent agent who is non-eternal, manifold, and non-omniscient.
Wherever there is the state of being an effect, there is an absence of having a single, eternal, and omniscient creator,
as in the case of a jar and so forth.
Even though some jars and such things may have a single creator, they certainly do not have a single, eternal, and omniscient creator.
This is because potters and the like are not omniscient and are subject to birth and death; furthermore,
the makers of chariots, gate-towers, and so forth are numerous,
non-omniscient, and impermanent.
Therefore, the meaning is that the reason is contradictory.

He concludes what was begun: "Thus, it is established that the pervasion between the probandum and the probans must necessarily be demonstrated by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*).
Pervasion is not established merely by repeated observation alone.
However, that [invariable concomitance] must be demonstrated by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within the example.

Some form of necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probans (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*), established by valid cognition, is required; and that [connection] is either identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*).
The claim that it is an "intrinsic relation" (*svābhāvika-sambandha*), however, is not established by valid cognition.
Therefore, the point is that an inference of an agent based on [the world] being an effect is not tenable.

Now, it may be objected: "Because of the difference in formulation, parārthānumāna (inference for others) is said to be of two kinds—namely, that which possesses similarity (*sādharmya*) and that which possesses dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
However, its general definition is: 'Parārthānumāna is the communication of a three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*').'"
In that regard, by means of the positive instance (sādharmyavat), only the positive concomitance (anvaya) is understood;
by means of the negative instance (vaidharmyavat), however, only the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is understood.
Therefore, the comprehension of the three characteristics (trirūpa) does not occur in a single [instance].
Therefore, one raises the objection that this definition is impossible, using the words "But surely" (*nanu*) and so forth.
He refutes this with the words "This is not a fault" (*naiṣa doṣaḥ*) and so forth.
If positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is understood through the word, then negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is understood by implication.
If the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) were understood from the word, then the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) would be understood from its meaning.
Therefore, he says—starting with "because it possesses similarity" (*sādharmyavatī*) and so forth—that both [types of evidence] express that which possesses the three characteristics (*trirūpa*).
He establishes their status as being implied by the meaning (*ārthikatā*) with the words: "the negative concomitance not being grasped... and so forth.
"Capability" (sāmarthyam) means this very capability.
And it has been stated by Dharmakīrti: "For even in an application based on similarity (sādharmya), the understanding of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) follows by implication."

"Because in its absence there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the reason with the probandum; likewise, through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) as well, there is no comprehension of concomitance, because in its absence—that is, in the absence of the probandum—the absence of the reason is not established. (Nyāyabindu 3.109).
This has been explained by the master Dharmottara: "But surely, negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) was not mentioned in the case of [the example] possessing similarity (*sādharmyavat*)."
And since there is positive concomitance (*anvaya*) even in the case of negative concomitance (*vaidharmya*),

how can this be called an exposition of the three-fold mark (*trirūpa-liṅga*)? To this [the author replies] with the words "only in the subject of the thesis" (*sādhyadharmiṇy eva*), and so forth (Nyāyabinduṭīkā 55).
The meaning is: "only a portion of the subject" (*pakṣaikadeśa*).

Regarding the phrase "the position of internal pervasion" (*antarvyāptipakṣa*): the meaning is that this is the position of internal pervasion because, for the sake of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), one does not rely on anything other than the subject itself.
Even by others, the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is accepted as occurring only within one part of the subject (*pakṣa*).

Since their position is that pervasion is external (*bahirvyāpti*), the meaning of "external pervasion" is that, for the sake of apprehending pervasion, one relies on something other than the subject itself. [For example:
"The disputed [entity], such as space (*vyoman*) and so forth, is not permanent..."
However, because existence is intended to be momentary—
meaning that whatever exists is momentary, just like a pot— the intention is that this constitutes an application of a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
What is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the pervasion (*vyāpti*)?
He says: "By means of the reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) and its reversal (viparyaya). He himself will demonstrate this immediately below.

In that context, when it is to be proven that the state of being a *śiṃśapā* tree is fit for the conventional designation (*vyavahāra*) of a "tree," the pervasion (*vyāpti*) must be apprehended through perception and non-perception in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
