The meaning is that the comprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs through perception and non-apprehension (*anupalambha*): because positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is understood through perception in the case of a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is understood through non-apprehension in the case of a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

Since both the fitness for the conventional designation "tree" and the property of being a *śiṃśapā* are specific intrinsic natures (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*) of a tree, their positive concomitance is ascertained by perception in other *śiṃśapā* trees which serve as similar instances.

The meaning is that the determination of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs through perception and non-perception, because in the dissimilar instances (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), such as things other than trees, the absence of those two [existence and momentariness] is not observed, and thus their exclusion is ascertained.
Regarding "of existence and momentariness":

he will later establish this by way of presenting an illustration, beginning with the words "as was stated previously," through the application of a reductio (*prasaṅga*) and its inversion (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*).
This is the intended meaning—the *prasaṅga*, which is the application of a consequence:
if momentariness were not present, then existence (*sattva*) would not be present. For existence is indeed the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).
This is not possible for that which is considered to be stable;
furthermore, the impossibility of that [causal efficiency] in what is considered stable must be understood from other sources.

Moreover, in the case of entities such as jars and the like, which are capable of causal efficiency, it is observed that they are indeed momentary—this being the reversal of the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*).
Regarding this, Śāntarakṣita stated in the section refuting the eternal entities such as space (vyoman) favored by opponents: "If they were devoid of momentariness, their existence would not follow,
because [existence] consists in the performance of causal efficiency (arthakriyā), whether successively or simultaneously."
"Entities are not stable; therefore, they are considered to be devoid of a [permanent] self.
Thus [it is stated in *Tattvasaṃgraha* 143].
And Kamalaśīla has explained: "But how is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this reason established? He says: 'If there were a separation from momentariness, etc.'"
Thus,

[the fact] that causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) is not tenable in entities (*bhāva*) considered to be stable has been demonstrated in detail by the passage beginning with "For instance" (*tathāhi*) and ending with "that [efficiency] does not cohere in stable entities" (*sā ca sthireṣu bhāveṣu na ghaṭate*) (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā 144).
"Or by the proof that sublates the opposite of the probandum (sādhyaviparyayabādhakapramāṇa).

This means that when the momentariness of all entities, such as jars and the like, is to be proven through their existence, there is a proof that sublates the opposite of the probandum—namely, permanence—which is characterized by the exclusion of succession and simultaneity.

By means of this proof, when the "counter-example" (vipakṣa)—such as space (ākāśa) and so forth, which is accepted by the opponent—is analyzed in terms of whether it is a real entity (vastu) or a non-entity (avastu), the pervasion (vyāpti) is determined.

This is the intended meaning: when the momentariness of all entities is to be proven, since a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is impossible, one must ascertain the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) as follows: "whatever is not momentary is not existent, such as space (*vyoman*) and so forth, which are accepted by the opponent.
Now, one might ask: what is this rule that whatever is existent must necessarily be momentary?
Why should it not be suspected that jars and other things, though existent, are indeed non-momentary? [To this we reply: it is not to be so suspected.
Or rather, let there be no existence for these [entities] either;
for existence is the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).
Whatever performs causal efficiency must perform it either successively or simultaneously.
The stability of entities is not tenable in either case;
therefore, they would necessarily be non-entities, like space and so forth.
Alternatively, if they were entities, they must be subsumed within the momentary alone.

[Objection: But surely, for those who do not accept the permanence of space and so forth, since space and the like—as the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)—are unestablished, how can it be said that [the reason] "subsists in the subject which is the counter-example"? [Response:
True;
even so, there is no inconsistency here, for in this case, the dissimilar example (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) need not necessarily be a real entity.
And so it has been said:
"Therefore, in a dissimilar example, the reason is not accepted as being without a locus.
This has also been cited by Kamalaśīla (*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā* 145).
"By means of the threefold perception and non-perception":
perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*anupalambha*); their combination is "perception-and-non-perception," by which [it is meant].
In that regard, there is one perception and two non-perceptions; thus, due to the distinction between its constituent parts, the aggregate is threefold.

The determination of pervasion (*vyāpti*) results from the ascertainment of the relation between cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) by means of the triad of causes characterized as perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*); this is the meaning.
The underlying intention is as follows: positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are the apprehenders of the causal relation;
therein, positive concomitance is cognized through perception.
The negative concomitance (vyatireka) is established through non-perception (anupalambha).
That smoke is perceived when fire is present is a matter of direct perception (pratyakṣa);
that it is not perceived when [fire] is absent is non-perception (anupalambha).
And this non-apprehension occurs both before and after [the effect], because prior to its arising the cause, fire, is absent;
and after [its arising], the cause, fire, has perished.
Thus, there are two kinds of non-perception based on the distinction between earlier and later times.

Ultimately, the determination of pervasion occurs through the determination of the relation of cause and effect by means of a triad of causes characterized by perception and non-perception. [This is expressed as:
"When there is smoke, there is fire."
When there is no fire, then there is no smoke; thus, the threefold nature [of the causal relation] has been stated through perception and non-perception in terms of time (*kāla*).

Now, "wherever there is smoke, there is fire; wherever there is no fire, there is no smoke"; thus, through perception and non-perception in terms of space (*deśa*), these three combined are the cause for ascertaining the relationship of cause and effect.
Intending to show that there are five causes, he says: "or by means of fivefold perception through apprehension."
Having stated the reason for ascertaining pervasion (*vyāpti*), he states the fault in failing to ascertain it: "If there is no certainty of pervasion, the fault is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).
"Like a jar" is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

"This is the reason" means that because the presence [of the reason] in the similar instances (sapakṣa) of the probandum is not certain, and because it is not certain that the absence of the probans in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa)— even though it exists— is necessitated by the absence of the probandum; thus, the reason "possessing breath," when employed by others to prove the possession of a self in a living body, is an "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) reason— this is the sense.
He states [the view] according to the opinion of others: "And another is the uncommon [reason].
For example: "Sound is impermanent because it is audible. This means, in effect, that it exists only in the subject (pakṣa).
"Like a jar, like space"—this is the sequential indication of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
Now, [one might object]: "But if this is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*," [then what follows?])

If it is argued: "That which exists in many places is manifold and subsists in many; [we hold that] the universal (*sāmānya*) and space (*vyoman*) are such. Since we, who assert that 'whatever exists is momentary' and that space exists, have not accepted either the universal or space as real entities, we do not here employ this pervasion (*vyāpti*) as a means of proof for establishing a specific property therein."—the sense of this is: what is the purpose of presenting this relationship of the pervaded and the pervader?
"Regarding the phrase 'for the sake of recollecting the pervasion' (vyāptismaraṇārtham):
this is the underlying intention—whatever resides in many things is itself manifold;

therefore, if one who maintains that a universal resides in many things must accept that the universal is indeed manifold, then for one who asserts that it is a single entity, the claim that it 'resides in many things' must be abandoned."

Thus, when it is intended to demonstrate an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*) to another, and the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between "subsisting in many" (*anekagatatva*) and "manyness" (*anekatva*) has been shown to one who maintains that there is a single universal (*sāmānya*) inherent in many, the point of the undesirable consequence— namely, that "either oneness must be abandoned or inherence in many must not be accepted"— is thereby brought to mind as the element to be demonstrated.

Just as, through the cognition of a single instance—such as in a kitchen—the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between all fire and smoke is established and recalled based on several instances of fire and smoke in several locations;
and this *reductio ad absurdum* (*aniṣṭāpādana*) ultimately results in the negation of the "universal" (*sāmānya*) postulated by the opponent.
Regarding the phrase "by the proponent" (*vādinā*): in a debate for victory (*vijigīṣukathā*), the proponent must formulate a formal argument (*prayoga*) to establish his own position.

By the examination of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) and inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), whatever is to be known therein has been made understood. Now, the pointing out of faults in the reasons (*hetu*) stated by others must be performed;
this introduction is undertaken for the purpose of making that understood, and thus the connection (*saṅgati*) for the examination of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) is demonstrated.
Regarding the phrase "the argument from deficiency" (*nyūnatādyukti*): "deficiency" (*nyūnatā*) refers to the deficiency of any one of the three required characteristics of a valid reason (*hetu*).
This is because [the reason] is that which possesses the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in a state of doubt.

Others maintain that proving what is already established is another point of defeat, known as *siddhasādhana*. However, the logical mark (*liṅga*) possesses three characteristics, and among these three, one is its presence in the subject (*pakṣasattva*).
The *pakṣa* (subject) is that which possesses the doubtful property to be proved (*sādhyadharma*).

If the *sādhya* were already certain, then because the state of having a doubtful *sādhya* would be absent, the characteristic of being a *pakṣa*—namely, its existence as such—would be impossible; consequently, the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*) would not apply. Thus, since it is included within the very category of the unestablished (*asiddha*), it is not a separate point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Therefore, the "lack of a locus for the reason" has been refuted—the uselessness of the reason has been discarded.
For that which is called "capacity" (sāmarthya) is not something other than the essential nature (svarūpa).
In a capable entity, what is called capacity is not some property distinct from the essential nature of the entity;
rather, it is the essential nature of the entity itself.

The meaning is this: since it has been stated that in the absence of that [reason], the very thing itself does not exist, the reason is ineffective; therefore, because the thing lacks substantiality (*avastutva*), it is included within the fallacy of "unestablished in its own nature" (*svarūpāsiddha*). For example, in the case of the proposition, "The self is omnipresent," the term "self" (*ātman*) is the indication of the subject (*pakṣa*).
"Omnipresent" is the statement of the thesis (*sādhya*). In this case, for the Buddhist, the self (*ātman*) itself is not unestablished;
for the subject (*pakṣa*) must be something agreed upon by both parties.
How, moreover, could its quality of being perceived in all locations be established?

Since the very self, which is intended as the subject (*pakṣa*), is unestablished, where could there be the establishment of the reason (*hetu*) intended as a property of that subject? Thus, it is stated by way of a *kaimutika* argument (an argument a fortiori) that [the reason] is unestablished. He demonstrates the non-establishment of the subject with the words beginning "For thus" (*tathā hi*).
And as for the claim that the self is established through mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), he refutes that with the words "of the mental [perception] also.
It is true that there exists the cognition "I am."
He does not rely merely upon "I" alone, [but also thinks],
"I am fair," "I am stout," and so forth.

The thought "I am emaciated" or "I am going" relies exclusively on external attributes such as stoutness; therefore, the implication is that the object of the notion of "I" must necessarily be the body itself, which possesses properties corresponding to that notion.
"Metaphorical, it is logical":
the meaning is that resorting to a metaphorical sense alone is logical.
"Because of the consequence of [the word] having a faltering application."
And Kamalaśīla says: "If this [notion of 'I'] were secondary (gauṇa), then its application would be faltering.
For in the world, when both a lion and a boy are present—one primary and the other superimposed—the cognition 'lion' does not occur unfalteringly with respect to both.
If it is argued that the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) has a faltering application toward the body and so forth because of the perception of their difference—as in 'my body' and so on—that is not so."
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that its application would also falter with respect to the self;
for even in that case, a distinction is observed in the form "my own self.
If it is argued that the difference here is merely conceptual, let it be the same in the other case as well.
Thus [it is said]:
"Because of the absence of a mark consisting of an effect or an essential nature" (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā 90).
The meaning is that there is an absence of either an effect or an essential nature as a logical mark (*liṅga*).
He establishes their very absence with the words beginning "by that which is eternally imperceptible" (*nityaparokṣeṇa*). If that [cause] were present, this would be its effect.

For it is through the observation of the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—namely, that "this [effect] exists when that [cause] exists, and this does not exist when that is absent"—that one can understand, "this is its effect.

Since the self (*ātman*) is accepted as being eternal and imperceptible, there is an absence of the perception of positive and negative concomitance due to the lack of spatial and temporal delimitation; thus, the logical mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the effect is not established.
Furthermore, since the self itself is unestablished, what possibility is there for a logical mark consisting of essential nature (*svabhāva-liṅga*)? This is the intended meaning.
"Others also [argue] by means of an inferential mark (liṅga)" refers to the following point:

regarding the inference presented as "the living body possesses a self because it possesses breath and so forth," since the probandum—the self—is unestablished, the pervasion (vyāpti) of the reason cannot be ascertained through it; therefore, the meaning is that this inference is not capable of proving the existence of the self.
"There is no disagreement whatsoever.

The intended meaning is that there is no disagreement on our part because what we accept as the momentary consciousness (*kṣaṇika-vijñāna*) is merely being designated by you with a different term as the "Self" (*ātman*).
Now, one might object: "But surely, the lack of pervasion (*vyāpty-asiddhi*) is also a logical flaw."

The meaning is this: why is that "unestablishedness due to lack of pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) not mentioned, which is included within "unestablishedness due to the opponent's own admission" (*parāsiddhi*) by virtue of being "conditioned" (*sopādhika*)?
[The author replies: "Not by means of the two specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
For indeed, every single object is a specific characteristic.
That which has its own specific characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is not characterized by any other concomitant universal (*sāmānya*).
Therefore, everything is momentary, being characterized solely by its respective individual manifestation (*vyakti*).

And because those various individual instances are delimited by distinctions of place and time, the apprehension of concomitance (*sāhacarya*) occurs only with respect to those specific individuals; thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) does not at all depend upon a universal (*sāmānya*).
The point is that pervasion is indeed to be grasped only through the medium of universals.
In that regard, [the opponent might argue] that the probans (*sādhana*) is pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*), and so forth.

The sense is that whether the apprehension of the pervasion between the probandum and the probans occurs preceded by the full knowledge of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) or otherwise, there would certainly be inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*); thus, it is not a separate fallacy merely by virtue of suggesting a deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Now, one might object: "For those who do not accept universals (*sāmānya*), how could the apprehension of pervasion occur through a universal?"—this is the doubt raised by the words beginning with "na hy anvaya... etc. He provides the resolution: "There is no such fault."

One might object: "Is 'exclusion' (apoha) not merely a difference in terminology, since even you admit that it must be something that accompanies multiple [individuals]? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Now, what is this so-called exclusion? and so forth. [He concludes: "It is indeed external."
The meaning is that it is precisely that external object, such as a cow and so forth, which is accepted; no other universal (sāmānya) is intended, as is held by others.
Furthermore, exclusion (apoha) is twofold: by way of relative negation (paryudāsa) and by way of absolute negation (prasajyapratiṣedha).
And exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is twofold: consisting of the object (*arthātmā*) and consisting of the cognition (*buddhyātmā*).
Thus it has been said:
"For exclusion is of two kinds, by way of relative negation (*paryudāsa*) and absolute negation (*niṣedha*)."
"Exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is also twofold, based on the distinction between that which consists of cognition and that which consists of the object" (Tattvasaṃgraha 396).
Therein, he first explains exclusion as consisting of the nature of the object— namely, "that from which something else is excluded."

That which is excluded—meaning set apart—from another, such as a buffalo, namely something of a different class like a brindled cow (*śābaleya*), is this very exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), which is *apoha*.
And this exclusion is of the very nature of the brindled cow and so forth, because non-existence (*abhāva*) is not a real entity; such is the meaning.

Although the Bāhuleya is not identical in nature to the Śābaleya, nor is the Śābaleya identical in nature to the Bāhuleya, nevertheless, both are indeed of the nature of the exclusion of non-cows (agovyāvṛtti).
And this has been restated:
"That form which belongs to a brindled cow does not belong to a black cow;
that form which belongs to a black cow does not belong to a brindled cow."
"The exclusion of what does not possess that form is considered equal for both [the object and the cognition].
Thus, "exclusion of what does not possess that form" means the exclusion of the non-cow (*ago-vyāvṛtti*).
And *apoha* is twofold: consisting of the object (*arthātmā*) and consisting of the cognition (*buddhyātmā*).
In that regard, the nature of the object has first been explained;
now he describes the nature of cognition with the words "as it appears," and so forth.

For one who perceives particulars such as the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and the black cow (*bāhuleya*), even though these are mutually distinct by virtue of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), there arises in the intellect a mental form (*ākāra*) whose essence is the appearance of the object, exactly as it appears.

The meaning is that this very thing is called *apoha*. Now, one might ask: why is the designation "exclusion" (*apoha*) applied to this? To that he says: "In this [term], that which is to be excluded (*apohya*)—that is, that which is differentiated—is [contained]. And it has been said:
“Those causes of a single unifying cognition that were stated previously—
objects such as fearlessness and the like— are by their very nature distinct from others.”
Depending upon them, that reflection of the object shines forth within cognition.
Even though the nature of objects is absent in conceptual construction, they are nonetheless determined as being simply "objects."
Because it is distinct from other appearances, it is a real entity excluded from others.
Because it is the cause of attainment, it also leads to movement by means of an unattached object.
That result which is the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is excluded from what is of a different class.
Or rather, because of the determination [of the object] within that [cognition], it is due to those whose [vision] is impaired by identity with it.
"In that regard, the designation 'exclusion of others' (anyāpoha) has been stated with its underlying justification" (Tattvasaṃgraha 317).
Furthermore, the nature of the essence of objects is demonstrated in that very same work:

"Even regarding its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because it exists as the exclusion of others. Thus [he speaks]. Now he explains *apoha* in the form of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)—namely, "according to reality" (*yathātattvam*).
This refers to *apoha* in the form of a simple negation.
The meaning is that apoha consists in the form of a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*).
And this has been stated: "And the non-presuppositional negation is: 'This cow is not a non-cow.'"
This exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is indeed understood with extreme clarity.
Thus (Tattvasaṃgraha 318),
it is "mere cessation";
that is to say, it is not something ceased, for that would be a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion).
For exclusion (*apohana*) is understood through absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*); thus he says: "having made 'exclusion' [the meaning of] 'exclusion' (*apoha*).

With the intention that, under the view of exclusion as absolute negation, in the cognition "cow," the object would be a mere positive entity consisting of the specific individual (*svalakṣaṇa*), and not exclusion, he raises an objection with the words beginning "But surely" (*nanu*), and answers with "No" (*na*).
Although apoha, being of the nature of a non-presuppositional negation (prasajyapratiṣedha), is indeed merely an exclusion,
its object in cognition is rather an affirmation qualified by that [exclusion],
not a mere affirmation alone; such is the meaning.

In order to strengthen the meaning already stated, [the author], while refuting the opinion of others, says: "As for what [is said]..."—namely, that "this is not the nature of a cow, nor is it the nature of a non-cow.
This is the nature of a cow.

The "negation characterized by simple exclusion" (prasajyapratiṣedhalakṣaṇa-apoha), namely "not a non-elephant," is understood subsequently through implication—that is, through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti);
however, first there is only the positive [cognition] of the thing-in-itself, the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa). This is the meaning.
He states that both these views are contrary to worldly experience with the words "That is not so," and so forth.
Now, in verbal usage, the word "cow" alone is uttered; the word "excluded from others" (anyāpoha) is not.
"How could there be a cognition of that which is excluded from others through a word?
For [it seems] the word is one thing, yet the cognition of the object is of another. With this intention, he raises an objection, beginning with "Even though... (yadyapi).
With the intention that the meaning of a word is indeed *apoha*, he offers a rebuttal with the words "even so" (*tathāpi*).
Strengthening the point that *apoha* must be apprehended at the very same time as the comprehension of the object from the word, he says "and just as," etc.
[He refers to] "of perception" (*pratyakṣasya*).
A person seeing a cow immediately apprehends non-existence characterized as an absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), namely, "this is not a horse"; however,
perception itself is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and possesses the power to produce such a conceptual construction.
Rather, the capacity to produce a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is precisely what constitutes perception’s grasping of a conceptual object;
for this very reason, one who sees a cow standing before them immediately arrives at the determination (*adhyavasāya*) that "this is not a horse. Such is the intended meaning.
The same applies to conceptual constructions as well.
Conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are cognitions arising from words.
Perception alone is free from conceptual construction regarding name, genus, and so forth; all other cognition—whether inferential or verbal—is necessarily of the nature of conceptual construction.

The capacity of these verbal conceptualizations to produce an execution corresponding to them— where "execution" consists of engagement or withdrawal— is precisely what is called the apprehension of the absence characterized as apoha.

This means: the determination through exclusion (*apohādhyavasāya*). Therefore, for a person hearing the word "Bring the cow," there immediately arises a determination through exclusion, and he acts in accordance with that determination.
Therefore, the sense is that it is well-established that the convention of words applies to what is excluded [from others].

He determines the nature of the relationship between word and meaning as that of the signified and the signifier: "Therefore, this is established," and so on; specifically, "only through conceptual determination" (adhyavasāyāt).
The meaning is: "Precisely because of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) through exclusion (*apoha*).
The determination occurs by means of the word;
therefore, it is for this very reason that the external object, as excluded [from others], becomes the denotation of the word—this is the meaning.

The meaning is that a word’s denotation of an external object consists precisely in its being the cause of the determination of an exclusion (apoha) which brings about the cognition of an external object;
it does not consist in the manifestation of a particular (svalakṣaṇa).
That is to say, it is not by means of bringing about the manifestation of a particular, as is the case with perception.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "as in the case of direct perception" (*pratyakṣavat*).
Here, he provides the testimony of an authoritative person (*āpta*), saying: "as he said.

Śāntarakṣita has defined the reality of the signifier-signified relationship (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between word and meaning for one whose senses are not engaged [by other objects] through verbal testimony.
In this regard, this first type of exclusion (apoha) by means of words is demonstrated:
because a cognition that determines an external object arises from a word,
and because a reflection having that form [of the object] is produced in the intellect from the word.
"This relationship between the signified and the signifier has arisen as consisting of cause and effect" (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā 318–319).
And it was explained by Kamalaśīla: "The first..."
It has the nature of a reflection of the aforementioned object.
(And the aforementioned object is apoha, which consists of exclusion by negation.
He states the reason for this: "by that which determines an external object," and so forth.
For that alone which appears in the cognition of a word is logically the meaning of the word;
nor is there here a determination of a simple negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha), nor is there an appearance of a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) as occurs in sensory perception. What then?

The meaning is this: a verbal cognition arises that merely determines an external object; therefore, it is that very reflection of the object which is rightly called the "verbal object" (*śābdo 'rthaḥ*), because it appears directly in verbal cognition as being identical with it, and nothing else.

Furthermore, the well-known relationship between a word and its object, characterized as the signifier-signified relation (*vācyavācakabhāva*), does not exist here as anything other than a cause-and-effect relationship.
Rather, he demonstrates that it consists precisely of the nature of cause and effect—by the words "of the reflection of that form," and so forth.

That which has as its form (rūpa), i.e., its essential nature (svabhāva), a form characterized by an externally determined existence is described as such; the compound is "that form" (tadrūpa) and "reflection" (pratibimba).

When that reflection, which belongs to the cognition, arises—that is, when it is produced from the word—then this relationship characterized as signifier and signified (vācyavācaka), upon being examined, is found to consist essentially of a cause-and-effect relation.
To explain: the word is called the "signifier" because it is the producer of the reflection, and that reflection is the "signified" because it is produced by the word.
Thus, in *Tattvasaṃgraha* verses 318–319,
he states the fault in the view that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is denotable by words in reality— beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
And this is set forth for those who remain within their own school (*svasamaya*) and do not accept the validity of verbal testimony (*śabda-prāmāṇya*).

This is the intended meaning: if it were accepted that, in reality, a word directly denotes an external object, then because of the resulting validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the word with respect to that object, the existence of the object understood through the means of knowledge that is verbal testimony (*śabdapramāṇa*) would be certain; consequently, the use of the word "is" (*asti*) in the expression "this cow exists" would be redundant, and the statement "it does not exist" would be untenable.
Therefore, he concludes that it is not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Immediately upon hearing a word, an external object is understood through a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) characterized as previously described, which arises in accordance with linguistic convention; however, its actual existence (*sattā*) is not apprehended.
Consequently, the employment of the word "exists" (*asti*) is justified for the purpose of making that existence known.
He clarifies the point already stated by means of an objection and its resolution—beginning with "Now then" (nanu).
He states the difference between perception and verbal cognition with the words "because the object of perception is non-determinative in nature," and so forth.
Then he says, "But of conceptual construction... (vikalpasya tu).
For perception grasps only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and not even a single conceptual construction; however, everything else is indeed characterized by conceptual construction.
Therefore, that which is other than perception is necessarily of the nature of ascertainment (*viniścaya*).
If a word possesses direct denotative power (*vācakatā*) with respect to an external object, then the comprehension of that object must necessarily be of a determinate nature (*viniścayātmaka*).

Consequently, since the existence (*sattā*) of that object—the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—is already ascertained by that very [determinate cognition], there is no need for the word "exists" (*asti*) to bring about its comprehension; this is the intended meaning.
"We do not perceive any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
He establishes this very impossibility of a means of valid cognition with the words "For instance" (*tathāhi*) and so forth.

That a universal (*jāti*) residing in a particular (*vyakti*) which is perceived by a certain sense organ is itself perceived by that same sense organ—this is merely a convention established within the circle of our opponents' own school.

For even when a person with open eyes is looking [at an object], nothing other than the color blue and so forth, and the specific configuration characterized by the dewlap, tail, and so on, enters the path of vision.
Thus, the point is that perception is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the universal (*sāmānya*).
Now, let it be granted that there is no perception of the universal; [but...]
Furthermore, even for a person who has experienced many individual cows while seeing one cow before him, there arises a certain cognition characterized by a unifying reflection (*ekākāraparāmarśa*);

in that case, some underlying cause (*nimitta*) must be postulated as its objective basis (*ālambana*), because otherwise it would be inexplicable. With the intention that this very [cause] is the universal (*sāmānya*), the author restates and refutes the objection raised by the opponent, beginning with "And not" (*na ca*).
"From the individuals themselves, whose powers are bestowed by their own causes.
This means that individual cows and other such things, being born from their own causes, are born as already distinguished by specific capacities (*śaktiviśeṣa*).

By virtue of these, even though they are mutually distinct, certain individuals alone become the causes for a single uniform conceptual reflection (*parāmarśa*) in the form "cow," and are thus denotable by the word "cow."

Therefore, the point is that one need not postulate a separate universal as an objective support (*ālambana*) in order to account for the occurrence of a cognition that apprehends a single form. To the question, "How can things that are distinct serve as the cause for a cognition that apprehends a single form?", he says: "Even though there is difference," and so forth.
Regarding this, he cites the consensus of authoritative persons (*āpta-saṃvāda*): "Even in the case of difference, some [things] are restricted [to produce a specific effect]," and so on.
"As in the case of the sense organs, etc. means:

just as, despite there being no difference in their status as sense organs (*indriyatva*), the capacity to perceive color is restricted to certain specific individuals while the capacity to perceive taste belongs only to others; so it is here.
By the word "etc.," myrobalan (*harītakī*) and other such things are included.
Now, one might raise the objection: "Even if recourse to a universal (sāmānya) is necessary, what is the use of a universal? The individuals themselves are sufficient;

it is their very nature (svabhāva) to be the cause of a single uniform reflective awareness. To ward off this doubt—that by resorting to such a nature one is merely denying an ontological reality established by valid cognition—the author says: "Furthermore... (kiñca).

This is the intended meaning: according to the view of those who assert that the universal (*sāmānya*) is a distinct, additional category (*padārtha*) excluded from substance (*dravya*) and the other categories, there is held to be an absolute difference between the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*).

Since [categories] such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and "horseness" (*aśvatva*) are even more distinct, then despite this lack of distinction in their being different, cowness inheres (*samavaiti*) only in individual cows and nowhere else.

When the question arises—"What is the determining factor that the universal 'horseness' inheres only in individual horses and not elsewhere?"—the answer they too must give by resorting to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is simply this: "It is the very nature of universals such as 'cowness' that they do not inhere elsewhere.
Therefore, what is this objection against us, namely, that "an answer based on intrinsic nature is inconsistent"?
"The distinction is this: the response being presented by us is authoritative because it relies upon intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), whereas that being presented by others is unauthoritative.
Refuting the inference relied upon by others as a means of establishing a general principle, he says: "And likewise, this other [argument]," and so forth.
To this, it is said: "In this regard..."
Having formulated the thesis, he refutes it with the words "of the qualified cognition," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "distinct qualifier":
that which is a qualifier distinct from the qualificand—that which appears as a qualifier in a qualified cognition while appearing as the qualificand itself, being distinct from the qualificand.
The meaning is that it is inseparable from the apprehension of that [object].
He states the refutation regarding the first alternative: "because there is no appearance of both in a perception that grasps a real entity.
The meaning is: because there is no appearance of both the qualifier and the qualified.

The claim that the perception of an object as "cow" manifests both the individual body (*piṇḍa*) and the universal (*sāmānya*) of cowness—which is distinct from it—is contrary to everyone's experience;
for the sense of one looking at something standing before them is that only the bare object (*vastumātra*) flashes forth.
He states another refutation: "and [the problem of] being a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*)."
He establishes the inconclusiveness [of the reason] with the words: "even without the apprehension of a distinct qualifier.
For example, as in the case of "the pot possesses its own nature" (*svarūpavān ghaṭaḥ*).
Indeed, the nature of the pot is not something separate from the pot itself.
Whether one says "cowness is a universal" or "it is a universal," the universal is not something other than cowness;
nor is the state of being a universal distinct from cowness itself.
But that [existence] is indeed its very nature.
He states the refutation regarding the second alternative with the words beginning "In the second...
He establishes the point of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) with the phrase "just as in the case of 'the pot possesses its own nature' (*svarūpavān ghaṭaḥ*)," and so forth.

The point is this: just as in the perception "this is a cow," which in reality grasps only the thing-in-itself, the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) is established by resorting to an imagined difference—as in the case of "the pot possesses its own nature"—so too, although the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is non-different from the individual body (*piṇḍa*), the relationship between qualifier and qualified can be established by resorting to an imagined difference; thus, there is no contingency of a different meaning (*arthāntara*). The uniform linguistic usage "this is a cow" relies solely upon the exclusion of the non-cow (*agovyāvṛtti*).
And he states that this exclusion is not distinct from the excluded object itself, saying: "because it is produced by the experience of the exclusion of the non-cow.

Thus, having refuted the argument favored by others as a proof for the existence of a universal, he demonstrates the argument that negates the universal, beginning with: "for the purpose of negating the universal"—namely, that "if something is present here and meets the conditions for perception, yet is not perceived [it does not exist]."
The reason (*hetu*) is its non-perception despite meeting the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*).
He dispels the suspicion that the reason might be unestablished (*asiddhi*) by stating, "and there is no possibility of it being unestablished.
[He further specifies: "accompanied by color and shape" (*varṇasaṃsthānasahita*).

The point is this: even when there is a conjunction with the sense organs and so forth, and when the collection of perceptual conditions is present and a particular individual is being perceived, the "cowness" (*gotva*) which is disputed does not appear at all;
rather, what is perceived is the individual's own nature, consisting of color and shape.
Since no universal "cowness" distinct from that is perceived, the reason [adduced in the argument] is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

He restates and then refutes the objection that "just as knowledge, though not within the range of visual perception, is not non-existent, so too a universal, though not within the range of visual apprehension, is not non-existent"—by means of the words "nor even," and so forth.
He concludes the refutation of the universal that was previously introduced with the words "therefore.
As for the phrase "nor even": this investigation has been undertaken as a secondary consequence of what preceded.

In the section on the examination of fallacies regarding the reason (*hetudoṣa*), while discussing the occasion of the unestablished (*asiddhi*), an investigation into universals (*sāmānya*) was introduced as a relevant digression.
That incidental discussion was concluded with the summary: "Therefore, every conditioned entity (*saṃskṛtavastu*) is empty of the universals imagined by others.
Just as every conditioned entity is devoid of universals, so too it is not produced by anyone; thus, this [discussion] has followed as a further consequence of what was already under consideration.
Is it not the case that this inquiry proceeds by following the exposition of a refined subject matter, which involves traversing various branches [of scripture]?
This is not so.
[For instance: "If the eternal agent is not the cause of the world, then what is its cause?"

Since the proof [of the self] is established by such statements as "the karma of sentient beings, known as wholesome and unwholesome," this serves as the gateway for one entering into the determination of the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
By this, the objection that "it is redundant because the Lord (*īśvara*) was already refuted as the creator of the world" is answered;
for here, the negation of him proceeds by means of a different method.

In that [previous section], there was a refutation of the formal argument (prayoga) put forward by others as a proof for the existence of Īśvara; here, however, the method of refutation is different, consisting in the demonstration that his status as the creator of the world and so forth is untenable.
To begin with, it is not logical that he be eternal.
"Eternal" means devoid of birth and death.
If it is incapable,
then to say "it is nonetheless an agent" is contradictory;
if, on the other hand, it is capable and eternal, [then it must always act].
Then he says that this is the fault: "while the agent is eternal and capable. Its essential nature (svarūpa) remains so even at the time of dissolution;
for the nature of that which is eternal cannot change due to a difference in time.
The sense is that if it were to differ, then impermanence itself would necessarily follow.
Having raised the objection that the non-simultaneity of creations and so forth is rooted in the absence of auxiliary causes, he refutes it.
Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of auxiliary causes" (*sahakārivirahāt*) and so forth:
since even an impermanent auxiliary cause is dependent upon that [permanent entity], the following objection applies equally here as well:
"If this permanent entity is capable, by virtue of being the cause of every effect, in producing its auxiliaries, why does it not produce them all simultaneously? This is the intended meaning.
Now, one might object with the following intention: "Granted that this [Lord] is capable and eternal, yet he is the Supreme Lord;

he would act if there were a desire to do so, and would not act if there were no such desire. Thus, there is no contingency of all effects occurring simultaneously. With this in mind, the author raises the objection: "Because the Lord possesses intelligence," and so forth.
This doubt might arise in the theory of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause independent of a presiding agent,
because of its insentience; however,
the point is that there is no occasion for such a doubt regarding us, who accept a conscious cause.
With the intention of asking why there is no simultaneity of desires, he says: "Those too...
[referring to] "by means of adventitious powers through the metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) of auxiliary factors.
The underlying thought is this: it is true that even the auxiliary factors are dependent upon this [consciousness].

These [powers] are specific forms of the power belonging to this [eternal cause], and while it is eternal and capable of producing all effects, those powers characterized as auxiliary conditions (sahakāri-lakṣaṇāḥ śaktayaḥ) are nonetheless adventitious (āgantukyaḥ); thus, there is no consequence of the simultaneous occurrence of creations and so forth—this is the intended meaning.
And that [cause] is eternal.
With the intention that its capacity is unimpeded and all auxiliary causes are dependent upon it,
yet the claim that those auxiliaries are only occasional is contradictory, he says: "In that case, even the mother would be [the cause]."
The meaning is that this is all insubstantial.
He objects by relying on a specific nature of the effect, saying: "But surely this is the very nature of the effect. He refutes this, saying: "That is not so."
Even if it were to become identical with the nature of another, why would it not accomplish its own effect?
The point is that if it does not accomplish it, then it is simply incapable.
He states another objection, beginning with "nor also."
For you indeed maintain that this creator produces entities sequentially;
however, it is untenable for an eternal and capable [agent] to bring about effects sequentially,
because the agent is independent and possesses [inherent] capability— this is the sense.
Regarding this, he states the corroboration from an authoritative source (āpta): "As he says.
"At the two times" means at the time of accomplishing the task and at a time other than that.

"Of one whose nature is similar"—that is, the essential form (*svarūpa*) of that which is capable and eternal never undergoes transformation; for if it did, the consequence would be impermanence (*anityatā*). This is the intended meaning. By the phrase "by this": [it refers to] the individual selves (*jīvātman*), who are regarded as eternal because of their eternity.

Regarding "non-momentary things"—that is, things such as jars and the like which are considered to be non-momentary—the point is this: the production of effects observed to occur sequentially is not possible for anything whatsoever that is considered to be stable. And it has been said by Śāntarakṣita:
For effects indeed delay due to the absence of their causes;
but when a capable cause is present, by what could their postponement be caused?
Thus (Tattvapañjikā 146).
For this very reason, it is well-established that all things capable of performing an action are momentary.
Now, one might object: "The momentariness of everything contradicts direct perception."

One might raise the objection that "it is indeed non-momentariness itself that is apprehended by perception," to which [the author] replies with the words "And there is no contradiction with perception here" (*na cātra pratyakṣavirodhaḥ*).
To this, they respond with the passage beginning "by perception" (*pratyakṣeṇa*), etc.,
[stating] "of the non-momentary" (*akṣaṇikasya*).
This refers to the state of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*).
"Not indeed" (*na hi*)—the underlying intention is this: perception (*pratyakṣa*) is indeed direct apprehension (*sākṣātkāra*).
And that [cognition] is momentary;
when it arises by itself, it grasps only the present thing-in-itself,
and not its connection with preceding or succeeding moments.
Furthermore, perishing itself in the next moment, it is not capable of grasping the connection of a single entity with multiple moments.

Moreover, the manifestation of the preceding and succeeding moments could not occur at the time of the direct perception of the present; for if that were the case, those two times would also result in being present. Thus he says: "Not before, nor after."

If, however, it were admitted that even the connection with preceding and succeeding moments is manifested at the time of perception, then the temporal continuity of the object being directly perceived—extending from its birth until its destruction—would also be manifested.
In that case, according to your own view, the very limit of the destruction of an arisen object would become known; with this intention, he says: "having birth and destruction as its limits."
Now, [the opponent] objects: "Does not the perception of recognition grasp the connection with two points in time? To this, he replies:

"By this... He establishes that recognition is not a form of perception (apratyakṣatva) by what is intended by the phrase "by this," namely through the passage beginning with "for knowledge is direct intuition" (*sākṣātkāri hi jñānam*).
That which is to be directly intuited...
This means it is capable of being directly realized. Furthermore, recollection is not perception;
the meaning is that recollection does not have the nature of direct perception.
Here, while setting aside the view of Kumārila, he raises an objection from that perspective with the word "atha" (now/if). [The objection is:
"It would not directly perceive its present state.
However, the word "ayam" (this) refers to the grasping of what is present.
And since that [cognition] depends upon the senses, the perceptuality of this sensory cognition remains entirely unimpeded;
thus, the point is that momentariness contradicts perception.
He restates the meaning already expressed in the verse with the words "yadāha" and so forth.
Regarding the term "atirekiṇī": it means distinct from memory (*smṛti*).
The meaning is that it is a means of valid cognition consisting of direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*).
He refutes this statement of Kumārila as follows: "In that case, recognition would consist of both recollection and apprehension.
[Objection: But surely this recognition is not distinct from memory.

Because there is no apprehension of it as "that" (saḥ) in the same way as "this" (ayam), and because the senses cannot function with respect to that which remains in a state of being remembered, it does not have the nature of direct perception;
and if it were apprehended in its present state, it would not have the nature of memory.
Therefore, it would follow that [the cognition] must consist of both remembrance and apprehension;
however, it cannot have the nature of a direct perceptual means of knowledge distinct from remembrance.
The point is that a single cognition possessing both forms is not possible.
Now, it might be argued: "The very same thing is remembered in one form, but perceived in another; however, its predominance is determined by the form in which it is being perceived."

However, the dependence on mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) pertains only to the aspect of the secondary characterization (*upalakṣaṇāṃśa*) of the object being perceived; therefore, with the intention that this recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) consists solely in the apprehension of the object standing before one, [the author] restates and refutes the opponent’s objection beginning with the words "yena hi... (for by which...). [The phrase] "it cannot be asserted by one who is not insane" means: [The opponent might argue: "If the cognition of a jar arises from the contact between the sense organ and the jar, then why does it not arise when there is contact with another jar? Furthermore, since the sense organ is not in contact with the jar at the time of the initial perception, how can the subsequent cognition of the jar be produced? Moreover, if the sense organ were to produce a cognition even without contact, then why would it not produce a cognition of everything else as well? And if it were to produce a cognition through contact with something else, then why would it not produce a cognition of that other thing? Therefore, the sense organ produces a cognition of the jar precisely because it is in contact with the jar. To this, [the author] replies: This is not so. For it is not the case that the sense organ produces a cognition of the jar simply because it is in contact with the jar; rather, it is because the jar possesses a specific nature (*svabhāva*) such that it produces a cognition of itself when in contact with the sense organ. If it were otherwise, then just as a jar produces a cognition of itself when in contact with the sense organ, so too would a cloth produce a cognition of itself when in contact with the sense organ. But this is not observed. Therefore, the sense organ produces a cognition of the jar only when it is in contact with the jar, and it does not produce a cognition of a cloth or anything else. Thus, the objection is refuted. Furthermore, the opponent might say: "Even if the sense organ produces a cognition of the jar only when in contact with the jar, it still does not follow that the subsequent cognition of the jar is produced, for the initial perception has already ceased. Since a cognition is momentary, it does not persist until the time of the subsequent cognition. Therefore, the sense organ must produce the subsequent cognition of the jar without depending on the initial perception. To this, [the author] replies: This is not so. For the subsequent cognition of the jar is indeed produced by the sense organ in dependence upon the initial perception. Just as a seed produces a sprout in dependence upon water and soil, so too the sense organ produces the subsequent cognition of the jar in dependence upon the initial perception. If it were otherwise, then just as a seed produces a sprout without depending on water and soil, so too the sense organ would produce the subsequent cognition of the jar without depending on the initial perception. But this is not observed. Therefore, the subsequent cognition of the jar is produced by the sense organ in dependence upon the initial perception. Thus, the objection is refuted. Furthermore, the opponent might say: "Even if the subsequent cognition of the jar is produced by the sense organ in dependence upon the initial perception, it still does not follow that it is a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), for recognition requires the synthesis of two cognitions. Since the initial perception and the subsequent cognition are distinct, they cannot be synthesized. Therefore, the subsequent cognition of the jar is merely a new perception, not a recognition. To this, [the author] replies: This is not so. For the subsequent cognition of the jar is indeed a recognition, because it apprehends the object as being the same as that previously perceived. Just as one recognizes a person seen before by saying "this is that very same person," so too one recognizes a jar seen before by saying "this is that very same jar. If it were otherwise, then just as one recognizes a person seen before, so too one would recognize a different jar seen later. But this is not observed. Therefore, the subsequent cognition of the jar is a recognition. Thus, the objection is refuted. In short, the dependence on mental impressions pertains only to the aspect of the secondary characterization of the object being perceived; therefore, with the intention that this recognition consists solely in the apprehension of the object standing before one, [the author] restates and refutes the opponent’s objection beginning with the words "yena hi...". [The phrase] "it cannot be asserted by one who is not insane" means: [the opponent's argument is untenable].
One who says that a single entity becomes two when its form (*rūpa*) is divided would indeed be insane;
for the meaning is that the division of form is not distinct from the division of its own nature (*svarūpa*).
"Even if [it exists]" means even if one accepts the existence of both recollection and perception regarding a single thing.
"It would result in being both perceptible and imperceptible" means that for a single cognition, there would follow both partial perceptibility and partial imperceptibility,
rather than perceptibility alone.
Therefore, the cognition of recognition is indeed erroneous because it lacks a real object (*nirviṣayatvāt*).
"Because it lacks a real object" means that it does not have as its object a thing as it actually exists.
And Śāntarakṣita said:
But surely, recognition arises in the form "this is that very same thing," occurring when the sensory faculties are functioning, being unshakable and uncontradicted.
Therefore, this sublation by perception (pratyakṣabādha) is unavoidable in all reasons adduced for the purpose of establishing momentary destruction; it is not tenable.
Indeed, recognition cannot be established as a form of direct perception,
because it is expressed through verbal designation and its object is not demonstrable as a distinct entity.
And recognition is erroneous, for it occurs with respect to each [object] as being distinct from that [other],
yet functions by means of a determination of non-difference even though the forms are different.

Thus, [the author] states the formal argument (*prayoga*) for the erroneous nature of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in the *Tattvaprakāśa* (157): "And the formal argument is as follows" (*prayogaś caivam iti*).
"That [recognition], in reality, does not have a single object" (*sa tattvato naikālambanaḥ*).
In reality, it does not have an identical object;
that is to say, its object is an imputed identity.
This is an "observation of what is pervaded by the contradictory" (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*).
He establishes the perception of the pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*) with the words "of unity and plurality," and so forth.
"Of unity and plurality" means of difference and non-difference.

He states that because there is a contradiction between the objects, there is also a contradiction between the two perceptions which have them as their objects, saying: "of those two objects as well."
Recognition is not a sublater of the inference of momentariness;
the point is that it is erroneous.
He raises the objection that there is no contradictory pervasion (viruddhavyāpti) with the words "If not... and so forth.

"From this very reason" means the following intention: [Objection] But surely this reason is contradictory; for recognition (pratyabhijñā) indeed makes known the connection with that same place and time of what was experienced at another place or at another time, as in "this blue is that very same [blue]," and this is its general rule.
Furthermore, there is a unity of the universal (*sāmānya*) in cases such as [grass] that has been cut and grown again;
thus, the nature of recognition is not contradicted by the fact that it does not have a single object, just as [the notion of] fire is not contradicted by water.
If it is argued that there is also inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā) precisely because of contradiction, we say no.
It has already been stated more than once that it is logically untenable for a permanent entity to perform an action either successively or simultaneously;
therefore, since the status of recognition as having a single object is not established, there is neither contradiction nor inconclusiveness.
[Objection: "But surely recognition itself (*pratyabhijñāna*) naturally brings about the understanding of the identity of an object.
[Reply: Not at all;

for it is precisely this—whether it is logical for that [recognition] to have a single object as its basis or not—that is being investigated today. Thus, he says, "And recognition itself... [in order to show that] the demonstration of the identity of an object through recognition is untenable.

He concludes the argument begun regarding the impossibility of the world being created by an intelligent agent: "Therefore, this remains established. Regarding the phrase "the world of beings" (*sattvaloka*):
"beings" (*sattvāni*) refers to living creatures.
The world characterized by height is the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*).
The receptacle-world (*bhājanaloka*)—the world that serves as the vessel or the support for sentient beings, that is, living creatures—is the receptacle-world.
It is this very mind that constructs this exceedingly diverse [world]; "mind," "intellect" (*buddhi*), and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) are synonyms.
The meaning is that it is the mind alone that appears as the external world; thus, the entire universe is merely a manifestation of the mind.

For it has been stated that the whole world is born of karma, and karma is nothing other than the mind. There are two kinds of truth: ultimate truth (*pāramārthika-satya*) and conventional truth (*sāṃvṛtika-satya*).

In this regard, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*pāramārthika-dṛṣṭi*), the mind alone is the root of everything; however, from the perspective of conventional truth (*sāṃvṛti-dṛṣṭi*), the entire world of sentient beings is born from karma.
Thus, the meaning is that apart from both karma and the mind, there is no root for the world whatsoever.
This is stated from the viewpoint of the speaker, relying upon the Vaibhāṣika system.
The internal divisions such as the Vaibhāṣikas and others arose after the Blessed One; that is to say, it is based on his words that the Vaibhāṣikas proceed.
Now, while establishing [the Buddha] as omniscient, he restates the opponent's doubt with the word "nanu" (but surely).
"What is the means of valid cognition?"—the meaning is that there is no means of valid cognition [to prove it].

Intending to show that inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he says: "It is said. One who possesses the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the four truths is omniscient (*sarvajña*);

and since direct realization is a vivid manifestation (*sphuṭāvabhāsa*), he demonstrates the formal application (*prayoga*) for their vivid manifestation with the words beginning "Whoever... The first sentence establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

And the second [member] is that which makes known the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*); therein, the reason (*hetu*) is "the quality of the mind accompanied by diligent, uninterrupted, and long-term practice," and the probandum (*sādhya*) is "fitness for becoming manifest."

The example is the form of a beloved woman as it appears in the mind of a lover; the forms of the objects of the four noble truths as they appear in the mind of one possessing the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) constitute the subject (*pakṣa*).

By means of this essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), once the capacity for the clear manifestation of the four noble truths is established, the proof of omniscience—which was previously obstructed by the possibility that clear realization might not occur—is thereby refuted.

This is what must be understood here: the intention of one who says that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for an omniscient being is this— that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not a means of valid cognition regarding him,
for no one is seen who perceives everything.

Nor is it inference, because that [inference] operates only among things of a perceived similar class; nor is it verbal testimony, because there is doubt regarding the validity of the words that would convey it.
Furthermore, omniscience is not tenable;
for no one is able to perceive objects that transcend the senses,
since objects are indeed manifested in dependence upon the senses.
Even at the height of wisdom, one cannot know anything by completely transcending the inherent nature of the sense organs and their objects. And it has been said:

"Even those men who are seen to possess excellence through the power of their wisdom, intelligence, and strength, do so only by degrees of slight difference, and not by perceiving what is beyond the senses."
For even a wise man, though capable of perceiving subtle matters,
excels other men by not overstepping the bounds of his own kind.
Thus [it is said] (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā 825).
Therefore, even when there is an excellence of practice, it is simply impossible for the objects and the sense faculties to transcend their own inherent natures.
As for the claim that the perception of supersensuous objects might occur through the power of yoga-practice—
That too is untenable;

for even that [meditation], when examined, is characterized by contemplation on an object and consists of an uninterrupted stream of memory, and is not itself of the nature of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*).

Since memory also has as its support an object previously experienced, one does not achieve direct perception of supersensuous objects even through the practice of yoga; thus, an omniscient being is not established.
The intention behind establishing the existence of the Omniscient One is this: as long as no subverting evidence is perceived, it cannot be determined that [the Omniscient One] does not exist;
for the non-existence of an object cannot be established by mere non-perception.
How, then, could the negation of an omniscient being be established merely by the non-perception of means of valid cognition such as perception?
Nor can there be a denial of those things belonging to dreams which are cognizable only by a particular person and not perceived by others.
As long as no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) is found, doubt regarding such matters will certainly persist.

This being so, how are you able to refute the omniscience of the Sugata? Surely an objection has been presented by the statement, "Omniscience is not possible," and so forth. To this it is replied: there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
Furthermore, this specific nature of the sense organs and their objects is such that the eye perceives only form and not sound or other objects, while the ear perceives only sound and not form;
likewise, form is perceived by the eye alone and not by any other sense organ.
"Sound is perceived by the auditory faculty alone, and not by any other sense organ.
This is true;
if it were perceived by a sense organ, then it would indeed be so.

If it is argued that this restriction does not apply to the mind (*citta*), [we reply: Is it not the case that the sense-faculty called "mind" (*manas*) would necessarily function toward an object only through the medium of the external sense-faculties? This is an inviolable rule. Not so.
There is no such thing as a faculty called "mind" (manas) that exists immediately [after consciousness];
mind, thought (citta), intellect (buddhi), and consciousness (vijñāna) are not different in meaning.
A stream of consciousness (cittadhārā), distinct for each sentient being, continues on.
And it becomes defiled by all the various impurities such as passion;
furthermore, the web of impurities arising from ignorance is adventitious,
and it is diminished through the cultivation of selflessness.
And through the cultivation of the four noble truths, there is excellence;

for just as the stains of passion and so forth are diminished by the cultivation of selflessness, so too does wisdom increase through the cultivation of the four noble truths that has reached its peak.

When the cultivation of the noble truths—which is characterized by yoga, continuous, diligent, and practiced throughout many lifetimes—has reached its ultimate limit, the four noble truths become directly perceived.
For even perception born of yoga possesses a vivid manifestation;
however, the restriction regarding the nature of sense-faculties and their objects applies only to sensory perception, not to all forms of non-conceptual (aparokṣa) cognition.
Through the direct perception of the Four Noble Truths, one becomes omniscient.
Regarding the statement that "the excellence of wisdom arises from diligent and uninterrupted practice," this is the formal argument (*prayoga*): "Whosoever [practices] diligently...
and so forth; it is just as, for example, the form of a young woman appears to a man filled with desire.
The phrase "capable of manifesting clearly" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
The mind of one who desires takes on the form of that which is desired; therefore, the form of the desired young woman becomes a quality (guṇa) of the mind.

Just as this form of a young woman, which has become a quality of the mind of one who desires her, becomes capable of clear manifestation when accompanied by diligent, uninterrupted, and long-term practice; likewise, the mind of a discerning person, when contemplating the forms of the Four Noble Truths, becomes such that this form of the Four Noble Truths— which has become a quality of the mind— is, through diligent, uninterrupted, and long-term practice, rendered capable of clear manifestation.
And because that [reality] appears clearly through direct perception, one becomes omniscient.
What are the four noble truths?
They are suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
The aggregate of form, the aggregate of sensation, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness—this pentad of aggregates is called suffering.
That which is the origination of this pentad of aggregates is origination;
that which is the cessation of suffering is cessation.
That which is the door to this cessation is called the path.

Establishing that the cause is free from the three types of defects, he establishes therein the absence of the fallacies of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) and the unestablished reason (*hetvasiddhi*), beginning with the statement "not, first of all, by way of the locus.
This refers to the subjects—the loci—which are indicated as the thesis (*pakṣa*).

For these [mental states], having entered the path of conceptualization, take on the forms of the four noble truths such as suffering and so forth, and manifest within the surface of the mind in each individual; thus, there is no lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
The word "mere" (*mātra*) in the phrase "merely a quality of the mind" has a restrictive sense.

Since the object of cognition possesses the form of the mind, the mere object is indeed the very form of the mind; thus, those mental qualities manifest within each individual, and therefore there is no lack of proof for the reason (*hetvasiddhi*).

Furthermore, since it is possible for the subject (*dharmin*) to possess the quality of being a mental attribute distinguished by diligent, uninterrupted, and long-term practice, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is not untenable.
Nor is this [reason] contradictory (*viruddha*).

"In the form of the beloved"—that is, in the form of a young woman within the mind of the lover; or alternatively, while the form of the beloved, the young woman, is being meditated upon by the lover.
For if the reason (*hetu*) is pervaded by the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), there is indeed a contradiction.
But it is not so in this case;

for those mental qualities—such as the form of a young woman—that are distinguished by practice that is respectful, uninterrupted, and long-term, are all indeed capable of clear manifestation, and it is not the case that none of them are capable of clear manifestation.

[Objection: Even if some mental qualities distinguished by respectful, uninterrupted, and long-term practice are seen to be capable of clear manifestation, what rule guarantees that all of them are likewise so?
Therefore, warding off the doubt that "this reason is inconclusive" (anaikāntika), he says: "And it is not inconclusive.
We do not assert pervasion (vyāpti) based merely on the observation of concomitance;
rather, we do so because of the necessary connection (pratibandha) consisting in the relation of cause and effect. He states this with the words beginning with "through repeated practice" (abhyāsa).
To the question, "How is the relationship of cause and effect established between these two?", he says: "By means of perception and non-perception.
This means by means of both perception and non-perception.
Furthermore, the relationship of cause and effect is established through the operation of positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka).

In that regard, positive concomitance (*anvaya-sahacāra*) is apprehended through perception, while negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*) is apprehended through non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).

Thus, by means of perception and non-apprehension, the causal relation between the two is established through a universal induction; therefore, the establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs through the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) characterized as the causal relation.
The state [of being].
In the present context, he establishes direct perception and non-perception by saying "for instance" (*tathāhi*).
"Existing within the mind of the lover" means existing within the consciousness of the lover.
"Established by three kinds of perception and non-perception" means that "perception and non-perception" (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) of these two; here,
"non-perception" refers to the single non-perception consisting of the state of appearing clearly (*sphuṭābhatva*).
The meaning is that there are two types of perception— namely, perception subsequent to practice and clear perception—
and the collection of perception and non-perception is endowed with these three modes;
that which is to be established by this is the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

This is what is being made known here: just as there are two types of perception—namely, the perception resulting from subsequent practice and the perception of clear manifestation—likewise, why should there not be two types of non-perception—namely, the non-perception of mental qualities distinguished by prior practice and the non-perception of clear appearance? In reality, however, one type of non-perception is defined as that wherein the effect is not perceived even when all other causes, including itself, are present.
However, when there is the perception of the effect upon the existence [of the cause], that is one instance of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
And thus, it is logical that the determination of the causal relationship is established through both direct perception and non-perception (*anupalambha*).

This being the case, if two instances of direct perception were to be produced by counting the perception of the cause and the perception of the effect separately—and if two instances of non-perception were relied upon by counting the non-perception of the cause and the non-perception of the effect separately—then...

Why should there not be a fourfold division? With this very doubt in mind, the previous statement— “the effect-reason, such as smoke, [is established] by means of three kinds of perception and non-perception, or five kinds of perception and non-perception, regarding the subject of the example, such as a kitchen, through [inference] with fire and so forth”— was formulated in an alternative manner.

However, as we observe the intention of the author of this treatise (*nibandhakāra*), it appears that the previous commentary does not follow the author’s own intent. He raises an objection with the words "Now, [is it not the case]...

(*nanu*). The intention of the objector is this: even if the direct realization of the Four Noble Truths is established, the realization of everything (*sarvasākṣātkaritva*) is not possible; therefore, how is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) established? Although [the Buddha] has no doubt regarding the four noble truths...
Not even a single entity [exists].
Nevertheless, clearly establishing omniscience, he raises an objection with the words "by means of the entirety" (aśeṣeṇa);
that is to say, by means of completeness.
Regarding the term "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*): the word *dharma* denotes existence in general.
That which has entered into the state of cause and effect—such as seeds, sprouts, and so forth—as well as mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), is conventionally designated as *dharma*.
Regarding the phrase "that which accords with valid cognition":

the reason (*hetu*) is the quality of stating an object that is ascertained through correspondence with valid cognition (*pramāṇa-saṃvādi-niścita-artha-vacanatva*); the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is the state of being preceded by direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of that object.
"Directly manifest cognition" means that which is a cognition directly manifest.
[The phrase] "either directly or through a succession" [is explained as follows].
The meaning is that it is preceded by direct realization, whether immediately or through a lineage.

When something is stated after one has personally realized the burning power of fire for oneself, it is immediate; whereas when the validity of a speaker’s word is applied based on another’s statement—without having personally experienced such knowledge for oneself—it is mediated through a lineage.
Likewise, regarding the statement of those who follow the Sugata that "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are indeed momentary," this is a "reason based on effect" (*kāryahetu*),
because the stated statement is the effect of the stated direct realization.

He establishes the absence of defects such as the unestablished nature (*asiddhi*) of the reason with the words "there is no unestablished nature for this," and so forth. This is because of the proof of the momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).

For momentary destruction is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena; and since this statement makes that meaning known, the reason—defined as the cognition of an object determined to be in accord with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—is not unestablished. This is the intended sense.
