Revealing the purpose of the qualification of the reason (*hetu*)—namely, that its object is ascertained by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—he wards off the charge of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*), stating: "even though mere speech may be preceded by doubt or error.
Regarding the phrase "of that whose object is ascertained by a means of valid cognition": it means of that sentence whose object has been determined by a *pramāṇa*.
Now, what is the proof for the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between these two?
To this, he says: "By means of perception and non-perception.
For a statement that accords with valid cognition has as its effect the direct realization of its own object.

The meaning is that, through perception and non-perception— namely, the observation of the effect when the cause is present and the non-observation of the effect when the cause is absent— the pervasion between cause and effect is indeed grasped without obstruction;
yet, even in this regard, if there is still doubt:
He says "otherwise" because there would be the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of the logical reason based on effect (*kāryahetu*).
Herein is the summary of the proof for the Omniscient One; this has already been elucidated by us elsewhere.
The object of cognition does not cease merely because the means of cognition cease;
for the cessation of that which is not pervading does not entail the cessation of that which is not pervaded.
Furthermore, that cessation of the means of cognition is not observed in all cases, and thus cannot serve as a proof.
The perception of that [omniscience] is difficult to grasp within the multitude of all cognizing subjects;
nor is any subverting proof found against the omniscient one. As for those who are indeed Bodhisattvas, they are by their very nature composed of compassion.
Through proficiency in the practice of meditating on the selflessness of all phenomena without exception,
they have become free from all obscurations and devoid of the stains of passion and the like;
by means of the excellence of wisdom, they have attained omniscience.
Through the power of the excellence of their compassion and the desire to uplift all sentient beings,
those Buddhas who remain as long as saṃsāra lasts— pure like clear crystal and unshakable by the winds of defects— are the benefactors of the world. Thus it is said.

"But what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the succession of existences?"—the word "what" here signifies a rejection; the meaning is that there is no such means of valid cognition. This is the doubt held by the Lokāyatas and their followers, because they do not reject anything else.
This is the intended meaning: let it be granted that for those who accept a permanent self, there might somehow be hope for rebirth;
but for one who asserts the momentariness of everything, how could the talk of rebirth be possible?
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "It is said," and so forth.

Even by us, who maintain the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), it is indeed admitted that for every sentient being, a stream of consciousness (*vijñānadhārā*)—which serves as the objective basis for the notion of "I"—continues from one existence to another;
specifically, that each preceding mind produces the subsequent mind according to its own nature.
Therefore, even the mind existing at the time of death possesses the capacity to produce another mind.
With the intention of showing that this is the logical application here, he says: "Whatever is a mind, that connects with another mind.
This means it produces it.
Furthermore, this relationship of producer and produced exists only between a preceding and a succeeding mind that belong to the same continuum.
The subject (*pakṣa*) is the mind existing at the time of death;
the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is the state of producing another moment of consciousness; the logical reason (*hetu*) is "being a mind" (*cittatva*);
and the present mind is the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Nor is there a deviation [of the rule] by means of the final mind of an Arhat.

The meaning is that even the followers of the Sugata accept that the final mind of Arhats—those from whom passion and the like have departed—does not produce another subsequent mind; thus, there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) in that case.
He dispels this suspicion of inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) by stating: "because that is known solely through scripture."

This is the intended meaning: one who asserts the invalidity of another's scripture should not raise the doubt of inconclusiveness by means of the final mind of an Arhat, which is established solely through that other's own scripture;
for if one accepts the position of another, then one must likewise accept rebirth as well.
Or, it is because [the final mind] gives rise to another mind free from afflictions.
This is the intended meaning: it is not accepted by all Buddhists that the final mind of an Arhat does not produce another subsequent thought;
indeed, some say as much.

In reality, even for those who are free from passion and whose roots of ignorance have been entirely removed, a stainless stream of consciousness (cittasantati) that is untainted by the impurities of the afflictions (kleśa) and so forth certainly continues; thus, there is no fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntika).
And it has been said by Śāntarakṣita:
"How could the consciousness of one whose outflows (āsrava) are exhausted fail to undergo reconnection?"
If it is argued that this is not so because of the doctrine of another [school], we say no,
because its authority is not accepted.
And those wise ones here who proclaim that the Jinas attain non-abiding nirvana, as well as the finality of those two vehicles;
For you, even when relying on a tenet accepted by the opponent, the example would be unestablished with respect to those [reasons] and would nonetheless be endowed with the property to be proven.
Thus Kamalaśīla has explained it in this way (*Tattvasaṃgraha* 538–539): "From what is it established that the death-consciousness of the Arhats does not link to another consciousness?

Or rather, it might be argued: in the Buddhist tenet system belonging to others [the Śrāvakas], it is recited: 'Exhausted is birth for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been done; I know no further existence beyond this.'"
Therefore, it is established that [the argument] is not a proof;
however, this is incorrect, because the opponent's tenet is not accepted as being authoritative.
How, then, could there be certainty based on what is accepted as lacking authority?
Because it would follow that there is also certainty regarding the next world.

Furthermore, showing that even by relying on the tenets of others, for certain Buddhists the example is not established as being endowed with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), he says: "And those wise ones here... (*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā* 538–539).
He says "let it be satisfied" according to this principle: because of the requirement for a qualification, namely, "when there is a cause, such as affliction.
The meaning is that the state of having a mind defiled by the impurities of passion and so forth serves as the cause.
The intention is that the dying mind of an Arhat is not of such a nature, and thus there is no inconclusiveness [of the reason].
And so it has been stated by Śāntarakṣita:
"The consciousness at the moment of death is capable of giving rise to its own effect,
because in one possessed of passion it is associated with attachment, just like a preceding consciousness."

This has been explained [in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, verse 535] as follows: "Whatever mind is possessed of passion is capable of giving rise to another subsequent mind that it itself has appropriated, because it is possessed of passion, just like a preceding mind; and this dying mind is indeed possessed of passion."

Having established that the mind existing at the time of death is preceded by the arising of another mind, [the author], establishing that the mind existing at the time of birth is itself preceded by a mind that serves as its cause for arising, says "here" (*iha*), etc.

By thus supporting the two states of existence—the prior and the subsequent—the continuity of multiple births is made firm. The reason for proving the future existence is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason).
He states that this "cause as effect" (*kāryahetu*) is the proof for the existence of past and future lives: "the cause as effect.

Now, an objection may be raised: since a stream of consciousness flows for every sentient being, and that stream persists through multiple births, how can descriptions of distinctions—such as there being many omniscient Buddhas—be logically consistent?

However, with the intention that emptiness alone is the accepted reality and that the very view of emptiness is liberation—this being the ultimate position—he raises an objection with the words "But surely... (*nanu ca*).
By means of this objection and its refutation, he introduces the distinctions between the systems of the Vaibhāṣikas and others.
"Beings"— that is, worlds. Since all beings,
whose minds are defiled by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of various stable entities due to the power of ignorance, cannot be suddenly established on the path to the highest good,
the Blessed One, whose heart was moistened with compassion, spoke this according to the nature of reality while establishing them on the non-dual path to liberation.

This is the underlying intention: since it is impossible to immediately introduce into the view of emptiness those people who, enveloped by ignorance, run after this and that object as soon as it is seen— without investigating its true nature, thinking "this is it, that is it"— and thereby fall into calamity,
the Blessed One first set forth the teaching on momentariness, [stating] that whatever is perceived here, such as the aggregates and sense-bases, is all momentary and not stable or unitary.

Consequently, in order to lead those who are defiled by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) regarding the distinction between knowledge and the object of knowledge away from that [dualistic state], there is the teaching of "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).

Then, having led them away from the view of the non-duality of consciousness toward the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which is exclusively conducive to the supreme good (*naiḥśreyasa*), there is the teaching of the emptiness of all things, stating "all is empty.

Thus, based on the distinction between the conventional and the ultimate, the various modes of teaching have proceeded as follows: "momentary, momentary," "consciousness, consciousness," and "empty, empty."
And so it has been said: "The Lord taught these entities for the sake of leading people into the world.

Having relied upon these various instructions undertaken for the purpose of leading those to be trained (vineya), a divergence of views arose among the followers of the Sugata; and that [divergence] is distinguished by the divisions of the Vaibhāṣikas and others.
To examine those divisions, he says, beginning with "For instance" (*tathā hi*).
Space and the two types of cessation.
There are two kinds of entities: the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Among these, the unconditioned consists of space and the two cessations—cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*).
The meaning is that everything conditioned is momentary.
Now, he states the view of the Sautrāntikas— namely, "the view of the Sautrāntikas"— by saying,
"there is no external object."
An external object such as blue does not appear [directly];
however, an external object exists,
and it is not within the range of visual perception.
The point is this: that which appears as "blue" is indeed cognition itself, having transferred the external form [onto itself].
These [opponents] are proponents of external objects that are to be inferred from cognition.
"Producing a cognition with their own form" means:
"visible"—that is, those things considered to be visible, namely external objects—such as blue and so forth;
these external objects, having imparted their own form to the cognition, themselves vanish.
But it is consciousness alone that shines forth, because what is insentient cannot be manifest;
this is the meaning of the phrase "if it is experienced."

If blue and so forth are perceived—that is, if they manifest within consciousness—then, by virtue of having the nature of manifestation, they too must be internal just like consciousness; how then can they be called external?
The meaning is this: that which manifests as "blue" must be stated to be "consciousness."
What is the connection between that which has fallen within the range of the eye and the mind,
such that when an object merely enters the path of vision, there arises the appearance "this is blue"?
That appearance is the manifestation of the mind itself.
Therefore, it is understood that the appearance of the form of blue belongs to the mind alone.
And if it were not perceived— that is, when it is not perceived and is not made an object by [the cognition] arising in proximity to the path of the eyes— then [it would not appear].
Now, how can there be externality for that [object], such that it becomes the object of a perception produced by an external sense-organ?
And thus, the non-perceptibility of external things is established.

If an external object is not apprehended by the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) consisting of perception, then, due to the absence of any means of knowledge regarding it, one must accept that reality consists of consciousness alone.
With this intention, he raises an objection: "Now, if...
He refutes it: "...because of the distinction," that is, because the object, such as blue and so forth, is distinct from the cognition.
He states the reason for this distinction with the words beginning "for not," etc.
"And not this" means:

even though each subsequent consciousness follows immediately upon each preceding consciousness, the appearance of blue occurs only in a certain place and at a certain time, and not at other times or in other places.
It is not tenable that [the mind] exists solely by the power of its own preceding material causes;
"distinct from the immediately preceding condition" means distinct from the immediately preceding causal condition.

Having thus examined the position of the existence of external objects as maintained by the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas, he now examines the Yogācāra view—the position of the existence of consciousness alone—and refutes the doctrine of external existence by means of an analysis: "But what is this external object? Is it a whole (*avayavin*)," and so forth.

The meaning of the alternative options is as follows: are they qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, which are considered to reside in another substance; or is it the ninefold substance; or are they atoms (*paramāṇu*)?

Although the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas do not accept the distinction of the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth, nevertheless, since even they must negate external objects in their doctrine of the existence of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), these categories are also included here.
The arrangement of atoms at the end—following the refutation of the whole (avayavin) and accepting only atoms—is intended to highlight the distinction between the Vaibhāṣika and Sautrāntika schools.
Although the whole was mentioned first, it is therefore refuted last; for it is appropriate to enter into the doctrine of atoms immediately after its refutation.

In that regard, it is not first of all "qualities and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), actions and the like are included, because they have already been refuted by the refutation of substance. How is their refutation achieved simply by the refutation of substance? He says: "And when the substance, which is the inherent substratum (samavāyin), does not exist..."
Therefore, he says—"even a refutation is not respected"—meaning that although other refutations exist, they are not taken into account here by us.
The meaning is that even if a separate refutation exists, it is not respected.
To the question "How is substance negated?", he replies with the words beginning with "And substance... and so forth.
In this regard, since this too is a proof for the negation of the self (*ātman*), the refutation of the self has already been performed; this is understood from the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase,
"that cognition which is occasional."
And this is the statement of the example (udāharaṇa) which demonstrates pervasion (vyāpti):
"having the nature of occasional cognition" is the reason (hetu), and "being preceded by an occasional cause" is the probandum (sādhya).
The example for the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is "like the cognition of lightning.
The statement of application (*upanaya*), "And this cognition of the 'I' is occasional," establishes the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

The sense is that by establishing the occasional nature of the referent of the 'I' (*ahamartha*), which is the cause of the grasping of the 'I', the claim that "the self is eternal" is thereby refuted.
He establishes that the reason is free from the three defects, such as being unestablished (*asiddhi*), by means of the passage beginning with "This is not unestablished" (*nāyamasiddha*).
Regarding the phrase "in the substrate *ahaṅkāra*":
*ahaṅkāre* refers to the substrate—the grasping of "I"—which is the subject (*pakṣa*) of the argument.

Having set aside the non-establishment of the qualified portion (*viśeṣyāṃśa*) of the reason, he precludes the non-establishment of the qualifying portion (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*) by stating: "nor is it occasional" (*kādācitka*). In the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), namely the cognition of lightning, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*).
It is directly perceived that as the flash of lightning (*saudāminī*) appears for a moment and then vanishes, so too does the cognition of it;
furthermore, there is non-perception of that cognition both before and after the lightning.
Thus, it follows that a cognition which occurs only occasionally must arise from an occasional cause, and so forth.
If it is argued that even for an occasional cognition, a non-occasional object might be the cause,
then in that case, such a cognition would never arise from an occasional object.
This is because it is admitted that the cause is not occasional (*akādācitka*).

If it is argued, "But [the effect] could arise even from what is non-occasional, as well as from what is occasional," then the implication is that this would result in the contingency of having no fixed cause, which would lead to the conclusion that there is no cause at all.
Furthermore, even so, there remains the fault of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).

The intention is that even when there is a restriction on the concomitance (*sāhacarya-niyama*) between the probandum and the reason through perception and non-perception regarding *saudāminī* (lightning) and the cognition thereof, there is nonetheless inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) in other cases.
The phrase "even well-known smoke and so forth" means that even though there is a restriction on the concomitance of fire and smoke in places such as a kitchen, [the same problem persists].
The sense is that even in that case, the suspicion of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) would follow, as one might ask: "Why should smoke not exist elsewhere even without fire?
Furthermore, etc.:
"Incapable of being a cause" means "inefficacious."

It is not tenable to claim that the ego-grasping (*ahaṃgraha*) is merely occasional; for since the cause is eternal and possesses the capacity to produce the effect, the ego-grasping would arise at all times.
This is because the cause, by virtue of its power to bring about the effect, must be in the very act of assuming the form of the effect.
The sense is that one might think, "It has performed its function" or "it will perform it," or perhaps "it does not at all.
However, for that which remains inactive even while performing its function, its status as a cause would result in being merely figurative;
or else, even while performing [the function], it would be [regarded as] only a single [cause].

The claim that "it would exist even while not acting" is contradictory, because there is a rule of distinction between those two; however, if there were non-difference, then by virtue of the identity of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the production of the effect would necessarily occur whether it is acting or not acting—this is the sense.
Furthermore, as for the phrase "of the ego-sense" (*ahaṅkārasya*).

If the self, which is itself non-occasional, were to produce occasional acts of ego-grasping (*ahaṃgraha*), then all the acts of ego-grasping produced by that single [self] in succession would have to arise simultaneously, because the instrument [of the self] remains ever-active and there is no deficiency in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). How could there be a deficiency in the causal complex when its capacity is present?
The sense is that if it were dependent on other causes, it would possess no efficacy at all.

Anticipating and refuting the objection that "the self is merely the objective support (*ālambana*) of the ego-grasping (*ahaṃgraha*), while the cause is something else entirely," he says: "Now, as for the ego... and so forth.
The point is that the state of being an object of cognition (*ālambanatā*) does not exceed the state of being a cause (*kāraṇatā*).
Thus, the self (*ātman*) as conceived by others has been refuted. Now, he refutes space (*ākāśa*) with the words beginning "Now, what is space? and so forth.
This is the intention: the Vaibhāṣikas, who are partial followers of the Sugata, maintain that space is a real entity (*vastu*).

While we ourselves, investigating whether it is a real entity or a non-entity, declare it to be indeed a non-entity—for a real entity must be capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), otherwise it is simply a non-entity.
Nor does space perform any purposeful action (arthakriyā).
If it is argued that it possesses the capacity for purposeful action characterized by providing room (avakāśa), we say no;
for where there exists a resistant object such as a jar or a cloth, [space is not perceived].
In that regard, even though space exists, it is not capable of providing room;
rather, when those resistant things are absent, room is established simply by their non-existence. What, then, is the use of space?
Since there is no room whatsoever that is distinct from the mere absence of resistant objects.
Therefore, it is untenable that space is a single, eternal entity.

For if one admits its expansion and contraction like a jar or similar objects, it would follow that it is finite (pariccheda). Furthermore, if one admits its destruction and origination based on the proximity or distance of obstructive objects, its eternity and unity would be contradicted.
Now, he refutes the method of establishing space (*ākāśa*) as favored by the Vaiśeṣikas, beginning with the words "But by others," etc.
Regarding the phrase "because all sounds are in the same state":

for those who maintain that space is eternal, unitary, and all-pervading, and who accept that sound has it as its substratum, every sound that arises has space alone as its location; thus, [they claim] "this is the location of this sound."
However, since it is impossible to specify that "this is its location," the perception of sound through spatial division would not be tenable;

for that which is called the "space of the ear" is not distinct from space itself, and thus it is untenable to postulate a distinction of parts within the supporting space such that one could say, "this sound is not near the space of the ear, but this one is near. Consequently, all sounds whatsoever would be heard.
If that which is separated were not heard,
then that other [word] which is said to be proximate would also not be heard, because the distinction of location is impossible to specify.
The point is that if they were heard, all of them would be heard; if not, not even one would be heard.
This refutation also implies the impossibility of the sequential production of sound.
And as Kamalaśīla has stated: "For if these [sounds] were inherent in the eternal, unitary substance of space..."
In that case, just like multiple sounds produced simultaneously, even those sounds belonging to other times would occur only at the intended time,
because their causes are unimpaired and they share a single substratum.
"And there is no dependence on another for that which is eternal" (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 208),
because space and time are unitary.
The meaning is: because of the admission of the unity of space and the admission of the unity of time.
This is an indicator for the admission of [space and time's] eternity and omnipresence.
By this [phrase "by this"]:
The meaning is: "precisely by means of the refutation of space, time, and direction";
that is to say, because the reasoning for the refutation is of a single nature.
He then restates and refutes the argument put forward by others to establish the existence of the mind, beginning with the words "due to the non-arising of cognitions simultaneously," and so forth.
This is the intended meaning: if the mind were not admitted, there would result the simultaneous occurrence of cognitions such as visual perception and the like.

This is because the all-pervading self is always in contact with the sense organs, such as the eyes, and thus the contact of the eyes, the sense of touch, and other organs with a flower or similar object placed in the palm of the hand could occur simultaneously.

However, when the mind is accepted as a sense organ, its atomic nature makes it impossible for it to be in simultaneous contact with multiple organs; and since the contact between the sense organ and the mind is also a cause of perception, there is no consequence of the simultaneous arising of cognitions.
Thus the Vaiśeṣikas maintain.
To this it is said here: that there is no simultaneity of cognitions is contrary to common worldly experience.
For those watching a dancer directly perceive both her form and her song simultaneously, and thereby experience a certain delight.
If the mind were accepted as some kind of subtle sense organ (*indriya*),
there would be a contradiction with the simultaneity of cognitions established by worldly experience; therefore, that mind postulated by the opponent does not exist at all,
and thus the mind is not something other than cognition.
It has been stated more than once that "mind," "aggregate," and "knowledge" are not different in meaning;
furthermore,
this person is hostile toward the fact that the simultaneity of cognitions is established by worldly experience.
Constantly conceptualizing with the mind, one does not perceive the loss of what is desired.
If the cause is eternal, how could there be succession in the effect?
For that which is capable does not depend on anything else, nor can that which is incapable be a cause.
Thus, the desired non-simultaneity of cognitions would never be established.
And it has been said by Śāntarakṣita:
"If the mind were eternal, cognitions would occur simultaneously;
therefore, the reason stated here becomes one that destroys your own desired conclusion."
Thus (Tattvasaṃgraha 209), earth and the other elements remain;
that is to say, they are to be refuted.
They are of two kinds, by way of the distinction between composite wholes and atoms:
the composite wholes are dyads and so forth, and the atoms are those that originate them.
"Non-perception is the subverting proof.
The non-perception of a whole (*avayavin*), such as a cloth, which is distinct from its parts, serves as the subverting means of knowledge (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the acceptance of such a thing.
If it existed, it would be perceived; however, no such thing called "cloth" is perceived that is other than the threads.
Likewise, a jar is distinct from its shards; the implication is that the same applies to threads, shards, and so forth.
Herein is the formal argument (*prayoga*): that which meets the conditions for perception but is not perceived in a certain place does not exist there.

Just as a jar, not being perceived in a particular location, is not perceived even there in that very place as something distinct from its parts— provided that the whole (avayavin) is intended to meet the conditions for perception.
One might object: "But this jar is perceived as one. [The author] raises this doubt with the words, "If the composite whole (avayavī) does not exist.

By the phrase "as oneness" (ekatvena), it is meant that oneness, when appearing, leads to the inference of a composite whole that is indeed distinct [from its parts]; otherwise, if only atoms were being perceived, that oneness would not be connected to them.
He dispels the doubt by introducing the statement of an authoritative source: "For they are indeed parts," etc.
Furthermore, there is this common usage of those who maintain the existence of a distinct whole (*avayavin*): "This is a cloth, a whole;
these threads are its parts."
And because this [object] possesses parts (*bhāga*), it is designated as "parts" in accordance with that;
for it is precisely the parts that appear in visual perception.
But no other entity consisting of parts—that is, something composed of parts—nor anything partless—that is, something indivisible—is perceived; this is the meaning.
He explains this very point, namely that "only the parts appear," by means of a question and answer beginning with "Now, what is this... and so forth.
"Appearing as accumulated atoms" means appearing as atoms gathered into a mass.

Many atoms, by occupying various directions and locations— remaining in a single place while occupying various directions and locations characterized as east, west, south, north, above, and below— are what constitutes a "mass."
He raises an objection with the words, "If this is so.
This doubt arises from one who does not understand the inner meaning of the statement.
He demonstrates that very ignorance with the passage beginning, "There is no cognition of the object in its own form," and so forth.
There is no cognition of an object—such as a gross form—in its own nature, that is, as the essence of the object;
rather, it is consciousness itself that appears in the form of the object.
Regarding this, he states the following: "The cognition of the object would be figurative."
The intention is that the statement "the cognition of an object" would be merely figurative.
He states the alternative explanation for the appearance of gross objects with the words "Therefore," etc.; what is meant is that the manifestation of grossness is an illusion.
In this very way, however, the venerable Śubhagupta maintains [this view],
and it is cited by Śāntarakṣita:
"Just as there is the delusion of permanence due to the arising of similar subsequent moments..."
"If there is the delusion of grossness when there is the apprehension of uninterrupted members of the same class" (Tattvasaṅgraha 552).
Now, [one might ask]: if the composite whole (*avayavin*) is not admitted, how can visual perception such as "this is gross" or "this is blue" be accounted for?
Regarding this, he says: "Even those atoms which are the initiators of that [composite], according to the Vaiśeṣikas.
This means they are intended by the Vaiśeṣikas as being the initiators of that [composite].
"Directly within the range of the eyes" refers to the system of the Vaibhāṣikas.

For those engaged in the refutation of external objects alone, the demonstration of the perceptibility of atoms is not strictly required. The intention is that this is stated according to the view of our own school (sayūthyas) when addressing one who is engaged in establishing the existence of the whole (avayavin). He states the distinction of the Sautrāntikas from the Vaibhāṣikas with the words "by imparting their own form" (*svākārasamarpaṇa*).
Now, rejecting external objects, he says: "Even those do not exist according to the view of the Yogācāras.
"Indeed, it is not one," etc.
The intention here is as follows: the innumerable atoms, each distinct from the others, [exist] in the form of an aggregate.
They are seen to exist [only] in combination;
never at any time do they exist independently, for each one,
but rather they arise only in combination and perish only in combination.
Therefore, there is no room for the objection: "If each [atom] seen in the state of an aggregate were to exist in its individual state, why would it not be perceived?
For it has been said:
"The possibility of individual atoms existing in isolation does not exist."
For this reason as well, atoms do not appear individually.
Thus (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 551), so say the proponents of external existence (*bāhyāstitvavādinaḥ*).
Here, this is considered: let [entities] arise only as aggregates, and let them perish only as aggregates.
In this regard, it must indeed be stated thus:
"This is one atom, this is one, and this is one; and these, taken together, are [the aggregate].
To this we ask: how can it be established that "this is one atom"?
Even that [atom], when subjected to analysis, cannot be a single entity. Why?

It is said: for that atom which occupies the center of another atom is joined with atoms on its four sides as well as above and below; thus, due to the division of spatial parts (*digbhāgabheda*), it necessarily falls into a state of having six parts, and its lack of unity cannot be avoided.
For that central atom, by whatever nature it is joined to a lateral atom,
it does not by that same nature join with an atom above or below;
and by whatever nature it is conjoined with the atoms above and below, it does not by that same nature join with a lateral atom.
If [atoms] were to combine without a difference in their intrinsic nature (svabhāva), then,
because the distinction created by spatial direction would be impossible to establish, they would result in occupying a single location;
consequently, the aggregate would be nothing more than the central atom itself.
If it is claimed that there is merely a facing toward one another—due to the difficulty of establishing mutual conjunction among atoms—even then, one cannot escape this very same fault.
Refuting it by another method, he says: "Now, as for this investigation..."

Nor is it a plurality of atoms. This is the intended meaning: [the opponent might object] "But surely this atom does not have a single nature; therefore, we say it is 'not one,' but we do not say it is 'not an atom' or that it is 'a plurality. To this, he replies: "No."
Why? Because a conjunction of that which is considered to be an atom with other atoms—atom by atom—that is, in an extremely minute manner—is impossible.
How could there be a conjunction of that which is considered an atom in a manner even more minute than that?
Furthermore, conjunction occurs only through the parts of the things being conjoined.

Therefore, if this [atom] possesses parts, how can it be called an "atom" (*paramāṇu*)? On the other hand, if it were partless and yet joined together, then because of its connection on all sides, the atoms would occupy the same location as one another; consequently, a mass would be no more than a single atom, and a mountain would be no more than the size of the earth.
"Of those two" means: of the lump and the atoms.
"Of the intrinsic natures" means: of the intrinsic natures of the atoms.
He corroborates his own refutation with the words of an authoritative source: "Because of simultaneous conjunction with six [atoms].
This has already been largely explained.
And Śāntarakṣita said this:
The form that is conjoined [with the eye], situated at a distance, arranged contiguously,
and facing a single atom, belongs to the eye located in the middle [of the visual field].
If that very same [atom] is postulated as being oriented toward another atom;
If this were the case, the accumulation of mountains and other such things would not be possible.
If it is maintained that the form facing another atom is distinct [from the rest], then how could those atoms not become a single atom? Such being the case, they would be one.

Thus (Tattvasaṃgraha 555): But how can there be the appearance of blue, yellow, and so forth, if the objective support (*ālambana*) is non-existent? How can there be the appearance of dreams if the object is non-existent?
Is it not by means of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)?
By those very same impressions, it is so here as well.
Is it not the case that objects are difficult to establish in a dream?
In this case as well, it is the same:
for those who do not investigate, the object is easily obtained; but for those who do investigate, there is only difficulty.
With the intention of demonstrating that insuperability (*daurghaṭya*) has also been established, he says: "If an external object... and so forth.
Now, alas! Does this not entail the consequence that there is no distinction between the dream state and the waking state?
Who can declare what the difference is?
Granted that there may indeed be a distinction regarding defects, waking cognition is nonetheless not different from dream cognition.

With the intention of providing a formal argument on this point, he says: "And [there is no difference] between dream-experience and waking-experience," and so forth, up to "because of the lack of a supporting object, it does not attain a specific form."
The meaning is that, due to the absence of an objective referent (*anālambanatayā*), no specific form is attained. This is like the perception of hair in the sky from a single [defective] eye;
by virtue of a visual defect, one sees something like hair whirling in the atmosphere.
This is like the perception of hair in the sky;
for the sky is not a real entity, nor is there any hair therein.
Therefore, this appearance is merely a manifestation of consciousness, independent of any external object;
and this particular distinction cannot be set aside by others as being due to some other kind of error.
For this very reason, this example has been adopted.
"Second" means that which is other than the perception of hair in the sky.
Now, [one might ask]: if there is no external object, what then exists for you?
However, consciousness alone is ultimately real;
thus he says with the words beginning "If," etc.
Here he cites the consensus of the ancients with the words beginning "As it has been said," etc.

"Free from the grasped and the grasper"— that is, free from the state of being the object of cognition and the subject of cognition. Now, if the state of being the grasped and the grasper does not exist,
by what would cognition be manifested?
It shines by itself;
therefore, it has no state of being an object of apprehension either, as he says: "There is nothing else to be experienced by the intellect," and so forth.
Here is the summary of this point, which has been determined by us elsewhere:
This stream of consciousness, like light in the expanse of the sky, is self-luminous; it flashes forth in various forms and in manifold ways due to latent impressions (*vāsanā*), as in a dream.
Being devoid of the duality of the grasped and the grasper, it is non-dual, consisting of mere cognition (*vijñaptimātra*).
This very same one alone brings forth the entire worldly transaction, independent of anything internal or external to itself.

In this world, it is conventionally regarded as having the nature of a grasper because it grasps knowledge and objects; however, it functions merely through conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*) and not as a real subject, for it is in fact empty of that.
Nor does it grasp a self, since it is by its supreme non-inertness of the nature of self-luminosity alone.
"And that flows continuously in an uninterrupted stream, eternally infinite through the diversity of sentient beings.

Among those who maintain that there is only consciousness, some hold that consciousness itself appears in various forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth, due to the variety of latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
others, however, maintain that it is in fact devoid of form.

Through ignorance (*avidyā*), [consciousness] appears as if possessing various forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth; yet even though it manifests by the power of those latencies (*vāsanā*), these forms—blue, yellow, and the rest—are merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*). In both of these positions, it is indeed agreed that consciousness is devoid of the relationship between apprehended object and apprehending subject. Thus, by examining the intrinsic nature of consciousness, the notion that consciousness possesses the capacity to grasp external objects is utterly discarded. He says: "In that regard..."
By the words "some," etc., he introduces the view of the Mādhyamikas, stating: "But for the Mādhyamikas," etc.
Upon investigation, no intrinsic nature whatsoever—whether singular or plural—is tenable for this [world].

Regarding the atom (*paramāṇu*) which is accepted by others as being external to the proponents of consciousness-only (*vijñānavādin*): is it of a single nature—or is it not of a single nature (is it of one form or of many forms)?
It has been stated that there is an untenability in both cases; the intention is that this very untenability is exactly the same even in the doctrine of consciousness-only. This he will demonstrate.
First, he corroborates the unreality of consciousness (*vijñāna*) by citing the words of authoritative persons (*āptavacana*), beginning with "As it has been said," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by way of a single or multiple nature":
for an entity must necessarily possess either a single nature or a multiple nature.
The sense is that for that which does not exist in such a manner, there is only non-existence, like a lotus in the sky.
"Bhāvas" refers to those things by which entities are defined—namely, external and internal objects.
As for the phrase "when, however": it refers to conceptualization—that is, to the determinate cognition consisting of conceptual construction (*savikalpa-niścaya*).

As for "anyasya"—when even direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is devoid of conceptual constructions such as name, genus, and so forth, lacks the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*); for its validity depends upon the existence of a real entity (*vastutva*), and since it lacks the nature of being either one or many, it is a non-entity (*avastutva*). Thus, where is there any occasion for its validity?
Now, when even the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself dissolves upon investigation, where can there be reality for anything else whose very existence depends upon it?
Thus, when everything dissolves, who is at fault?
Since the emptiness of all entities is their very nature, they are equal; therefore, there is no occasion for the dependence of one upon another.
[Objection: But would not even the established distinction that "this one is bound" and "this one is liberated" be contradicted?
[Reply: True;
this distinction also exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛttyā*), and not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).
And emptiness is precisely the absence of intrinsic nature.
This has also been stated elsewhere:
"These entities, as propounded by ourselves and others, are devoid of intrinsic nature from the perspective of ultimate reality."
Because it is devoid of a nature that is either one or many, like a reflection.
Thus [it is asked]: what then is reality?
"Neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither; the Madhyamikas have declared that reality is free from the four extremes."

He demonstrates the formal argument (*prayoga*) regarding the non-ultimate reality of entities due to their lack of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): "The formal argument, moreover, is as follows" means that it does not possess the nature of being either one or many;
that is to say, it is neither of a single nature nor of a manifold nature.
This is known as the "non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
Being either of a single nature or of a manifold nature is a pervader of ultimate existence;
its non-perception [is established],
and through the non-perception of the pervader, the cessation of the pervaded— ultimate existence— is proven.

Establishing the presence of the reason (*hetu*) within the subject (*pakṣa*), he wards off the suspicion of its being unestablished (*asiddha*) by stating: "The reason is not, first of all, unestablished.
This is because, in the case of cognition possessing an image (*sākāra-vijñāna*), the incompatibility of an external object with having either a unitary or a manifold nature is perfectly clear.

Regarding the external object that is desired as a collection of atoms (*aṇu-samudāya*) such as blue, yellow, and so forth, the fault has been pointed out that this atom cannot be of a unitary nature, nor can it be of a non-unitary nature; thus, it is untenable in either way.

The meaning is that this is quite clear: even for the Vijñānavādin who asserts that it is consciousness alone which appears as the forms of blue, yellow, and so forth, the [objection] is exactly the same.
He demonstrates this very clarity with the words beginning "For where... and so on.

The proponent of the existence of all things (Sarvāstivādin) maintains that the external object consists of an aggregate of atoms—blue, yellow, and so forth—which is designated in the world by the term "this" as "this is blue" or "this is yellow.

However, the Proponent of Consciousness (Vijñānavādin), asserting that consciousness itself appears in various forms as if it were external, accepts blue, yellow, and the like as being the forms of consciousness. Thus, while blue, yellow, and so forth are not rejected in every respect, the dispute concerns only their ultimate internality versus externality.
The point is this: the objection raised against [the objects'] being external applies equally to their being internal;
for the refutation is not based on their being outside [of consciousness].
Indeed, the objection was not put forward as a defect on the grounds that blue, yellow, and so forth exist outside of cognition.
However, this applies merely to the admission of blue, yellow, and so forth.
Thus, whether it be external or internal, the fault remains exactly the same; such is the intended meaning.
Now, one might object: "By one who accepts external blue, yellow, and so forth, it is admitted that they are corporeal (*mūrta*);

however, for those who say that these are mere consciousness (*vijñānamātra*), they become incorporeal (*amūrta*). Thus, this doubt would not apply to the incorporeal. Anticipating and dispelling this objection, he says: "The cause of corporeality," and so forth.
This is because if there were a formal aspect (*sākāratā*), even cognition itself would be corporeal.
To the question, "If there is a form (*sākāratva*), how can there be corporeality (*mūrtatā*)?", he says: "For this very form of cognitions is their corporeality.
The meaning is that this very form which is desired [as the object] constitutes the corporeality of the cognition.

However, in the doctrine that maintains the ultimate reality of mere formless consciousness (*nirākārajñānamātra-pāramārthya-vāda*), a fault common to all entities has been described at length in another place by way of a different approach.
"Neither from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause,
do any entities ever exist anywhere as having arisen.
— *Mādhyamakakārikā* 4.1.

By such means as these— the details of which should be understood from that [source]— and by repeatedly contemplating [the subject] with an eye attentive to the treatises of Dignāga and others, I, though possessed of limited intellect, have composed this commentary on the *Tarkabhāṣā*.
Let the wise either censure or applaud this work;
for who indeed could be free from seeing faults, or what work could be entirely devoid of them?
This man, residing among the Gurjaras and honored by many rulers, [has composed it].
Like an actor, he assumed various forms for the sake of others;
even while dwelling in a realm perfumed by the joyous fragrance of the lotus-feet of Padmanābha, he performed the deeds of a Tathāgata.
As I traverse many times through the wilderness of numerous tantras,
may the unimpeded path of Viṣṇu depart from my heart.
Thus ends the commentary on the Tarkabhāṣā.
